1t was another hot day to-day, the mer-

ant, however, comfortable breeze having

Charles Gray and Miss Maggie Cossman,

SAN Francisco, Sept. 7.-Early this
morning there was a fight in China
town, and two Chinese were shot. The
Ping King Tong company were holding
an outdoor religious service on Waverly
place, when members of the Chez Kong
Tong company interfered. Instantly
knives, revolvers and clubs were drawn,
and two shots were fired. Chin Moy,
of the Ping King Kong So
ciety was wounded in the left
thigh. Chinese focked to the scene
from every quarter, and two China
town watchmen who drew revolvers were
swept away by the mob. Ping Ting
Kong men then rushed to Shafferd alley
where the Chez Kong Tong society was
holding an outdoor festival, intending to
retaliate by smashing their idols.
Another melee ensued and Ping King
Tong man was wounded. By this
time five regular policemen had reached
Shafferd alley, and with drawn revolvers
kept the Chinese at bay Back of the
police stood the fighting men OF the
Chez Kong Tong company, ready to
meet the expected attack. The Chinese
refused to disperse, and menaced the
police until reinforcements arrived from
the central station. 1t is expected that
there will be further trouble, as the two
societies which are at war swear they
will have revenge.

MONTREAL, August, 11.-Twenty-five
hundred Grand Army men, with their
wives and children, left Chicago for
Boston, via Niagara Falls, the St. Law
renee river, and Montreal, Friday. Yester-
day morning five big steamer loads left
Kingston to go through the rapids ofthe
st. Lawrence. The Bohemian the largest
of the boats had between 600 and 700
passengers aboard. About O'Clock in
the evening great thunder clouds began
to gather in the west. A big storm
was predicted. There was yet one series
of rapids to go through, the Cretan, as
dangerous as any on the river, when
there was brilliant flash of lightning
and rain began to fall in sheets. Sud-
denly sound OF cracking timbers was
heard, and women shrieked and tainted.
The upper deck beams of the Bohemian
had cracked, and the floor, in sinking,
had jammed the tiller chains, and the

Richard, surnamed Strongbow, also Joined
him with the understanding that he should
marry Dermid's daughter and succeed to
the sovereignty of Leinster.


One morning in May some fishermen in
the bay of Bannon saw a strange fleet of
swift ships blowing the blue waters and
headed for O creek near by. On nearer APP
proach they were seen to be fllled with a
host of men clad in such armor as had
never before been seen on human form,
and word was sent inland that
Dermid had returned. King Rod
part of the island enforcing their claims,
founding lectorships at Armagh, partition
ing Meath, and occupying themselves with
such matters as kings in those unruly days
found to do, and day after day ships of
strange build came stealing INTO little Irish
coves and bays with troops of Dermid's
Norman hirelings. The darkest days Of
sorrow the land had ever known was COM
ing. Yet the gallant o'Conor paid no
heed, but looked calmly forward to long
succession of prosperous days.


One morning as the sky in the East grew
from grey to scarlet and gold the watch
men from the walls of Wexford looked out
over the valley and saw the whole country
glistened with shields and helmets. with
the Melted steel hauberks of knight and
squire and the spiked breastplates of war
horses. Carelessly Jung over the armor
of the encircling hosts were capes of silk
and satin, cloth of silver and gold emblaz-
oned with the arms of the wearer, and over
all bristled the points ofswords and lances.
Here and there were strange looking
machines-scorpions or huge cross-bows;
the balista which seemed to shower stones
to almost any distance; the catapult with
its deadly night of darts and arrows, the
war wolf" the battaring RAM besides
movable towers of all shapes and sizes.


All this nlled the Irish with wonder and
dismay. The battles they understood were
fought hand to hand with spear, lance and
battle-ax. This long-distance combat,
where men fought behind impregnable de-
lenses, and individual bravery and muscle
counted for little beside discipline and
strategy, was new thing, and the town of
Wexford, though bravely defended, soon
fell. The foot of the Norman was planted
to remain forever in a land which the wild
sea kings never could touch.


The news of the disaster soon reached
King Roderick, and in few days there
was grand muster of the Irish at the hill
of Tara, whence they marched to Dublin,
and there awaited the onslaught of the
Normans.


Dublin did not fall then, but a treaty
was made between Roderick and Dermid
which confessed to- the weakness of the
Irish, and paved the way for future VIC
tories for the Leinster king. Dermid
bound himself by secret agreement to
admit no more of the Normans. and the
upright OConor believed him.


Within two months after the signing of
this solemn agreement Dermid was well
coming to Ireland and to Wexford another
son of the fair Nesta, Maurice Fitzgerald.
Meantime he continued to write urging
Earl Richard to hasten to Ireland, accord
ing to the terms agreed upon at Bristol.


Richard was polite, and though anxious
to pluck the Irish plum was not willing to
displease his sovereign, Henry III. AS a
compromise he sent over force under his
Uncle Herve, which landed at Waterford
harbor. Here they were attacked by 5000
Irish, who, while chanting the songs of
their ancestors, rushed blindly on to the
battle. A sudden and deadly discharge
from the Welsh and Flemish cross-bows,
for which they were totally unprepared,
sent them scuttling back faster than they
had come, while $50, who had been made
prisoners, had their legs violently broken
and were then hurled into the sea.


This was Ireland's hrst taste of the re-
venge of the banished Dermid.


Trouble came thick and fast after that.
In the following winter Earl Richard left
his Pembroke castle, and marching
through North Wales, picked up the Hover
of the lighting men along his route. On
the eve of St. Bartholomew's day, with 200
armored knights and 1 oo0 infantry, he
landed safely. under the earthworks of
Dundonolf. and the doom of the ireland of
Brian and O'Conor was sounded.


The fair city of Waterford, though
bravely defended, soon fell, and the be-
siegers waded TO the walls of the city
through Irish blood.


Then, amid the ruins of the fallen CITY
and the scowling faces and muttered male
dictions of the grief-stricken defenders,
the ill-omened nuptials of Eva McMur-
rogh and Earl Richard were gaily cele-
brated and the iniquitous compact of three
years previous carried out.


In the midst of the marriage ceremonies,
word came that Asculph MacTorcall, the
Danish lord of Dublin, had invoked the
aid of Roderick OConor. The king and the
whole force of the invaders, marched on
the ancient capital. Doubly bitter was
Dermid by this time. King Roderick had
beheaded his son, given as a hostage, and
the city of Dublin had killed his father
and inferred his body with the carcass of a
dog. Treacherously, while the archbishop
was negotiating for peace, the Normans
entered the city and ruthlessly put the
citizens to death.


What came afterwards all the world
knows. The Normans grew into the coun-
try and in the wake of Earl Richard came
the feudal systems and the landlords.


In the kalends of the May following the
conquest at Dublin, Dermid died, as the
ancient chroniclers say, sat Fernamore,
without making a will, without penance
without the body of Christ and without
JUNCTION as his evil deeds deserved"

PORTLAND, Ore, April pa shooting
affray occurred this morning at Dandy,
fishing station on the Columbia river,
between union and non-union fisher
men. Jack Hayman was killed, and
James Wilson and man named Olsen,
probably fatally shot. Olsen and Will
son were brought here this afternoon on
the steamer Telephone, and taken to
the hospital. A party of union fisher
men came from Astoria to Dandy last
night, and when the two factions met
this morning, the shooting took place.


Morgan Backus, who arrived this
afternoon in this city, states that Jack
Hayman, Harry Olsen and Charles Will
son, union men from Astoria, were in a
sail boat, and passed number of nom
union men, who were fishing.
They ordered the non-union men
to draw in their nets and quit fishing,
claiming that they had been selling SO
cents lower than the union price, After
some words the union men sailed on and
came near scow anchored near the
shore. Suddenly a number of shots
were fired from the scow, one of them
striking Hayman in the head and killing
him almost instantly. Wilson, who had
rifle, returned the fire. The shooting
was kept up for some time, and Olsen
received shot in the back which will
prove fatal. Wilson was shot three
times in the legs, but will probably re-
cover. No arrests have been made as
it is impossible to find who did the
shooting, but the supposition is that it
was done by the non-union men, as
threats had been made at different times
by the union men against the non-union
fishermen.

match been shot, as the conditions prescribe,
under the Hurlingham instead Of American
rules, Bassford's bird would not have been

CHICAGO, Dec. 29.-One of the most
daring robberies known in Chicago was
perpetrated today by three stock yards
toughs, undoubtedly the same who re-
Gently robbed the cashier Of the Aller-
tons packing house. A few min
utes past noon three men en-
tered the Merchants Exchange bank,
on Commercial avenue, South Chicago.
Cashier Wilder and Bookkeeper Willis
had gone to lunch, and the only person


left in the bank was Frank Lynn, assist
ant cashier. Two of the men went to
the windows in the bank railing,
DO inted revolvers at Lynn and ordered
him to open the door at the rear and let
the third man in. Lynn did this,
after which the robber knocked
him down and kicked him in
the stomach until the young man was
completely helpless. Then he entered
the vault, took from the safe three $500
packages Of bills, some change and box
containing deeds and mortgages. Then
he picked up Lynn, threw him into the
vault and locked the door on him. The
burglars then put their spoils into
sack, and taking buggy drove down
the street. Book-keeper Willis passed
the men at the entrance to the bank land
in getting inside was surprised to
find the vault locked and no one pres
ent. He hurriedly opened the vault,
when young Lynn fell out, bloody, and
groaning that the bank had been
robbed: Willis rushed outside, and met
Police Lieutenant Jenkins and Sergeant
Powers. The patrol wagon was called
out in minute, and started in hot pur-
suit OF the robbers, whom they could see
a mile ahead. The lash was piled mer-
cilessly, and the police were gaining
rapidly, when the horses began to give
out. The lieutenant ordered the officers
use shot guns as soon as they could get
within range, while he jumped out to
order another wagon. At the corner of
South Chicago and Cottage Grove ave-
nues, the robbers deserted the buggy, get
ting into the covered meat wagon of
Charles Mullin, evidently with the idea
that they would thus elude the vigilance
of the police, but their pursuers were
too close, and volley from shotgun
soon caused them to desert the wagon.
When it was caught up with, Mullin
was placed undsr arrest, although pro-
testing he knew nothing about
the matter, waile the officers
continued the chase of the others. One
OF them, John Corbert, soon surren-
dered, and after long hunt the others
were found in barn. They opened fire
on being discovered, ,and Patrick O'Brien,
watchman with the police, was shot
in the thigh. The sight of the shot
guns, was too much for them, however,
and they soon gave up, surrendering all
their spoils. They gave their names as
Frank Bennett and Henry Featherstone.
The latter is known to the police by
several other names.

SAN Francisco, Aug. 25.-Judge Sawyer.
in the United States circuit court, handed
down his decision this morning in the case
of Lee Sing. releasing the Chinaman from
custody and making void the Bingham
ordinance. Lee Sing was arrested for liv-
ing in Chinatown when the ordinance de-
clared that all Chinese must remove from
there. He was released from custody on
writ OF habeas corpus. returnable before
Judge Sawyer. The decision is very full
and quotes from several authorities. The
court holds that the ordinance conflicts
with the constitution of the United States,
and by the treaties with China the Chinese
are entitled to the same privileges as other
foreigners.

FOUNTAIN, Colo, May IA north
bound freight train side-tracked in the
Denver and Rio Grande yards last night
to allow the Trinidad and Durango ex-
press, south-bound, due at 2 81 a. M, to
pass. The freight crew left the switch
open, and the express engine, baggage
car, smoker and one coach were thrown
from fourteen-feet embankment. The
engineer OF the passenger train saw the
open switch, but was unable to stop the
tram, being on down grade. The en-
gine was badly damaged and Fireman
Sipes was killed. Engineer Dan Mack
escaped by a miracle, with only
few bruises. There were very
few passengers in the smoker
and coach, as nearly all were in the two
sleepers which did not leave the track.
Those in the cars that left the track es-
capped without injury, other than a
shaking up. The tender, baggage-car
and smoker were turned over; the day
coach was thrown on the side, and one
sleeper was derailed, but none of the
passengers experienced any bruises.
Fireman Sipes was 81 years old and
married. His body was taken to Pueblo.

SAN Francisco, Dec. 25.-Soon after
the baseball season came to close, the
California players who returned to the
coast from their season with eastern
league clubs, arranged with the local
players to play series of Sunday games
here during the winter. Some of the
members of the league clubs went south
to play ball in Los Angeles and San
Diego; others remained here to play
with the All-Californias, and for the past
three Sundays the games at Paige street
have been we'll attended. However,
news was received at baseball head
quarters here that the league players
who went south were coming money,
and that at San Diego crowds of 5000
and 10000 were turning out to see the
games. The news created sensation,
and the local players hurriedly packed
their grip-sacks today and boarded the
train for Los Angeles. The team is
composed of Coughlin and Knell,
pitchers; Stevens, catcher; Dooley, first
base; Mcdonald, second base; Wilson,
third base Ebright, shortstop; Levy,
left field; Sweeney, center field ODay,
right field. The team will make
an exhibition tour through the south
ern part of the state, and expects to
obtain some of the baseball money float
ing around Los Angeles and San Diego.
1t will play today (Christmas) and Sun
day in San Diego, and New Years day
and the Sunday following in Los An
gees. On its return trip it will prob
ably play at Bakersfield and Fresno.
The departure of these players will
close the game here, and there will be
no more baseball until the opening of
the regular season in March.

The new year is heartily welcome. karefy

New Year wishes for other peoples may not

some that might prove a most questionable

brighter than in the assurance that ballot re-
form will he secured in many of the States, and
some provision made that in National elections

The New Year wishes for the rulers of our
country include the happiness which comes from
the consciousness of duty well done. Nor can

bers of Congress, who were chosen and pub
licly promised to perform certain duties unless
they repair the defects in the tariff which hos
tile interpretations have produced, or which

the new year They dream that the year may
bring them larger industries, and the ripe
fruitage Of the improvement begun last year

find the greater Britain of the West passing
her at last in the production OF iron. They
dream that destruction Of combinations against
the people may come with cheaper sugar and
paints, cheaper meats and other products for
the needs of the millions They dream that
the year may bring steps toward better educa
tion for all, better marriage, divorce, and
land-title laws in the different States, and
toward wiser and more practical temperance
legislation in many. They dream that the new
year may unite all American nations IN har-
mOny OF interest and effort, and perhaps IN
common monetary system based upon universal
circulation and exchange OF certificates repre-

wear may bring 20 the great kindred nations

promoting conviction that, in the not remote
future, SUCCESSORS of Victoria and William Will

ALBANY, Ore, June 12.-News was re-
ceiyed here today Of terrible tragedy
enacted early this morning, seven miles
northeast of Lebanon For about two
years Grant Aarnspaugh has resided
with his family, consisting of his wife
and two children, in a country home
near his parents, having moved there
from California. A sister of Mrs. Aarns-
paugh has been living at the home of
Aarnspaugh for some time. A sus-
picious circumstance led Mrs. Aarns-
paugh to believe that her husband was
too intimate with her sister, About 5
O'Clock this morning, missing her hus-
band from her bed, and hearing noise
in her sisters room, Mrs. Aarnspaugh
fastened to the room and entered She
found her sister sitting in her husbands
lap in chair, both in their night robes


This is not the first time this has
happened" she said, "and | am going
to put a stop to it,


Producing a revolver she aimed it at
her husband and fired, the ball entering
his breast. He fell to the floor, while
her sister fled from the room and out
into the yard. Mrs. Aarnspaugh then
ended the tragedy by shooting herself in
the head. She died in a short time
Mr.. Aarnspaugh lived several hours, and
confessed to the above facts before sew
eral neighbors and men from Lebanon.


Justice Wallace was called, and with
a coroner's jury found verdict sub
stantially as stated above.


Yesterday Mrs. Aarnspaugh wrote to
her mother in California, charging her
sister with working against her and try
ing to break up her home, and there
seems little doubt that Mrs. Aarnspaugh
had grounds for her rash act. The affair
has caused great excitement throughout
the community. The participants in
the tragedy were quiet, unassuming peo-
pie, always remaining at home and asso-
ciating with but few persons.


Later particulars of the shooting show
that Mrs. Aarnspaugh shot her husband
while he was asleep. She had found
her sister and husband in a compromis-
ing position the night before, and had
upbraided her sister about it, when the
guilty couple taunted her with threats
of eloping together. The wife waited
until her husband was asleep this morn
ing and shot him, then killed herself
The baby, lying between them, was un-
injured. Her sister ran into the room
on hearing the shots and found both
diving.

To jest and dance to strains of music sweet.
Through waning hours around the banquet, there
They revel in the gay and festal scene;
Yet on those lovely faces, unaware,


Rests oftentime discontented MEN,
For all this life of ease and pleasures sense
They give no thanks no worthy recompense.

Full many years within this humble nook


An honest yeoman and his wife have been
A still, sweet hamlet, where the even flow

A grassy strip of fruitful garden plot


The narrow limits of their circle bound;
life of toll and labor is their lot,


Yet, year by year, the family gathers round,
And tho one sunny child is missing there
The father calmly bows his head in prayer

WASHINGTON, January 26.-Commis-
sioner Roosevelt makes report of the
investigation of the violation of the civil
service law in the New York custom
house prior to the last Presidential cleo
tions. The report is scathing con-
demnation Of the political contribution
system, which the law has not yet sue
ceeded in eradicating, which is charac.
terized as nothing but blackmail. The
report finds that in the naval office un-
der Burt, the law was observed in letter
and spirit. But the Collectors office,
under Magone, was different. There was
a general, but not always successful,
effort to make the clerks "come down."
bnt no threats were made. In the Sur
veyor's office, under Beattie, contribu-
tions were universal, and especially were
the Republican hold-overs compelled to
pay assessments. This was accomplished
by an ingenious and widespread system
of threats and intimidation, which Roose-
velt details at length. Many petty per-
secutions are instanced. The commits
sion will probably take action.

The town Of Burke, Idaho, in the Ceur

and the terror-stricken inhabitants have fed to

The disaster occurred Tuesday afternoon.
With scarcely q moments warning a tremen-
dous mass Of snow and rocks swept down upon
the town from the west side of the narrow
gulch in which 1t is situated. Five men were
buried beneath the snow. Two were rescued,
but the others are dead and their bodies have
not yet been recovered

through which Canyon creek pours its water
into the south fork Of the Ceur d'Alene. 1t
had about two hundred inhabitants, who have
deserted their wrecked or menaced homes
and places of business. The nearest town is
Gem, also upon Canyon creek and three miles
down the stream.


Later in the day another disastrous ava
lanche swept upon a boarding house con-
nected with the Custer mine, which Is stu
ated upon Nine Mile creek, about five miles
from Burke. The boarding house was full of
miners, six OF whom were killed; the others
had narrow escape and . number were in
jured.


The disasters were not q surprise to those
familiar with the topography OF that section
The towns are situated in very narrow gulches
on either side Of which abrupt mountains arise
The snow fall this winter has been unprece-
dented in the history Of the country. Within
the last few days 1t has been raining hard,
which had the effect of loosening the deep
snow banks and precipitating them upon the
town and the houses below

| Sullivan mines, perhaps the greatest nssure

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 10.-The loss
of six men from the whaler Charles w.
Morgan, which arrived Saturday from
the Okhotsk sea, has just been MADE
public. The men left the vessel IN
small boat September 1st, in pursuit OF
awhale. The whale was successfully
harpooned and started off at rapid
rate, towing after him the boat which
contained the second mate, FL. A. Mar,
tin and five seamen. Another boat had
been launched, but the party failed to
catch up with the first one, and a Jog
setting in, they returned to the vessel.
Nothing was ever found OF the boat con-
tanning the second mate and five men,
and it is believed the whale smashed
the boat, killing the occupants. The
whaler Norwhal, from Fox island, re-
ports six men washed from her decks
during gale, but two of them were for
tunately thrown back alive by the re-
turn wave.

Forty-four happy little boys and girls sat
down to superb Thanksgiving dinner at
the Orphans Home yesterday. They
fairly revealed in turkey. Such turkey,
too. 1t is safe to say that in no home In
the city were fatter or more tender birds
served with cranberry sauce. This neces-
sary feature Of the days repast had been
furnished by the police department, whose
members are acknowledged judges of the
good things of this life. They did not 20
half way in their gift. either, for the bros
were sent ready dressed and cooked, so
but to cut and carve for the plates OF the
little ones.


And it was not only in this part of the
dinner that the children had been amply
provided for. A prodigious quantity Of
pies and cakes and sweetmeats of every
description had been contributed by the
pupils of the public schools along with
other things. such as clothing. shoes and
underwear. An immense contingent Of
the school children from Mercer street
school. South and Central schools arrived
at the Home about $3.50 on Wednesday
afternoon carrying their offerings, which
they deposited in the dining-room, almost
filling that capacious chamber. Never be-
fore had so many children congregated in
the Home, and for the space of an hour the
place was enlivened with their presence
and resounded with their happy laughter.
And before they left they took good care to
carry the good things they had brought
into the lar0er and closets, and behaved
altogether, as the matron said, Tin beau
tifui. kind way that did ones heart good to
see."


It was o'clock when dinner began, The
turkeys were carved and huge platefui,
with cranberry sauce galore, was laid in
each little urchin's place. Then when this
was accomplished the dinner bell rang, and
first the sixteen girls filed in and tosk
their seats. and then the twenty -eight boys
took their seats, and when grace had been
said all set to with q will, and the way that
turkey disappeared was marvellous to be-
mold. And alter the turkey came the pies
and cakes, and they were hugely enjoyed.
Surely there never was such banquet
served to them before. 1t mattered little
that some Of the little eyes were larger
than the little stomachs. The remem.
brance of that feast will linger for many
long day with the orphans at the Home.

Two Young Men Arrested In Richmond


and Brought Back.


Detective Raft returned from Richmond yes
terday afternoon with Philip, alias Peter Ferris,
and John Harcourt, the young men who hired
bicycles from Atwater and offered them for
sale in Richmond The prisoners are nice
looking young men and this is probably their
first offense. They were attired in flannel
shirts and suits of clothes that showed that
they had been travelling about the coun-
try. Ferris is from New York and Harcourt
came from Boston. They hired the bicycles
a week ago and were three days on the road
between here and Richmond. 1t was through
the efforts OF q colored porter in bicycle store
In Richmond that they were arrested. When
they reached that city they were short of funds
and had become tired of roaming about the
country, and they thought they would raise q
stake on the bicycles and turn back toward the
homes that they had left.


The man in the bicycle store did not want to
purchase the wheels, but the colored porter
followed them outside and told them to meet
him later in the day, when he would have them
purchasers. The purchasers were two police
men In citizens clothes, and when they placed
the young men under arrest one drew razor
and the other q pistol, but the officers quickly
disarmed them and locked them up.


They came back without the Formally Of q
requisition, and this morning in the Police
Court they plead guilty to charges of grand
larceny. Judge Miller committed them to jail
to await the action OF the grand jury. -

WASHINGTON, Oct. 25.-The members
of the Iron and Steel institute, who
have been on tour through the south,
began to arrive in Washington last
night, and came in large numbers this
morning. They were taken in charge
by a committee, were first taken to
hotels, and after a short rest were es-
corted to the patent Office, where they
evinced much interest in the details OF
the American patent system. They then
visited the postofice department, calling
on the postmaster-general. The pro-
gramme for the day included visits to
the other executive departments, re-
ception at the white house at 3 O'Clock,
and promenade concert at the Airing
ton hotel tonight.


All of the visitors are enthusiastic
over the success of their tour. They were
unanimous in their praise of the coun-
try and the people. President Harrison
gave the visitors special reception at
the White House ins the after
noon at 3 O'Clock. The lower portion
of the house, with the exception of
the blue parlors, now under repair, was
thrown open for their inspection, and
the beautiful eastroom where the recep-
ton proper took place was tastefully
decorated with potted plants. AS a
special compliment the Marine band
was present and played selections of
English, German and American airs.
The receiving party consisted of Presi-
dent and Mrs. Harrison, Secretary and
Mrs. Noble, Attorney and Mrs.
Miller, Secretary and Mrs. Window,
Secretary and Mrs. Rusk, Secretary
Proctor and Mrs. Dimmick. They were
accompanied by Assistant Secretary
Adee OF the state department, and
Colonel Ernest of the army, who
assisted in making the presentation.


Owing to the fact that the executive
mansion is still in the hands OF the dec
orators and refurnishers, thus render
ing many of the rooms unavailable, the
reception was necessarily informal and
consisted solely Of the personal presen-
tation to President and Mrs. Harrison
of each OF the visitors. After the recep-
tion most of the visitors repaired to the
Corcoran art gallery, which was espec-
tally opened for their benefit.

The comprehensive mind Of Rev. DIR. McCosh
has grasped the details of confederation of
Protestant churches for parish aud other mis-
sionary work. The scheme does not contem-
plate consolidation Each church preserves its
full identity. According to the philosophers
plan the Episcopalian remains under his bishop,
the Methodist under his conference, the Pres
byterian under his presbytery, the Conyrega-

under his convention. The prime purpose is to
prevent the overlapping of church work and to
insure a strong. united effort in districts where
now little is done by any denomination This

Indian Agent Mclaughlin Tells How


Sitting Bull Was Slain.


WASHINGTON, Dec. 15.-Indian Com
missioner Morgan this evening received
from Indian Agent Mclaughlin the fol-
lowing dispatch, dated Fort Yates, N.
D., December 18th:


''Thirty Indian police arrested Sitting
Bull at his camp, forty miles northwest
of the agency, this morning at daybreak
His followers attempted to rescue him.
and fighting commenced. Four policemen
were killed and three wounded. Eight
Indians were killed, including Sitting
Bull and his son, Grow Foot. and several
others were wounded. The police were
surrounded for some time, but main
tanned their ground until relieved by
United States troops, who now have
possession of Sitting Bulls camp with
all the women, children and property.
Sitting Bulls followers, probably one
hundred men, deserted their families
and fled west up the Grand river. The
police behaved nobly and great credit is
due them. Particulars by mail"


THE PRESIDENT INFORMED.


Commissioner Morgan showed this
telegram to the president late this even
ing. The president said he had regarded
Sitting Bull as the great disturbing ele-
ment in the tribe, and now that he was
out of the way, he hoped a settlement of
the difficulties could be reached with
out further bloodshed.


sCHoFIELD AND PROCTOR NOTIFIED.


An Associated Press reporter commu-
nicated to General Schofield and Secre-
tary of War Proctor the first information
they had about the battle in which Sit
ting Bull was killed. General Schofeld
was disinclined to discuss the matter.
He INDUCED the hope expressed by 9TH
ers. that it would hasten the settlement
of the trouble. He thought it would
make more definite line between
friendly and hostile Indians.


Secretary Proctor said he did not
think the killing will have any bad
effect on the friendly Indians. They
had not been kindly disposed toward
Sitting Bull, and had no love for him.

A shocking accident occurred at Baden
Station, on the line Of the Southern Pacific
Railroad Company, at 4:30 o'clock yesler-


day afternoon and resulted in the death Of
five persons-three women and two chill
dren, and the injury Of five others.
No greater tragedy has ever taken place
in the history of the Coast Division of this


road, which is in charge of Superintendent
A. c. Bassett.


The catastrophe happened to party of
German picnickers who were returning
from their day Of pleasure, little dreaming
that the shadow of death was hanging over
so large a portion of their number and that
their hours of exhilerated enjoyment should
be followed by wailing and woe.
ANTICIPATED PLEASURES.
About a week ago picnic party was


arranged by Charles Roschmann, beer
bother for the Bavarian Brewery, Henry
Strobel. George Eberlin, c. Beach and
Others for days excursion to the Crystal
Springs dam in San Mateo County. About
forty people were invited to participate in
the affair.


The party made arrangements to be sup
piled on large scale with everything In
the way of solid and liquid refreshments,


the main beverage, however, being beer in
kegs and bottles. as a great number Of the
party were connected with different brew
cries in this city.


STARTING FOR AN OUTING.
The nucleus of the party left this city


about o'clock yesterday morning, taking


up the other persons invited as they went


along. There were three conveyances em-
ployed-two wagons and one cart, each


containing from twelve to fifteen persons.
One of the wagons was driven by Rosh-


mann, and the second by man named
Rozewitzer.


The course lay out the San Bruno road,


then along the beach to the Fourteen-mile
House, and then further on to the Seven


teen-mile House. The final destination,


however, was the Crystal Springs dam,
which was finally reached.
GAY AND FESTIVE.
Here the day was given up to unre-
strained enjoyment, dancing, singing and
drink king. The spirits of the party ex-
panded like the mercurial thread of ther-


mometer on warm day. Toward 3:3C


o'clock the party began to think of return


ing home and took the county road


Nothing trauspired of interest until Baden


was reached. The conveyances were then


progressing in the following order. First


came the cart, then the wagon driven by


Rosch mann, the wagon driven by Roze-


witzer bringing up the rear of the procession


of pcnickers. At the time they were all


laughing and singing, their mrth being


commented upon by passengers waiting at


the station for the train.


The cart passed over the crossing, which


is about hundred feet from the station


where the train slows up.


APPROACHING DEATH.


Next came Roscbmann's wagon with its


merry occupants. But it never crossed the


track.


A Menlo Park train, the one due in San


Francisco at 5:13 o'clock. struck the con-


veyance, crushing the frail structure like an
eggShell, and tossing its human freight


about like so many nine-pins.
The collision was q terrific one, and left
those who beheld it spellbound with horror.
A MODERN MIRACLE.
The cow-catcher struck the rear part of
the wagon. The driver had almost reached


the other side when the engine came thun-


dering along. 1t was just slowing up, but
the momentum was sufficient to cause the
destruction that followed.
One of the strangest facts connected with
the catastrophe was tHat tle nOTSeS at


tached to the wagon were uninjured. But
the cow-catcher made III for their escape
by carrying death among the occupants.
THREW OUT HIS CHILD.
Henry Strobel, who occupied the rear
part of the wagon with his wife and three
children, saw when too late that the wagon
could not escape collision. and he threw
his youngest child out on the roadway.
Then came the fatal encounter of the re-
cietlpsa lOPnmntiya and the fraUiip


ance with its fifteen occupants, who but a


minute before had been singing at the to D


of their voices. The women in the rear of
the wagon suffered most, as that was
where the cow-catcher struck.
HURLED INTO SPACE.
Shreks rent the air as the bodies of the
occupants went flying IN all directions,
falling upon the ground many feet away,
some dead, others with broken limbs, man


gled legs and heads cut.


Some cried feebly for help, others were


unconscious, and others slept the sleep that
knows no waking.


Henry Strobel was thrown thirty feet in
the air, but had miraculous escape, being
but slightly injured about the body.
One of his children was horribly man
gled, being but an unrecoguiZable mass of
flesh. His third child was sligatly injured.
IMMEDIATELY KILLED.


Mrs. Strobel was killed outright, her head


coming in contact with the hard ground


about fifteen feet away and being split
open.


Mrs. Rosehmann, the wife of the driver,
was thrown about twelve feet away, and


never spoke after her fall. She presented a


spectacle horrible to behold. Her skull was


laid open and the brain exposed, and one OF
her arms was literally torn from its socket.


A ten-year-old child Of Mrs. Roschmann


met with the same fate as its mother, being


crushed to DEATH


IA irI l. lodi hrC


Eberln, a cornice- maker working for


George Cronin, her death beingi caused by
injuries received about the head in her fall.
THE INJURED.
Among the injured were Charles Beach,


a teamster, George Eberlin, Lille Eberiin,
Mrs. Gesner, who received internal injuries,
Miss Beach, Miss Gesner and Otto Strobel,
7years of age


The driver, Roschmann, being in the front
seat, escaped with the horses. He was
thrown to the ground. but was only slightly
bruised.


Immediately after the collision scene of
indescrbable confusion ensued. The
frightened passengers knew by the shock
that something had happened. and thought
an accident had happened to the train. The
locomotive came to stop Immediately
after the collision. and the trainmen and
passengers did all they could to ease the
sufferings OF the injured.
TENDERLY CARED FOR.
The dead were tenderly cared for, and
were stretched out on the platform of
| the station, where their pallid faces
and mangled limbs were viewed by hun
| dreds. The train was delayed a half hour
while the unfortunate victims were being
| cared for.


Not far away from the scene Of the
| tragedy lay the silent burial ground known
| as Holy Cross Cemetery. 1t was a strange
| coincidence that the picnickers should have
| lost their lives SO near the burying grounds.
| They probably never thought how short wai
| the distance between the pleasure ground
| and the grave.

California Farmers Pleased with the


Outlook for Good Crops.


SAN Francisco, May 9.-The Erominer
has advices from all the counties in the
state affected by the late rains, and,
with few exceptions, the reports are
gratifying, and the farmers are pleased
with the outlook. In Monterey county
several thousand acres of early-sown
grain was injured, and other
counties report damage to hay and
early grain, but nearly all the reports
coincide in stating that late-sown grain
will be greatly benefited. In the south
ern counties the rain, though light, was
especially welcome, and where it fell
plentifully the barley crop is expected to
be nearly doubled. Orchards and vine
yards are fourishing, and with the pos
sible exception of plums, prunes and
pears, largely increased crops are looked
for.

rounding country, the military, floats
with young ladies representing the
states and territories, societies, 49ers,
cavalcade OF horsemen, carriages with
the orator and committee and those par
ticipating in the literary exercises,
which took place in the grove adjoining
the town. After these exercises which
were most successfully carried out there
followed the barbecue, athletic sports
and racing.


The orator of the day was Hon. j. w.
Mitchell, of Los Angeles, and his effort,
which was most excellent literary pro-
duction, was ably delivered and closely
followed by the large audience present.
Mr.. Mitchell, in the latter part of his
speech, left the beaten field usually fol-
lowed by orators on this occasion, and
held that, while the founders of the gov
ernment had anticipated this rejoicing
and celebration of this anniversary, they
never imagined that upon this day-one
hundred and fourteen years after their
act-there would or could be such a
state of affairs as the press of the day
chronicled. The speaker then took as a
supplemental text, the headlines in the
morning HERALD Starving Workmen,"
Homeless Families Walk the Streets
Without Shelter" and argued from this
that there were two sides to our great
ness, and that such state of affairs
warned the return to the principles
taught by the forefathers, whose teach
ings were that all men were 'born free
and equal" The speaker handled the
subject most forcibly, and made a
marked impression on his hearers.


Taking in all, the celebration at Dow
ney was most successful and creditable,
and reflected credit upon those having
the exercise in hand and the commun-
ity at large.

and put up at the hotel. He left Saturday
morning before any person was astir.

the murder. Kolmer was quiet, steady
man and had many friends. Hatton has not
been captured at the last report.

and Fireman Blown to Atoms--A Bad
Collision on the Erie Road.


DETROIT, August 15-The North Shore
limited, one Of the Michigan Central
was badly wrecked this afternoon, at
Augusta, Michigan. The limited struck
a producing car Of a freight train which
had been side-tracked. The engine
jumped the track and crashed into the
depot, completely wrecking the build
ing, and two boys who were inside were
killed. After striking the building the
engine exploded, blowing Fireman
Gregg to atoms, and instantly killing
Engineer McRoberts. Particulars thus
far received do not mention any passen-
gers being killed, although the number
injured lis given at from twelve to fifteen.

PATERSON, N. j., August Is, = The
Chicago and Grand Trunk express

into a freight train, near the bridge
over the Passaic river this afternoon.
The fireman was probably fatally in
jured. The passengers were hurled in

of the passengers were hurt. The killed

Charlie MCGEE, Alton. and James Muir
ray, OF st. Louis. All the injured, are
badly hurt and several will probably

text:
From the Minneapolis Tribune


While all others at Kohlman's Lake last Sum
day evening were distracted with grief and
shock by the disaster wrought by the tornado
Mrs. Eachus, wife of DIR. Eachus, preserved
her presence of mind with extraordinary forti.
tude. Her mother and her brother dead, she
did not allow her grief to interrupt her untir-
ing efforts to assuage the sufferings of the
others. The hotel, which had been turned
into a hospital was the scene of her heroic
work. She labored all night ministering to
the wants Of the wounded, cheering those who
had lost friends and relatives, despite hers
was the deepest grief of any. Her devotion
was wonderful. The surgeons found her skilled
and of the greatest benefit and the afflicted
are earnest in sounding praises of her noble
work, her care for the suffering people and
her tact in ministering to the wants of the
wounded and cheering up the despondent. All
this while her heart was breaking, for more
than any one else was she bereft.


Nor had she escaped injury. She had been
ruthlessly tossed by the tornado, cut and
bruised until she suffered untold pain. Her
name should be recorded with the heroines Of
the world

A story of Indian revenge comes from Idaho.
Two Indians belonging to the Missoula tribe,
accompanied by their squaws and young In
dian girl, have camped for the past four months
near Sand Point, Idaho. The girl attracted the
attention of Black, section foreman ON the
railway. By purchasing fruits and other arti-
cles from the girl Black gained her confidence
and betrayed her. She confessed to her
parents. An Indian who could speak English
went to Black, but was slapped in the face and
kicked off his premises. The Indians said they
would avenge the wrong with Blacks blood.


On Tuesday the Indians, learning that Black
was going about ten miles down the track the
next day. packed their utensils and started the
women to the reservation, while the men with
two ponies remained in camp. About noon on
Wednesday they started toward the reservation.
The next day news came that Black had been
murdered and his scalp taken. Officers hurried
to the scene, but the Indians had made their
escape to their tribe, where they we're sheltered
and disguised, so that it is thought that IL will
be impossible to apprehend the murderers.
The settlers along the valleys arc terribly ex-
cited over the affair, and have ordered every
Indian In the valleys to leave.

The steamship Idaho of the Dominion line
went ashore at South Point Anticosti As miles
southeast of Montreal, at 7:30 O'Clock YESTERDAY
morning and will probably be a total wreck,
although II was at first supposed that the ship
would be gotten of with but little damage.
The following particulars of the wreck
have been received: The steamship Idaho,
Capt Brotherton, which sailed from Montreal
on Monday for Avonmonmouth docks, England,
had clear weather until midnight Tuesday,
when, while the ship was coasting the south
shore of the Anticosti, she entered a dense fog
bank The ships engines were Immediately
slowed down and she proceeded at half speed
until daylight, soundings being frequently taken.
AT 4:3O yesterday morning, the fog tighten
ing, the ship once more went ahead full speed,
but shortly after O'Clock the fog again began
to reef down.


Shortly after this the sound of a gun was
heard. This was believed TO be the fog signal
gun at the light house at Heath point although
the officers of the ship did not suppose they
had run so far yet as the lead showed deep
water. 1t was thought that the most easterly
point OF Antlcosti had been passed and the
ships head was Immediately pointed for the
straits of Belle Isle. An hour later. when the
ship was steaming almost dead slow. the look
out shouted Breakers ahead!' but before the
engines could be reversed the ship struck
heavily and remained hard and fast on the
rocks. Although the sea was almost calm, still
there wac considerable surf and panic almost
ensued on board. No land could be observed
through the darkness Of this fog bank and for
a time the ships officers had no idea where they
were.


Fortunately, there were but few passengers
on board, and Capt Brotherton and his officers
soon restored oroer. Then the bosss were
launched and manned, for the pumps being
sounded il was found that the ship was making
no water, and boat in charge OF the third
officer was sent off. Getting into the breakers
she became unmanageable and drifted ashore
On her return to the ship it was learned that
the Idaho was stranded nj South point, about
two miles from the light house and about so
miles 10 the westward of where her officers sup
posed her 10 be, the gun which misled them
being probably fired by some fishing schooners
in the fog Fears are entertained for her crew
and passengers.

TACOMA, March 1.-THE British ship
Craigend, Captain Hamilton, arrived
from Wales about three weeks ago, and
the vessels colored crew complained to
the authorities of maltreatment during
the voyage. They brought suit for six
months wages, and Justice of the Peace
w. @. Patrick decided in the favor,
libslled the vessel and put Constable
Sweeney and officers aboard in charge of
her. When the stevedores sought to re-
move the ballast from the vessel prepara-
tory to loading her with wheat, the
deputy constables repulsed them, and
Manager Hamilton, Of the stevedore
company, was thrown into the water by
Constable Sweeney, who overturned the
gang plank. The officers subsequently
went ashore, taking the vessels compass,
quadrant and chronometer as security
for the sailors wages. The opinion is
expressed that the Justice of the Peace
exceeded his powers in libelling British
ship, and that the taking of the vessels
property ashore may lead to inter-
national complications.

HARTFORD, Jan. 15-The electric wire
claimed it's first victim in Hartford to-day.
Oscar Williams. an employee Of the Cushman
Chuck Works, was almost instantly killed. His
death is the result OF his own carelessness.
Along tho west side OF the factory run two
wires OF the Hartford Light and Power Com
pany. These wires are SO near second story
window that by bending out of the window ono
can reach down and grasp them. The work
men in the factory have been in the habit of
thus reaching down and receiving slight
shocks. The electric company found this out
and sent a warning to the establishment, and
Mr.. Cushman forbid the practice.


To-day was very wet day and insulation
was almost useless. Late in the day Williams
went to the window. and. leaning out Rrasped
the wires. He leaned over a steam radiator
and circuit was formed. Instantly he ut
tered piteous shrek and blue smoke was
seen rising from his body. The smoke blew in
through the window Two employees ran into
the room. and. seizing the unfortunate man
by the legs. pulled him by main
force of the wires in through the window.
He was unconscious and died in less than ten
minutes. Two fingers Of the right hand were
burned to the bone. Death resulted from the
thing, says Williams only grasped one wire
and that his wet clothes-he had Just been out
in the rain-leaning against the iron steam ra-
diator formed the circuit. The current was an
alternating one of about 1000 volts.

LONDON, May 12.-Gladstone spoke at
the Golden Club tonight. He said the
fiee traders must recognize with great
disappointment how much ground has
been lost by their doctrine within the
past twenty-five years. Militaryism,
which lay like vampire over Europe, was
responsible for much of the mischief, but
not for all, because free trade receded in
countries where militaryism did not pre-
vail-in the United States and the Brit
ish colonies. Protection was applied
now in America, not only to goods but to
persons, as instanced by the treatment
OF the Chinese. The great republic had
never accepted the doctrines of free
trade. AT one time there had been quail
flied progress toward them, but this
being checked, the opinion became actu-
ally retrogressive. Still, the growing
strength, activity and clearness of con-
viction of the free trade Amer
lean party gave favorable
promise OF ultimate triumph at the
polls. On looking over the world the
prospects OF free trade certainly were
not encouraging. This state of opinion
has emboldened the champions of pro-
lection, long lurking in their holes, to
venture out and renew the struggle un-
der the name OF free trade. Regarding
bimetallism, Gladstone said it was a
movement in the direction of protection.
Since the adoption of free trade the
wages of laboring men had improved
fifty per cent. England was working
out great social and economic problem
for the benefit Of the world He was
confident free trade, though Temporal
rily discredited, was destined to become
the universal charter of trade, and OBJ
tain the general acceptance of the civil
lied nations.

moned and pronounced the woman's

plainants. The opinion was written by Com
missioner Veazey. 1t states that the COM
plainants are large manufacturers of
common soap at Cincinnati. Ohio.
In the official classification common
soap stands in the fifth class in carload lots


The defendant railroad companies have always
given it the rate of fifth-class articles but for
many years prior to May, 1885, they charged
the complainants for only net weight, the gross
weight being one-sixth more than net weight


but since said date they have charged for
gross weight without diminishing the rate per
hundred pounds. The effect Of this was to
charge one-sixth more for the same service
than had before been charged. The charge for
transportation under the net weight practice
was reasonable and just aud without complaint
on the part of shippers or carriers. Held, that
the increased charge by the device OF charg-
ing for the gross weight, being one-sixth ad-
vance for the same service, was unwarrauted.
AZ it operated to make the rate unreasonable.

CLEVELAND, o., Sept. GA frightful
accident occurred at the Wilson avenue
crossing Of the New York. Chicago &
St. Louis road at 80 O'Clock tonight, by
which at least a dozen persons were
terribly injured, some fatally. The
crossing is on steep grade down which
runs the electric street railroad line. At
the time the accident occurred, a freight
train was standing close to the crossing
on the south track An electric motor,
drawing one car, was approaching
from the south. The safety
gates were up and the road
apparently clear. Just as the motor
crossed the railroad track, locomotive,
running about twenty miles an hour,
dashed out from behind the freight
train. The engine of the train struck
the electric train between the motor and
trail car, tearing them apart aud hurl-
ing one to each side of the track. At
least score of persons were on the
trail car, and were tumbled about in all
directions, some being hurled a dozen
feet away, and others pinned under the
car, which was demolished. The street
railroad barns were close to the scene of
the accident, and rescuing party was
soon on hand. The victims were taken
from the wreck and hurried away in
ambulances to the hospital within
short space of time. All of them were
so badly injured that they had to be
carried from the wreck.


There was no warning whistle, and
the bell was not rung. The engine
ploughed right through the street cars,
and the screams of the frightened pas
sengers rose above the crashing of the
frames of the cars. A moment later the
injured passengers were lying about
groaning in agony. Two sisters, Louisa
and Minnie Mock, were in the
car. They were lifted out tenderly and
partially revived. Minnie's body
was terribly crushed and blood trickled
from an ugly wound in her head. She
was taken to St. Alexis hospital, and
died in half an hour. Her sister Louisa
was badly hurt about the head and
arms, the muscles of her right forearm
being torn away from the bone. She
will doubtless recover. The wrecked
cars were bespattered with blood, and
the hands, faces and clothing of the res
cuers were covered with the crimson
fluid.

hospital.

left leg lacerated.

face cut.

arms.

riously, cut and bruised.

Thirtv-two Thousand Pounds OF Dead


Fish Taken From Fox River.


Thirty-two thousand pounds of dead fish
were taken from Fox River near North
Aurora, recently. The river presented an
unusual spectacle, every available inch Of
water being covered by dead minnows, pike
and bass. The cause of this fearful mortal
ity emanated from the glucose works at
North Aurora. All the refuse matter from
these works is thrown into the river, poison
ing the water wherever it penetrates. and
Yesterday the attention of the State Fish
Commission was called to the wholesale de-
struction. A thorough investigation was
made along the river from Batavia to
Geneva and only four dead fish were found.
This made the evidence against the glucose
factories conclusive, and further eXamin-
alton of the refuse matter where the dead
fish were found brought the guilt home to the
Pode Manufacturing Company. Commits
siOner Buck was ordered to call on the COM
pany to present the report of the commission
on the cause of the wholesale poisoning.
The Commissioner placed the matter before
the company in strong light and notified
them that they must start pumping that
matter from the river Immediately. If they
failed to carry out the order of the COM
mission they would be held to the Grand
Jury. There were 5000 minnows, from three
to four inches long, hauled out of the river.
The remainder were pike, pckerel and bass
from four to six pounds each.-Chicago
Herald.

JOLIET Qll.), June 14.-The heaviest and
most damaging rain ever known here fell
steadily all last night, commencing with a
waterspout, which completely inundated
the northern, eastern and southern portions
OF the city,


At an early hour this morning the people
in the southern part of the city were COM
PEELED to move out in boats. Small out
buildings are floating around, ard men and
boys are sailing about on RATS and in boats
picking up articles of household furniture.
Street-car tracks in many places are three
feet under water and the electric-road is
stopped. Great damage to fences AID gar
dens has been done. Many railroad bridges
in this vicinity are washed away and trains
delayed. The food pegan subsidng this

ROCKFORD Qll). June 14-Never since

VERNON, La, May 13.-Two Mormon
elders, hailing from Utah, have been
tramping through Washington and
Holmes counties, distributing their re-
ligious tracts. They had proselyted to
a considerable extent, and especially
among young unmarried females. A
party Of eight women was secured to go
west. Adam King has two daughters in

neighbors, pursued the party, and cap
turing them, they tied the elders to
trees, and after flogging them unmerci-
fully, loosened them and began firing on
them. The Mormons ran into the
swamps. They have not been seen since,
and undoubtedly perished. The young
women were returned home, and every
one OF them well chastised, their par
ents making each one whip the other.

at Fort smith, Ark.


Fort SMITH, Ark, January 16.-The
hanging of the six condemned murderers
took place at 1912 p. m. The men
executed were Austin, the Choctaw,
John Billy, Thomas Willis. Sam Coin,
Jimman Burris and Jefferson Jones.
The crime for which Austin paid the
penalty was the unprovoked murder of
Thomas Elliott, in May, 1888
John Billy and Thomas Willis,
both full-blooded Choctaws, were
convicted jointly of the murder
of white man whose name was sup
posed to be A. B. Williams. Williams
had refused to give the Indians whiskey,
and they killed him. Sam Coin and
Jimman Burris, also Choctaws, MUIR
dered Houston Joyce, of franklin,
Texas, in November, 1888, for his
money. The last RAN was Jefferson
Jones, another Choctaw. His victim
was an old man named Henry Wilson,
whom he killed while going through the
Territory on the 18th of March last.


The prisoners bore their fate with
much nerve, standing on the scaffold
fully twenty minutes while the prepara-
tions were being made. The work, how
ever, went with precision and dispatch,
and when the fatal drop came there was
but slight groan from one of them, a
gentle swing of the six black bodies. not
tw:tch or a shrug. All were dead in
from three to six minutes, and George
Malodeon, who had hanged seventv.five
persons before, performed the work
apparently with relish.

Where yonder nymph with music takes
Across the fields her silver way,
With mirthful melody she wakes
The browsing minstrel of the day.
There from his ripple haunted dream
The meadows blithest chorister,
Enraptured by the singing stream,
Clears his brown throat and sings with her.
The amber air with music fills;
Like seeds, the notes sown in the hush
Blossom in song between the hills
Whence echo answers to the thrush.
Dear Bird whose liquid carols come
To me across the valleys span,
l dream you are descended from
That older minstrel, shaggy Pan.
For as the nymphs with dance and song
In olden days his piping graced,
This sylvan maiden steals along
Beside you in melodious haste.

Minnie Worley, aged twenty-five, telephone
exchange operator at South, Bend, Ind. and
Frank Middleton, aged twenty five, in like
position at Michigan City, became acquainted
over the wires during their night watches.
Finally Middleton proposed in fun that they
get married by telephone and Minnie con-
sented. A Michigan City justice was called in
and performed the legal ceremony, but without
the necessary state license. This occurred last
week and passed off as a joke. Now eminent
legal counsel pronounce the marriage legal and
binding. and say Justice Dibble is liable to i'm
prisonment for performing the ceremony with
out the necessary license. The groom will go
to South Bend to see his bride and divorce pro-
ceedings will probably be instituted unless they
agree to live together.

Chicago railroad, which resulted at the annual
meeting yesterday, was accompanied by reports
that either the Pennsylvania or Louisville and
Nashville road had obtained control Little
satisfaction could be obtained from the officers
OF the Louisville and Nashville road, their only
statement being that they knew nothing about
the matter while the new directors of the
New Albany appeared perfectly willing to have
the public understand that q great system
was behind them. The representatives Of the
old board. however, state positively that they
have been assured by both the Pennsylvania
and Louisville and Nashville companies that
they have nothing whatever to do with the
new board and have no interest in the road.

kenney and John Jacob Astor died and caused

LA LIBERTAD, San Salvador, July "a
News has just been received confirming
the reports Of the success of the San Sal
vadoran forces beyond the frontier in
Guatemalan territory. The San Saliva
dor army has now gained six battles and
captured quantity of arms and ammu-
milton. Many have been killed and
wounded on both sides. The San Saliva
doran forces are pushing their way into
the interior of Guatemala, and meeting
with success at every step. Great en-
thusiasm prevails. The intention is to
overthrow the government of President
Barrillos before coming to any agree
ment with Guatemala. San Salvador is
determined to free herself from the yoke
of Guatemala, and assume her own lib
erty and independence.


The Guatemalans Claim a Victory,


Cry OF MEXICO, July 24.-Advices
from Guatemala have been received to
the effect that Ezeta's army attacked
the Guatemalans near the frontier In
Guatemalan territory yesterday; that
the Salvadorans were defeated and
routed, leaving on the field many dead
and wounded and three cannons, which
the Guatemalans captured. Advices
from San Salvador are entirely contrary.
These dispatches report five separate
victories for the San Salvador troops,
who are said to have captured large
amount of booty.


MexicO's Neutrality.


President Diaz has authorized the AS
sociated Press correspondent to say that
not a single Mexican soldier has been
moved to the Guatemala frontier; that
there are only two regiments on the en-
tire line, the same number that has
been stationed there for three years, and
that Mexico will observe, as she is now
observing, strict neutrality.


BERLIN, July 24.-Dispatches from the
City of Mexico state that the Mexican
government will maintain neutral atti-
tude in the disputes between the Cen
trail American republics; also, that the
United States and Mexico will offer to
act as arbitrators.


Trying to Force Ezeta to Resign.


SAN Francisco, July 24.-Consul Cen
eral Estrada, of Guatemala, at San
Francisco, has received dispatch from
Dieguez, minister of Guatemala at the
City of Mexico, dated July 22d, saying
an agreement was signed on the Goth
inst. between all the Central American
republics to force President Ezeta to re-
sign his power and re-establish amnesty.
Guatemalan forces continue ON the bor-
der without orders to attack. No battle
has been fought between Guatemala
and San Salvador. Ezeta has circulated
false report.


Designed to Crush San Salvador.


CRY OF MEXICO, July 24.-The opinion
here is that the alleged alliance of all
the countries of Central America against
San Salvador is for the purpose of crush
ing out of existence that small republic,
under the plea that anarchy prevails,
and that General Ezeta's government is
not desired by the people of San Saliva
dor.


The seizure of rifles aboard the steamer
Coima by the Guatemalan government
has been the constant theme of CONVEX
sation here. Many believe that owing
to the fact that the seizure was made
before hostilities occurred, and before
the Central American compact was
signed, the United States will ask
Guatemala for an explanation of her
conduct.


Later advices state that the number
of rifles seized was 200, and that they
had been ordered from San Francisco
before any revolutionary movement
had broken out in San Salvador, and
were destined for the newly-formed
mounted police.

The weather crop bulletin of the Signal
Office says: The week ending August % was


unusually cool throughout the central valleys.
the northwest and the lake region, the mean
daily temperature in the northwest ranging
from degrees to IL degrees below the normal
for the week, while it was from degrees to 8
degrees cooler than usual in the lake region
and central Mississippi valley. On the Atlantic
coast and IN the south Atlantic and Gulf states
about the normal temperature prevailed, but it
was slightly warmer than usual generally
throughout the cotton region. The tempere-
ture tell to freezing In the extreme northern
portions of Minnesota and Dakota, and light
frosts occurred IN southern Dakota, Michigan
and northern Wisconsin. There was more than
the usual amount of rain throughout the north
ern states east Of the Mississippi and in Arkan-
sas. Missouri, Tennessee, Kentucky. Virginia
and the east portions of North Carolina and
South Carolina Excessive local rains also oc
CURED In the northern portions of Alabama
and Georgia and In portions OF Mississippi,
Louisiana and Texas, although generally
throughout the gulf states the rainfall was less
than the normal The precipitation was un-
usually heavy, ranging from two to four inches
in the Ohio valley and in the interior of New
England and the middle Atlantic states. The
rainfall for the season continues in excess gen.
orally over the lake region, the Ohio and GEN.
tral Mississippi valleys, in the middle Atlantic
Bates and northern New England.


The weather during the week in Minnesota
and Dakota was too cool for late crops. Al
though wheat has been nearly all cut some
helds late sown in the extreme north have been
injured by frost. Light frosts also extended
over the extreme northern portions Of Iowa
and Michigan, but caused no material damage.
The recent rains have greatly improved the
condition OF crops throughout the corn belt.
extending from Ohio westward to Kansas and
Nebraska, and IN this section the conditions of
corn and potatoes are much improved and the
ground Is in good condition for blowing Fa-
yorable weather also prevailed generally
throughout the southern states Throughout
New England and the middle Atlantic states
all crops were improved by the favorable
weather. except the tomato crop in New Jersey
which requires more sunshine. A large corn
crop in Pennsylvania almost assured and
tobacco Is being housed in good condition
tirapes and hops are reported as promising In

CHICAGO, June a. - One thousand
freight conductors, brakemen and
switchmen of the Illinois Central struck
last night, followed by three hundred
passenger trainmen this morning. Not
a wheel was turning on the road here
today. Everything isquiet. The strike
is for the discharge of an obnoxious SUI
perintendent, Russell, and the rein
statement of two minor officials.


The strikers this afternoon ordered all
the branches of the road in Illinois,
Wisconsin and Iowa tied up. 1t is said
not a wheel is moving north of the Ohio
river.


The men insist on the dismissal OF
Superintendent Russell, whose jurisdic-
ton extends over the lines in Illinois,
Iowa and Wisconsin. They have many
grievances against him. Train-masters
were discharged by him as mentioned in
these dispatches last night.


The men did not want to be held re-
sponsible for interfering with the United
States mail or express matter, and con-
sequently attached the mail and express
cars to the New Orleans mail train
today. The general superintendent,
however, refused to start the train until
passenger coaches were attached, and
the strikers warned him that he de-
tanned the mail and express at the COM
pany's risk.


General Manager Beck and General
Superintendent Sullivan had confer
ence with the strikers this afternoon
The men stated their determination not
to return to work until Superintendent
Russell was dismissed. The only con-
clusion arrived at was that the company
would resist the mems demand.


The tie-up will cause serious trouble,
not only locally, but throughout large
section of country both west and south
The suburban traffic of the road is
enormous, the largest in the United
States. Trains run in and out of the
city every five minutes from O'Clock in
the morning until midnight, and are
crowded. All the people, many of whom
live beyond the cable-car limits, are now
thrown upon their own resources for
transportation. But it is not this that will
trouble the commercial world. To stop
the freight traffic of the Illinois Central
means to prevent thousands of people in
Northern Iowa, Southern Illinois, Ken
lucky, Tennessee, Mississippi and Louis
lana from getting their products to
market.

text:
Boston dispatch TO the New York Sun to
day says: Two Of the astronomers from the
Lick observatory in California-Profs. Burn
ham and Schaeberle-who journeyed to Cay
enne, French Guinea, to observe the total
eclipse of the sun last December. are now visit
ing Harvard university. Their experiences
differed from those of the astronomers who
visited other parts Of the globe. The astro-
nomical instruments startled the natives, and
When the party landed from the steamer they
were surrounded by . chattering, half-clad
crowd. who guessed that the visitors were for
eign invaders armed with q new-fangled sort
Of Calling gun. The French fortress III q few
miles from the town and the natives are pretty
familiar with weapons of warfare.


On the day of the eclipse the professors re-
sorted to the actual use OF cannon. Everybody
knows that unenlightened people regard with
superstitious dread any extraordinary darken-
ing Of the solar orb. Ecllpses Of the sun, par
ticularly when they are total. fill their minds
with forebOdings of war, famine and death.
When, therefore, through the announcement
OF the astronomers the common people learned
that the sun was about to hide his face they be-
come more than ordinarily terror stricken and
imagined again that the astronomical instru-
ments were death dealing agencies and that
they would be used to annihilate the town
during the period Of the eclipse. For this rea-
son the astronomers were careful not to expose
their precious apparatus to the possibly violent
curiosity of the mob. After the instruments
had been fixed for the observation of the
eclipse they were surrounded by small cannon,
which increased the apprehension of the ma
tives, but nevertheless kept them at a respect
full distance. They were manned by convicts,
who proved intelligent and faithful.


Entire success attended the scientific work of
the expedition. Early ON the morning of
December ~. the date of the eclipse, the
weather was unfavorable, as it had been almost
ever since the party reached Cayenne. The
sky was dark and cloudy. Between the moment
when the earth's shadow began to creep over
the surface of the sun and the period when the
sun was totally obscured there were two
showers. The second rainfall, occurring only
half an hour before the totality Of the eclipse,
was SO violent that it was necessary to cover
heavens quite clear. Still the conditions were
fairly favorable to. the purposes Of the
observation. When the photographs were
taken. and these were the chief objects OF
the work, there was only slight haze.
Photographs were successfully made of the
were obtained, of which four we're developed
with satisfactory results at the point of
observation. The remainder will receive the
attention of Profs Durham and Schaeberle
when they get back to San Francisco. As yet
they are unable to define the scientific results
OF their observations. Before doing SO they
will have to study carefully the negatives made
at Cayenne and also compare them with those
secured from former eclipses. 1t may safely
be said, however that these negatives show as
much Of the corona as any photographs here
tofOre taken. The plates used were of the
most sensitive kind, made especially for this
expedition, and the times Of exposure were
varied between wide limits The corona OBJ
served at Cayenne very closely resembles that
seen in California on January /, 1889. 1t is
elongated at the SUMS equator, but short at
the poles,

In days of old, of poetry and story,
when the flocks and herds roamed the
fields tended by their faithful shepherds
when truth and right prevailed, and
there were no magistrates TO punish or
threaten; when the grand old trees had
not been cut down to furnish timber for
vessels; when war was unknown; when
the earth brought forth its increase
without labor in plowing and sowing;
flowers sprang up on every side, and
the whole land smiled with plenty; per-
petual spring reigned Pan wandered
DER the fields and through the wood
lands playing his pipes and dancing
with the dryads; when all was serene
and fair in this glad golden age, which
the old poets hoped might yet return;
in the days of paganism, when every
stream and woodland, flower and tree,
represented some deity, and the gods
inhabiting Mount Olympus looked upon
a crude though beautiful world; when
man, rude and uncultured, looked up
ward to the stars, each god endowing
their great son with gifts that were to
control and rule the world, Prometheus
giving him fire, and with this gift he
made weapons to subdue, tools with
which to cultivate the earth, and intro
means of trade and commerce; then
passed the Golden Age of the poets, and
the Iron Age of art and industry began.


Coming down to our day of civiliza-
ton and unrest, when nothing seems
beyond the ambition or creative genius
of man, when there is so much labor
and such great results, why should
agriculture languish and man not cult
vate this beautiful earth, which God has
given him for habitation, here
in glad free, great, glorious America,
with its beautiful States, with their
great mountains, with their minerals,
their great streams, their grains and
fruits, their flowers, their noble men
and glorious women? All should be
peace and prosperity, and no want
known in the land labor and capital
work for the common good, the Skilled
workman everywhere finds a full recon-
pense TO- mis- labor.


Here in California, State celebrated
for it's climate, its fruits and flowers, it's
grains, it's wealth, there is an awakening
W lIlc lull VI 1to
interests. Its great-souled, great-hearted
men have: inaugurated a movement
which should be encouraged by every
one claiming home or any interest in
this matchless State. Acting in harmony
with these "noblest works of God," in
a few years our fair land will blossom as
the rose, and Illinois, extending her
hand in greeting to her beautiful sister,
will look with pride on her majesty and
growth.


Our noble Chamber OF Commerce,
with it's public.spirited men, it's ambi-

see the great ships on the broad bosom

SAN Francisco, Oct. 8.-A fierce wind
sprang up off the coast this afternoon,
and tonight it developed into terrific
gale. At 6 O'Clock the wind was blow
ing five miles out at the rate of forty
four miles an hour, and at 10 O'Clock
was blowing still harder. Five
schooners left during the day for
northern coast ports, and two of them
returned to port tonight, both being
badly damaged by the high wind. The
schooner Gussie Kloss encountered a
gale fifteen miles out. She was unable
to withstand the tempest, and after her
foresail and mainsail were blown away,
she managed to turn about and return
to port. The schooner was
bound for Coos bay. Soon
after the schooner Portia returned with
her foresail and fying-jib gone. She
was bound for Salt Point. At 10
O'Clock third schooner whose name
could not be learned, was making
slow headway at returning, being
about four miles out. The Pacific
coast steamship City of Puebla, which
arrived in port at O'Clock, caught the
edge of the gale few miles north of the
heads. She experienced no trouble,
however. Captain Debney made the
trip with the Puebla from Victoria, in
55% hours.

obligingly complied, when instead of
crackers. Rube drew forth two six-shoot-

Tested their impatience of the delay by

hands and stamping of more or less delicate

Settlers.


One of the noted characters OF the Rogue
River Valley and Southern Oregon was
Umpqua Joe, civilized Indian, who per-
formed many valuable services fol the
white settlers during the Indian troubles,
and the news Of his tragic death was re-
ceived with regret by his many friends
throughout the State, says an exchange
UmpQua Joe served in the Mexican War
and was a trusted scout with General Ere
mont in the Rocky Mountains and during
his Indian warfare on the PACING Coast
When the early settlers of Oregon began TO
locate in the UmpQua and Rogue River val
leyS Joe did active and valuable service in
warning them of impending danger, kind
ness which was greatly appreciated. lie
finally squatted on a piece OF land In the
Rogue River Canyon. between Grants Pass
ard the Galice Creek mines. Here he es-
tablshed ferry, which, together with his
orchard and garden patch, furnished HIM
self and family with q comfortable
living, lie received land warrant
for 100 acres Of land from the Government
as a reward for his efficient services during
the Mexican War, but one time, when under
the softening influence of fire. water, he al
lowed speculative Missourian to euchre
him out of the land warrant for mere
trifie. Joe raised large family of sons
and daughters. but lost his wife several
years ago. and shortly afterward one Of his
sons was killed at Grants Pass in drunken
row. His Oldest daughter married stoIid
brute of an Indian. who finally betrayed
another unmarried daughter This was too
much for Joe's pride, and, crazed by this
and the death of his son, led to a double
murder. In September, 1886, when the
writer was living in Grants Pass. messen-
ger came for the Coroner one night, with
the news that Joe and his son-n-law were
both dead. The Coroner found them both
lying within few feet of each other. The
daughter and wife testified that they had
both fired their rifles simultaneously and
each dropped dead instantly. - Spokane
Falls Spokesman, June Dist.

aced homes and places Of business. The

that the Mississippi River has risen fifteen
points during the last twenty-four hours at
all stations between Vicksburg and Baton
Rouge. The Nita creyasse is widening and
the water in the Atchafalaya is rising
steadily. Four new breaks are reported in
Bayou de Glaise. The Yellow Bayou levee,
eighteen miles north of this city, is reported
as giving way, and the water is running
over two miles of the leYee above Turner'S
bayou. How the people are going to escape
the seeming watery fate is now the all-ab-
sorbing question.


The Illinois Central tracks are covered
with water for distance of twenty miles
near Ponchatoula. The railroad company
has big force of men at work strengthen
ing the weak places. Large numbers of
deer, driven out of the swamps for sixty
miles from the Nita crevasse to this Sec
ton, are running all over the vegetable
farms, eating young vegetables and corn.

ROCKFORD, ILL.,, June 14.-Never since
1857 when the waters rose and over
whelmed nearly all of Rockford, has
such disastrous flood visited this Sec
tion as last evening. 1t is estimated
that the damage to property will reach
half a million dollars. Rain fell in tor
rents for three hours, ompanied by
vivid lightning and deafening thunder
In short time every street was river,
and soon devastating floods were sweep
ing through the Kent and Keith creek
valleys. Down the Keith creek district
came the flood, sweeping everything be-
fore it. The water spread over the low
lands, filling cellars, creeping up into
the first stories of houses and driving
people from their beds.


The basement stories of the Co-opera-
tive and Forest City furniture factories
were flooded many feet deep. Lumber
piles besides the factories were picked
up and carried along, planks and heavy
timbers proving battering rams which
took down bridges spanning the creek.
The fire department and police worked
hard all night conveying people from the
flooded districts to places of safety.
Many fled from their houses when the
water began to run into their cellars,
fearing they were about to be carried
away. So far as learned no lives were
lost.


The city this morning presented a
scene of desolation. The entire lower
portion was lake covered with debris.


The Illinois Central and Milwaukee
railroad companies are the heaviest
losers. Many cattle and sheep were
drowned, and considerable damage done
to the residences which were flooded
The waters receded today almost as
quickly as they had arisen.
