A bold highwayman appears to have
established shotgun toll gate in the
Pipestone pass, about twelve miles south
of Butte, Mont, and is demanding his
tolls with regularity that smacks of
the good old days.


About month since slender, soft
voiced young man, wearing a piece of
overalls for mask, commenced asking
for contributions from people passing
this point, and all were made tributary,
not even the wood haulers being exempt,
and he made up in numbers what was
lacking in individual amounts. This
was kept up for few days, then the
Pipestone was deserted, and the Cham
pion stage was brought under the per-
suasive influence.


Today word comes to this city that
this modern Claude Duval has returned
to Pipestone, and that five new victims
have been added to the list. The
amounts taken in each instance have
been small, but the frequency of the de-
mand has made it burdensome, and the
people living in that section are organic
ing to endeavor to discourage his efforts
in that line.-Cor. Minneapolis Tribune.

magnificent specimen buck deer was

100.-Duluth Cor. st. Paul Globe.

PORT TOWNSEND, WASH, March 10
The American war ship Iroquois arrived
in port today in distress, with four ship
wrecked sailors aboard. The lroquois
LETT Honolulu November goth, for Samoa,
to relieve the United States ship Adams,
and stopped at Marshall and Gilbert
islands. Three days after leaving Gill
bert island the engine broke down, and
the ship began leaking. A succession of
heavy gales from the eastward prevented
the vessel from returning, and she was
forced to 60 north. Provisions and
fuel ran short, and the officers and crew
have been on half rations since Febru-
ary 18th. The crew suffered greatly
from the sudden change from tropical
climate to the intense cold of Cape
Flattery.


While at Marshall islands five of the
crew of the American trading schooner
III. l.. Herman, of San Francisco, were
taken aboard. The schooner capsized
November 25th in heavy squall, and
eleven passengers were drowned, all
South Sea islanders.


The officers, crew and nine native
/ q ,sengers were saved, after being in
ships boat for six days with very little
water. They were taken to Knox, Mar
shall islands, where they went on a
small schooner to Mile islands. The
mate, cook and two 8 amen took passage
on the Iroquois. Ned Good win, the
cook, (colored), died at sea February
18th. The vessel was owned by A.
Grifiths, San Francisco, and was fully
insured. The Iroquois will take fresh
supply of provisions and fuel, and await
instructions from Mare island. All hands
are well.

This seems no city of the dead,


No gloomy, weird and haunted place;
The birds sing gayly overhead:
The squirrel moves with sudden grace;
The fountains play, the flowers bloom,
The yielding sward is fresh and smooth;
Art wells the secrets of the tomb;
And all seems planned to cheer and soothe
But from this calm height glancing down,
We spy the outlines shadowy
Of life's quick haunts, the fevered town,
The living city and the sea.
There the wild chase goes ever on,
With scarce restful hour to spare,
Till each brief life is spent and gone;
Few pause to think of Greenwood there
Beneath that overhanging veil,
That dins with mist each busy street.
How many aspirations fail,


How many weary spirits meet!
To them these tranquil paths and bowers
Would scarce suggest the mournful tear
How they must long, in secret hours,
For such repose as waits them herel
And they will come, the busiest there,
Tired Of the battle, ripe for peace,
Bowed by an avalanche of care,
And signing for their last release;
Will come, patient Greenwood, come
To seek thy quietude and rest,
AS children come at evening home
To rest upon the mothers breast

lasted until October 20, the present session,

UTICA, N. Y, May S.-The larger por-
tion of the Chenango county buildings, To-
Gated at Preston, near Norwich, was
destroyed by fire at midnight last night,
and ten inmates, possibly more, were
burned. The buildings destroyed were
the asylum, in which were about thirty
inmates, and the pauper house and
idiot wards, in which were forty in
mates. Both were three-story wooden
buildings, in good repair, having wings
two-stories in height. They were valued
at $25, 900, insured for $40, 900, and are a
total loss. Probably the worst part of
the disaster was the burning OF ten
idiots who, penned in their cells, were
roasted alive.


The origin OF the fire was probably
smouldering sparks of slight fire which
had occurred Wednesday afternoon.
Deborah Dibble, feeble-minded old
woman, was smoking pipe and set her
clothing and bedding on fire, and was
burned fatally before the flames could
be extinguished. 1t is supposed the fire
started from some undiscovered smoul-
dering sparks from this event. The
keeper was awakened by q pauper and
attempted to release the idiots, but was
driven back by the fire. He then ran
through the other buildings in his night
clothes, rescuing the inmates.


The patients, who had, some of them,
to be forced out, fought against their re-
lease, but all were saved. Most of them
were taken to the Methodist and Uni
versalist churches till other quarters
were procured. Some escaped and took
to the woods, where the sheriff and dep
uties were hunting for them today.


The names of ten idiots who were
burned are: Sarah Mills, Sarah Gala
CHER, Arvilla Atwood, Sarah Bailey,
Laura Gray, Deborah Dibble, Mary
O'Daniels, Almeda Austin, Lucy Warren
AMI Adelia Benedict.


Keeper Mainwaring rescued several
at the peril of his own life. The scene
at the burning was indescribable, and
the horrors of Tongue Pointe were re-
enacted on small scale. The demented
and terror-stricken inmates wandered
around the burning piles in a hopeless
manner. The great wooden buildings
lit up the hills for miles around. A
bucket brigade was formed and about
100 labored to save the small buildings
in the rear, with success.


Norwich, N. Y, May S.-The excite
ment over the destruction of the poor
house and county insane asylum this
morning is intense. All who had friends
among the unfortunates eagerly sought
information as to their fate. Preston is
six miles from any railroad, and pro-
cession of all sorts of vehicles has been
going there all day. The smoke and
stencil from the holocaust are percept-
ible here. At the scene of the disaster
the stencil is sickening. The idiots
were locked in and roasted like beasts.


Keeper Mainwaring said: con open
ing the door leading from the hall to the
idiot department, was thunderstruck
to see the interior mass of flames. /
attempted to rescue the poor inmates,
who were all securely shut in
their cells as usual, but was
driven back by the heat and smoke.
l saw that the idiots were doomed,
and nothing could save them. / then
aroused 4e paupers. In some instances
the poor people were dazed, and it was
necessary to carry them bodily from the
house and turn them loose in the yard
and fields. There were twelve inmates
of the idiot asylum, and they must have
been overcome by the heat, for l heard
nothing from them, and they were

The steamer was put about TO return to

rolled fearfully, and, the guys of her smoke

hold her. The sea washed the decks, and
the cargo of lime was soon wet and began
generating great heat. Steam and smoke

work.

saving the vessel. Captain Benjamin had

struck not far from the land when one of

jsmin. She has been on the Sound

sured for $4,000. Her cargo Of
lime was for Gillette & Wiley of this city

Its golden lines are drawn.
Dreaming of long gone summer days like this,
Feeling the winds soft kiss,
Grateful and glad that falling ear and sight
Have still their old delight.

ask, sis this the last?'
evil never more for me the seasons run

For me to rise and set?'
Thou shouldst be here or should be with thee
Wherever thou mayst be,
Lips mute, hands clasped, in silences of speech

novel duel was fought near Moore Station,
Tex, the other day between two Mexican cow
boys named Jose Carrasco and Manuel Bosco,
Carrasco was in possession of fine mottled
COW which Bosco claimed belonged to him and
had been stolen some time previous.


The two men met in the roadway. They were
both on horseback and their lariats hung from
the pommels of their saddles Bosco hailed
Carrasco and demanded the return of his COW.
The latter became furious at the suggestion
that he had come into possession of a stolen
COW and his hot Mexican blood began to boil.
Words of a sulphurous nature began to pass
between the cowboys, when Bosco called Car
rasco a liar. Scarcely had the word been spo-
ken when, quick as a flash, the irate Carasco
grabbed his iasso from his saddle and, whirling
1t with quick movement over his head, sent
it with a swish toward Bosco's neck. The latter
ducked his head and grabbed his lariat as he
did so.


Then began one Of the fercest bloodless
battles that the past has recorded. Up and
down the roadway the two horsemen dashed,
the lassos of the duelists flying and circling in
the lassos fell short of their mark they were
Jerked quickly together, and with twirl over
the head each cowboy endeavored to encircle
the others neck


The horses were fecked with foam and both
OF them dashed away in the same direction
seeming to realize the fight to the death going
on between their riders On sped the horses,
but not a word spoke the fighters.


Bosco finally turned his eyes from the other
cowboy for an instant, and quick as a flash,
Carrasco dropped the moose of his lariat over
his adversary's neck, swung his pony around
with a jerk, and, putting spurs to the animal.
started of in the opposite direction.

SOUTHAMPTON, England, Sept. g.
Strikers made riotous demonstrations
tonight and were only dispersed at the
point of the bayonet. The trouble be-
gan with the dock laborers preventing
the departure of several trains. Two
companies of infantry arrived and drove
the mob away from the rails. The dock
men made desperate attempt to break
the line formed by the troops. Some of
them took horses from the cabs and
charged furiously upon the soldiers.
The troops, however, stood firm and re-
peatedly repulsed the strikers. A
number of horses were bayoneted and
some of the riders seriously wounded.
Volley after volley of stones was thrown
at the troops, and several soldiers were
severely injured. The mayor read the
riot act, and this only added to the fury
of the mob, which stormed the mayors
business premises, and smashed every
window in the place. The troops were
now supplied with ball cartridges and
ordered to charge. For moment the
rioters made resistance, but seeing many
of their number fall, pierced by the bay
onets OF the soldiers, the mob broke and
fled in wild disorder. Excitement
throughout tonight is intense, and fur
ther trouble is feared.


Midnight-No trains have passed into
the docks excepting those carrying mails
The strikers have telegraphed Davitt
and Cunningham, and asking as
sistance.

LONDON, May 4.-Today's labor dem

cent success, and excelled in point of
numbers and orderly enthusiasm all
working class gatherings since the great
reform assemblage OF 1866. The splen-
did organization of the different sections
taking part in the professions brought
together in the park half million peo-
pie, who met, went through their busi-
ness and dispersed without single in
cident occurring of disorderly charac-
ter. The leading sections were the trade
councils, which included eight groups
representing the leather trades, metal
and cabinet workers and shipping,
clothing, printing, paper and building
trades. Those bodies, in which were
numerous related trades, mustered in
specified districts of the metropolis early
in the forenoon and marched, headed by
their leaders and with bands
and banners toward the Thames
embankment, the central point, whence
the marshaled array was ordered to
start for the park. The gigantic pro-
cession moved off at 3 O'Clock amid
thunderous cheers and blending music
of many bands. The route toward the
park was along Bridge street, st. James
park, Bird Cage walk, which were lined
with spectators, Masses of artisans
joined the paraders on the way until on
entering the park the estimated number
OF men in line was 100000.


Sin1u ltanaOuS1v with tbp anpparanca
in the park of the trades columns, sec
tions of the Social Democratic Fedora
ton began to enter. Some of them
joined the main body ON the Thames
embankment, while others, marshaled
in distant suburbs, marched from points
converging toward two platforms in the
park especially allotted to Socialist
speakers. The Railway Workers. Union
had also special professions, some of
which swelled the embankment columns,
while others marched isolated towards
the platform centers. The total number
taking part in the various professions is
estimated at 10000, and these were
almost lost in the vastness of the assem-
blage gathered around the thirteen plat
forms upon which the Labor day advo-
Gates held forth After the paraders
formed around the platforms, the speak
ing commenced. Shortly after o'clock
resolutions demanding eight hours as
days work were put and carried amid
the acclamations of the multitude, and
by 5 O'Clock, when the paraders had
reformed in line, the assemblage began
to disperse. Half million is moder-
ate computation of the guthering, the
character of which bore everywhere the
unmistakable stamp of the solid, re-
spectacle artisan classes, the rag-tag and
bobtail being conspicuously absent. A
notable feature was that the bands
eschewed revolutionary music. The
speakers included Davitt, Cunningham,
Graham, John Burns, Thomas Mann,
Benjamin Tillett, Mrs. Aveling and
Annie Bisant.

The President today remitted the 800 fine
imposed on James C. Lovins, convicted last
May in the district of Kentucky for illicit dis
tilling. This is done to relieve the estate, Mrs.
Lovins, the widow of the convicted man. being
the petitioner.


The case is a rather startling one in some of
its features. Both father and son were con-
victed on the same day of the same
offense, the former being given
thirty days Imprisonment and 500 fine and
the latter five months and 800. A few days
after they went to Jail a gang of men, enemies
of the family, burned their house and barn.
Upon the expiration of the thirty
days, his fine having been paid.
the father left the jail and started
for home, but while on his way was shot by the
same parties who had burned his property.
Just before the sons term expired he obtained
a remission of his fine, and upon
being released set out for home. At
about the same place where his father had
been shot he was waylaid and slain, fully
twenty bullets being fired into his body. The
father had died from the effects of his wounds
the day before.

sponded that the only terms were the

Diaz has ordered the authorities on the

generally throughout the districts east of the
Mississippi and in the northwest, while about
the normal temperature prevailed on the
Pacific coast. There was more than the usual
amount of rainfall during the week in southern
Virginia and North Carolina and thence west
ward over Kentucky, Tennessee. the extreme
northern portions of the gulf states and still
farther westward to New Mexico, including

ern California, northern Illinois and northern

orally occurred over the states of the Ohio val
ley and lake region and over the greater por-

Nebraska. western Iowa and over the interior
of New England and eastern New York. The
weather during the week was especially favor
able for farm work throughout the northwest.

proved very favorable for crops, although the
planting of cotton was retarded by rains dnr-
ing the week. In the middle Atlantic states
the weather during the week was the most
favorable of the season for blowing and seed
ing and great progress was made in the plant
ing of early vegetables. Reports from New
England indicate that but little farm work has

sing favOrably in the southern portions.

CHICAGO, April 2O.-The action of the
two rival conferences of the Evangelical
Church in each appointing the pastor
for every church in the State resulted in
serious trouble at the Humboldt-park
church, this city, today. Rev. Morloch
was to preach his farewell sermon and
his successor was to be installed. The
adherents and appointees of both con-
ferences were on hand. Bishop Esher's
conference had appointed Rev. John
Vetter and the other faction Rev. A.
Heilman. When Pastor Morloch and
Pastor-elect Heilman attempted to
close the Sunday school. preparatory to
the other services, Superintendent
Kreuzer and Pastor-elect Vetter de-
manded their authority. Immedi
ately the congregation leaped from
their seats, and one party seized Vetter
while Heilman jumped down from the
pulpit. The confusion was made worse
by the women and children rushing for
the door, Vetter's friends shrieking:
"They are killing our PASTOR" while his
opponents yelled: "Out with him."
Vetter was finally landed outside, and
notwithstanding his license from the
conference, was refused admittance by
Heilman, who stood in the doorway
when Vetter's adherents had retired.
Rev. Morloch preached his sermon, de-
ploring the occurrence, but saying Christ
was the only bishop they were recogniz-
ing at present. The excitement in that
quarter over the affair is intense.

The correct story of the terrible railroad
disaster at Lake Labish, near Salem, Ore
gOn, on the 18th inst. must forever remain a
mystery says the Portland Oregonian of
November, 18th. But two men ever knew it,
and they are both dead. They were En-
gineer McFaddcn and Fireman Neaie. The
tramp who was passing wood for them, in
return for which lie was allowed to Tide on
the tender of the locomotive, was the last
who ever saw them alive. but he knows moth
ing. His leg was broken IN the wreck
When he was liberated he disappeared, but
some one has found him.


A gentleman who arrived from Salem yes.
terday reports him as saying that he remem
berS when the accident occurred. Both eugl-
ncer and fireman seemed to realize that all
was up with them when The locomotives
wheels began TO cut through the ties. They
looked each other full in the face, resigned
ly, but neither spoke, and an instant later
both were dead. That is all the tramp re-
members.


SO far all the facts brought to light add
strength TO the company theory that rail
was misplaced for the purpose OF wreckIng
the train. That the rail is gone from its
place there is no doubt. 1t is fifteen feet
away on the other side of the track. Nor is
there any doubt that the spikes were drawn
out of the ties and the fish plates uu-
screwed, lOT tileTc is lNe imprint OF Tie
pinch-bar that was used in drawing them.


The reason for the company's adherence
to this theory are already known. The dis
cUvery that rail was missing from the point
where the engine jumped the track and the
finding of the same rail on the ground six
teen feet below, and fifteen feet west of its
original position, were the first circunl-
stances considered. Then it was ascertained
that pinch lar and wrench had been
stolen from the Salem yard the night before
where the rail was misplaced revealed i'm
prints evidently made by the bar when /. was

All that the company then needed to com-
plete its theory We're the bar and wrench {.
These were fund yesterday morning in Il
wild rose. bush 200 feet west of the nor them
end of the Lake Labish bri1ge. They were

deposited with great care. The handles of
both were partly under the dead branch of
a tree, and two small twjgs crossed them
Tom Graham and Charles Pipka, who are
employed on the section, found the tools.


Another circumstance In favor Of the
misplaced all theory is that the destruction
began at the very place from where the rail
was removed. Then it was that the loco
motive left the track and began blowing its
way over the rails, swapping them as though
they were straws, and leaving death and

Entwined in each Others arms, Minnie

ice that thinly sheets Lake Calumet ypster-

When school was dismissed the children

as they have done ever since winter locked
the waters. For half an hour they whirlei
on the slippery ice, hugging the shore with
childish timidity. Bat, growing holder,
Hand in hand they swung along.
The other children paused and watched

their own bravery, went further on and
out Their red scarfs snapped behind them.
Their faces grew ruddy in the wind and
they screamed with delight. Their COM
rades heard them and joined in the shouts.
Suddenly they saw the ice bend and roll
like long swell and then thoy heard it
creak. Long cracks rushed toward them
and the girls went down. The other chill
dren heard the two little ones scream again,
but the scream was not like the others.
They saw the red scarfs flutter and the
bright heads go down under the gray ice
The children were too small tn have presence
of mind enough to save their playmates
They were bound to the banks for while
and they ran wildly up One Hundred and
Eleventh street and told of the accident,


The word got to the Pullman Police Sta
ti0n and the big officers dashed down to the
lake. 1t was just o'clock when the girls
went down. The police. with long planks,
worked carefully on the swaying Ice, but
could not see the girls, and it was o'clock
before they drew the dripping bodies from
The water. They tenderly carried them to
the staring crowds and the sobbing parents,

The New York bank wrecks are all repaired.
The third of the burglarized institutions, the
Lenox Hill, opened its doors yesterday after
noon. But the repairs have not been made by
the wreckers. but by the chief sufferers. The
chief offender, Peter Claassen, last night slept
at his own residence after an expensive sojourn
Of five days and nights in Ludlow street Jail.
The $4,000 bail necessary to release the ex-
bank president was furnished in the afternoon,
the sureties being Mrs. Ella Claassen, his wife,
and Bernard Cohn, a real estate dealer aud
builder.


Within few minutes after the Lenox. Hill
bank opened several checks had been paid and
deposits received amounting to $1,000 Presi-
dent Jordan made a statement to the board of
directors and today the bank assets will be ex-
amined and there is no doubt the bank will be
declared solvent by Monday. He said the res
ignation of President Wallack and other direc-
tors had been accepted but the resignation OF
Cashier Vanzandt had not yet been acted on
Conrad Jordan was elected president of the
bank.


Thus all three Of the banks that closed their
doors a week ago are doing business, but some
body has lost $3.50 900, whose whereabouts still
remain mystery.

telegraph communication was inter-

swept pretty much all of Northern Ohio,

LOUISVILLE, May 14.-The features of
the opening day of the spring meeting
OF the Louisville Jockey Club, were
great crowds, some very lively though
not heavy betting, and mud, and then
the Kentucky derby was run in the
slowest time on record. 1t rained heav-
lily all night and until 10 O'Clock this
morning. At 2 O'Clock the heavens were
clear, and when the bell called for the
first race, fully twenty thousand people
were present. While the bets placed by
individuals were not heavy, except in a
few instances, the aggregate of money
that changed hands was very great. A
good many were unable to place their
money as the jam was 50 great. The
track was slushy at the opening The
slightest canter scattered mud for several
feet on either side, and with every great
bound in running mud and water were
dashed yards away in every direction
AS the racing progressed the mud dried
little and became more sticky.


Initial Events.


Five furlongs, 2-year-olds-Grandpa
won, Liberty Bell second, General Cald-
well third; time, :O71a.


Mile, all ages-Uncle Bob won, Clock
ner second, Warpeak third time, :464.


The Derby.


Next came the derby, and Riley won
it. None of the other five could touch
him on that muddy track, and it is
doubtful, even, if Bill Letcher. who was
alone proved to be of the same class,
could have pushed the great son of
Longfellow over dry track. Isaac
Murphy's riding was superb. The occa-
sion required jockey who could keep
his horse in hand and prevent his killing
himself by running away. Murphy did
this admirably He had his horse under
complete control throughout. He held
him back to let the others set the pace
through the mud, kept the way open
before him to take advantage OF every
favor the dreadful track offered, and win
the race.


The Entries.


There were six starters-Riley (Mur-
phy), Prince Fonso (Overton), Palisade
(Britton), Bill Letcher (Allen), Robes
pierre (Francis), Outlook (Breckin-
ridge).


Following was the pooling in the
morning: Robespierre, $40, Riley. $25;
Prince Fonso, $40; Bill Letcher, SIS;
Palisade, $40; Outlook, $5. w. g. Nor
ris and Rosemeade were scratched.


The Race.


They were off at the first tap of the
drum, with Letcher in the lead, Pali-
sade second, Outlook third, others
punched. At the quarter Robespierre
led, Outlook second, Palisade third, 9TH
ers scattered. At the half Riley was
first by head in front of Robespierre.
AT the three-quarters Riley be-
gan his race and the rest be-
gan whipping for life. Riley went
to the frcnt, Bill Letcher second, Robes
pierre third, the rest struggling. In the
stretch Riley was two lengths in front of
Letcher and coming easily, and Robes
pierre third. Letcher then began to
come under q heavy whip, and for a
moment it looked like his race, but Muir
ply loosened the reins and Riley re-
sponded nobly, coming under the wire
the winner by length and three-quar-
ters, Robespierre a length behind
Letcher, Palisade back two lengths more
and Fonso nearly neck and neck with
him, and Outlook ten lengths in the rear.

The Vigilant came up to the capsized
schooner first and managed, although a
nasty sea was running, to make line fast
to her main boom, which showed above the
wreck, but as soon as the strain was felt on
the line the boom carried away. The Vigil
lant's boat, containing the TWO men who
were making the lines fast, capsized and

1t is usual when tugs want to get hold of
capsized vessel to place on the upturned
keel man or two, who bore a hole through
it so that line can be attached for towing.
In this case this was impracticable as the
sea was too rough, Captain Mccoy says.
and the men would have been washed off.


Captain Lockyer proposed that the two
tugs join hawsers aud by letting the blight
down under the vessel, where it would
surely catch on the mast or rigging, the
two boats could together sweep" her
down to this port or into smooth water,
and the two share the salvage. To this
proposition Captain Mccoy demurred and
the schooner was left to her fate.


When sighted. the schooner had drifted
with the wind and sea considerably to the
southwark of Point Reyes, and when last
seen by the tugboat hen was about two
and half miles to the northeast of North

BERLIN, Aug 23.-To-night the news from
Peterhof conveys the distinct impression
that the imperial meetings have had a
highly satisfactory result for Emperor WILL
lam. The officials of the Foreign Office
maintain an absolute reticence regarding
the nature of the German Emperor's pro-
posals, but admit that there was immense
political significance in the interviews.


Advices from various reliable sources all
confirm the announcement that Emperor
William desires that another European
Congress be held, with the preliminary
cessation Of further armaments. Whatever
the nature of the inducements offered the
Gar it is certaiu he has met the Emperor's
overtures favorably.


Since the Cars first conference with
Chancellor Won CapTiyi communications
have been passing between the authorities
here and at Vienna, with a view to expe-
diting meeting between Emperors William
and Francis Joseph. Austrian official circles
regard the impending change in position
with intense distrust. Hence the semi
official press Of Vienna throw doubt on
the probability Of holding another European
Congress, and profess incredulity as to the
EmperOTs presence at Peterhof causing
great political transition.


At the same time there comes news from
Vienna that Emperor William has asked
the Emperor of Austria for a conference
within fortnight, preparatory to the pro-
jected reception Of the Car in Berlin in
October.


The Munich Neuste Nachrchten states
that the Gar and Emperors William and
Francis Joseph will meet on Austrian soil
before definitely agreeing to the holding of
a Congress.


After the court banquet tonight the En-
peror will start for Kronstadt on board tine
imperial yacht Hohenzollern. His Majesty
proceeds to LoetZen. where he will witness
an attack upon the Notifications there. He
will arrive at Potsdam Friday, and his new
departure as regards his foreign policy.
though only vaguely known, has aroused
the ire of the old Blsmarckian press.

the farm of Thomas Habon, late Repre-
sentative in the Legislature, three miles
north of Waldron, have been destroyed for
farming purposes and great holes have been
blown in the earth. The course of Flat
Rock Creek has been turned up stream, and
birds. snakes, rabbits and fish are thor
oughly cooked in the heated waters. All
this has been caused by the upheaval of the
waters. A log fire was blazing in the midst
of ten acres, when, without warning, the
earth belched forth flame, great trees were
hurled skyward and all the waters of Flat
Rock converted into foam and steam. A
vast pocket Of natural gas burst forth and
the scene was beautiful to behold. The gas
took fire, blaZed fiercely above the trees and
continued all yesterday and az night To-
day 5000 spectators viewed the phenome-
non. The fire has been extinguished, but
the gas is still escaping. Some claim that
other agencies have been at work, that the
gas is not the cause of the phenomenon;
but the general conviction is that no other
agency could produce such an effect on the
water. Not drop Of Flat Rocks flood has
gone below the cavern since the upheaval
The great cavern has taken in the current,
and a wild, foaming Niagara has been
created,

A breezy little incident on Sixth avenue
last week furnished amusing proof that there
are some strangers in town to whom the ele-

New York By the help of civil passengers
they succeeded in passing steps. ticket

and yon, indifferent to the approaching
train. On she came, slowed up, gates were

partners the gentlemen in truly independent
country fashion stepped briskly aboard, ex
pecting the ladies to follow. But the ladies
had seen no necessity 10 hurry themselves,
so, with clatter and bang OFF the cars
started. leaving the trlm Didos behind.
Then most painful scene was enacted.

locomotive, jump overheard. and yell out
consolation and directions to their wailing
wives, much to the diversion OF hard- hearted
citizens crowding the platform. The train.
however whiSked around curve. and the
concentrated passion of the week-old BRIDE
Sro0ms had no power to reverse the course
of prosaic elevated coaches.

soothed. They wept and wrung their hands,
requiring the combined efforts Of the officials
to still their worst fears. When the chop
per assured them it was all right about the
tickets, and they might board the next train,

sudden sort OF machine and inquired their

TExARKANA, Ark, June 10.-The
west bound cotton belt train, which left
here at midnight left the track at a
spur switch two miles from town. An
unknown man, stealing a ride on the
baggage car, was instantly killed, and
the passengers and trainmen badly
shaken up. The engineer and fireman
had scarcely recovered from the shock
when six-shooters and Winchesters
we're rarnmed in their faces and they
were ordered to lead the van in march
upon the express car. The robbers had
turned the switch and caused the
wreck. They entered the express car,
and, after a short resistance from Mes
senger Nesbitt, went through the safe,
securing, it is claimed, less than 5000.
After they had gone through this car
the robbers marched the engineer and
fireman and messenger about 500 yards
from the track, seated them on log,
and told them to remain there with
their eyes shut for one hour. When
the bandits had gone distance of about
fifty yards they turned and fired volley
at the men on the log. The messenger was
shot through the left hand, and another
bullet pierced his ear. The robbers then
disappeared. 1t required but short
time to notify the officers here, who are
now in pursuit of them. One party has
been arrested, but not fully identified

SPOKANE FALLS, April 7.-Nineteen
prisoners confined in the county Jail
made their escape early this morning.
Immediately after the jailor made his
rounds at midnight, the bars were
wrenched off, and four prisoners crawled
through the break they had made. The
wick of lamp burning in the window
sill, was turned up high, and cry was
raised by the other prisoners for the
jailor to come and put out the light, or
the lamp would explode. Turnkey
Beard responded to the cries, when he
was felled to the floor by blow on
the head from one of the prisoners.
The others then came out from their
hiding place, assisted in binding the
jailor with ropes and gagging him. After
liberating the prisoners in the upper
tier they made their escape, locking the
Jail gates behind them. The jailor
lay in this position about two
hours, when one OF the remaining pris-
oners reached through the bars of his
cell and united his hands. Sheriff
Hinchcliffe was awakened by the noise
and quickly summoned a posse and
started in pursuit. At late hour
tonight three of the prisoners were cap
tured.

WASHINGTON, Aug. 12.-Last Friday the
State Department received from Minister
Miner a telegram saying that during the
battle in the city of San Salvador, the forces
of the Provisional Government seized the
American Consulate of that city, hauled
down the flag and damaged property. The
department the same day instructed Miner
to demand full reparatlon of San Salvador,
the reinstatement and protection of the
Consul, and to see that all rights of the Uni
ted States and its citizens were observed.


Last night the department received word
from Miner stating that the provisional
Government of San Salvador had hosted
our flag over the United States Consulate
the day before, at the same time saluting
with twenty-one guns, and that the Consul
had been reinstated and the rights of the
United States and its citizens guaranteed.


Acting Secretary Wharton said to-day, it
is most gratifying to be assured from this
news that Salvador is DESTROYS and anxious
to recognize and protect the rights of cti-
Zens of the United States and make all the
reparation possible, whenever any disre-
gard or infringement of them is brought to
It's attention.

The most delightful person at sum-
Iner resort is the woman with Sunday
husband. She is always to be found in
some of the quieter resorts near the large
cities; she is always pretty, usually
young and the most devoted wife in all
the world-on Sundays. During the
week, while her husband is down in the
city, she is the leader in all the gayeties
that are going on. She plays tennis with
the college boys like the best of them;
she flirts with the elderly men, who
quite understand her, and she turns the
heads Of all the quite young men, who
don't understand her. All this during
weekdays. But on Saturday night every
thing is changed.


When at dusk the big stages come
E1mbling up to the little hostelry, with
their long seats filed with tired, dusty
looking men, she stands, the best dressed.
the most eager eyed, affectionate little
woman in all the assembled crowd OF
guests, and when Tom comes stepping
mp to the piazza she gives one wild little
cry and settles down ON his coat collar
as if she had done nothing all the week
but mourn for his absence. And Tom
pats her a.Ify Lead and feels sure that
he has the dearest little wife in all the
world, and they walk off, she clinging
Yondly to his arm quite like pair of lov-
CTS, while all the men who have been
her slaves all the week look foolish and
would like to punch Toms empty head.
But they don't know, poor souls-and
neither does Tom-that the whole thing
was gotten up for their benefit. For a
woman always likes to show a man the
endearments that may be in store for
some man, even though she has no wish
or purpose that they should be for him.

NEW YORK, Dec. 27.-ISpeciai. yellow

savers say they have undertaken in years.


The storm of ice and snow struck the
Melissa Trask yesterday, but she contin-
ned to beat her way northward, and Just
before midnight she was off Sandy Hook.
The snow was still coming down in blind
ing gusts and the wind, which had lulled
somewhat in the early evening, began to
blow with hurricane force. Captain Hat
wood had one of the anchors

stiff. and the masts were covered with ice

showed signs of falling. Slowly the
schooner drifted toward the beach, and the
benumbed crew, seeing the inevitable re-
suit, shouted with all the strength of their
lungs. and signals of distress were burned.

than three minutes two large mortars were

4 life line was shot from one of the NOR

Here new difficulty was presented. The
schooner's crew did not understand work
ing the life-saying apparatus and instead
of hauling in on the line to secure
stronger cable, which was to carry out the
breeches buoy, the men simply made the
line fast.


Enormous seas were sweeping over the
little schooner and she was rolling fear
fully. with her decks and rigging solidIy
coated with ice, which was constantly
growing thicker The life-savers were at

selves hoarse, and burning several signals,

launch one of the surf boats, as it was
plain that the schooner's crew would sue

being done Trask's crew, to Captain Pat
terson's JOY, began hauling on the
line. Within a few minutes the cable
was in position and the breeches buoy
brought ashore the first man. His clothing

almost had to carry him 10 the station.

One brave man, with the muzZe OF his re-
peating rife pointed steadily at the door Of the
state prison work shop, yesterday afternoon
held at bay 500 yelling and infatuated convicts
until they were overpowered by the police.
This man was Officer Howard Of the prison
force on guard upon the wall facing the Jail
work shop. The plan OF the convict uprising
was to shoot this man and then for such as
could to scale the prisonwall and run away, but
the hand OF the man appointed TO kill him was
unsteady, and although fred at twice, Howard
was not hit Then the riotous convicts, not
daring to venture out within reach of Howard's
rifle, ragged back and forth in the work shop.
smashing doors and windows, breaking every
thing breakable and shouting and cursing. 1t
was not until more than one hundred police
officers, each with a drawn revolver. entered
the prison gates and forced their way into the
work shop, that the revolt was checked


This trouble at the prison, which was the
most threatening that has arisen for long
time, dates back i've or six weeks, to the time
when the Berthrong measurement system Of
obtaining and recording descriptions of the
prisoners was put into force. The prisoners
then became noisy and insulting, and during
one night kept up a constant camor in their
cells. The locking up in close confinement OF
about twenty of the ring-leaders and the de-
tention of the remainder of the ten IN their
cells for three or four days put an end to the
Gistur bance for the time. but the atmosphere
remained charged with insubordinaaon, and
any unusual event was sufficient to excite the
men to overt tactics. This came In the sue
cessfui escape OF Moore last Sunday and the
subsequent unsuccessful effort of Chicken"
WEIGH, q notorious Boston criminal and leader
of the Albany street gang" recently impris-
oned.


THE SIGNAL FOR AN OUTBREAK.


There are 593 convicts in the prison, great
part of them being employed i'll the shoe shop.
At 2:35 yesterday afternoon, evidently upon
some preconcerted signal, nearly all of the men
in the shoe shop broke out into terrible shout
ing. yelling and all sorts of disorderly noises.
In the shop where the disturbance occurred
many Of the albany street gang were said
to be at work, and it is supposed that they
raised the row in the hope that some of them
might escape during the excitement and con-
fusion. The new prison officials IN the shop
were utterly unable to uuell the riot and fled
for their lives. Officer Howard was patrolling
the prison wall opposite the door which opens
from the shoe shop INTO the yard


1t would appear that the plan was to intimi-
date the shop officials and then to shoot the
man on guard and scale the wall. William
Evans. one of the rin9leaders, had become pos
sessed of a revolver and two cartridges. Two
minutes after the outbreak began Evans, stand
ing by the open window. aimed his revolver at
Howard and fired. He missed. Again he fired
and again he missed The men, who had
clustered Just inside the door, only waiting for
Howard to fall before making rush for the
prison wall, retreated with bowls and curses
Howard stood on the wall like statue, covering
the workshop door with his rifle, ready to
shoot down the first maQ who crossed the
threshold, but not a man ventured forth.
Meanwhile aid had been summoned from sta
ton Is, near by, and within five minutes the
patrol wagon from the station with twenty-five
men, under command of Lieut.. Brown, das he'd
up to the entrance of the prison. Police aid
was also summoned from the city proper, and
patrol wagons from the Boston stations loaded
with policemen hurried over to Charlestown
with the greatest possible speed.


More than 100 men were on the ground as
soon as possible. Lieut.. Brown ordered his
men to draw their revolvers, and they dashed
up the steps leading from the prison to the
inner door of the workshop. As the lieutenant
crossed the threshold hammer was thrown at
his head. 1t missed him and struck the officer
behind him in the hip, disabling him. The
sight of the twenty drawn Tevolvers cowed the
rioters, and no further demonstrations were
attempted. They threw down the shoe knives
and hammers and submitted, one by one
They were searched by the officers and then
conducted to their cells and locked in. It was
$3.50 before this was completed and comparative
quiet reigned. The Boston police superintend-
ent has detailed 100 officers to report at the
prison at o'clock this morning for fear Of
further trouble.

Carlist leader, the Marquis D'Errallbo,
at Valencia today was made the occasion
of an anti-Carlist demonstration. Thous-
ands Of anti-Carlists met at the station,
and followed the Marquis to his hotel.
They smashed many windows. and tried
to set fire to the hotel, when a detach-
ment of troops charged and dispersed
the mob. Many persons were wounded.

Carlist club and set fire to the furniture.
When the firemen came the mob tried
to obstruct them. Another mob tried
to burn church, but was prevented
by detachment of troops. The troops
have failed, however, to disperse the
constantly gathering crowds, who have
built two barricades in the streets. The
military authorities have taken posses
sion of the city, and the whole garrison
is under arms.


At midnight the rioting continues. The
troops have made several charges. Many
persons have been injured and some
killed, though orders were given to avoid
bloodshed as long as possible.


Several members of the Carlist club
fired revolvers into the crowd and three
were wounded. The mob also attempted
to attack the Jesuits' college. Order
was restored after midnight. The troops
occupy various points throughout the
city

Something Beside Pressure Which

Trees which grow in exposed situations
have their tops always leaning away in the
opposite direction from the prevailing
winds. and the casual observer concludes
that the branches have been bent by the
constant pressure of the wind and retained
their position. Now, although such tress
have the appearance exactly Of trees bend
ing under gale, still it is not pressure in
that way which has given them th.ir shape.
The fact is, they have grown away from the
blast and not been bent by 1t after they
grew. Examination of the branches and
twigs will show this. says writer in the
Garden.


We hardly realize the repressve effects of
cold wind upon tree growth, which 1t par
TALLY or altogethersarrests. according to its
prevalence. Conifers show the effects Of
this more distinctly thaR, other trees
Owing to the horizontal habit of growth Of
the branches they point directly to the
teeth of the gale from whatever directioa it
comes. and cannot, like the oak, lean over
and grow in the opposite direction, hence
c0niferous trees growing in exposed stua-
tons produce good long branches on their
lee sides. while on the windy side the
branches retain their rigid horizontal posi-
ton, but make comparatively little growth
which is simply suppressed.


Example: measured the branches of a
Nordmann's spruce, growing in position
fully exposed to the north and south. One
branch Of the north side of the tree had
fifteen annual nodes or growths, and was
seven feet long, and Its opposite had the
same number Of nodes, but was nearly two
and one-half feet longer, all the lateral
branches being propoftionately long and

IAN old woman" used to be term OF
contempt, and yet what pleasant picture
it may call up, writes correspondent to
the Inter Ocean of Chicago. There are
those who have been soured and hardened
by pain, disappointment and failure, yes,
and even by prosperity. They sheer and
taunt and complain, having exaggerated
every i'll, and passed over every good with
out cOmprehendng that it was good A
Grabbed old man, selfish, emblttered old
woman, what torment they are to them
selves, and what suffering they inflict upon
all with whom they come In contact.


But there are others, whose souls have
ripened and sweetened, even under the
chilling winds OF adversely. Those whom
they loyed have been taken from them !;
that which they most ardently desired has
been denied them. that which they would
not have chosen has been laid upon them,
and out of it all they have extracted sweet
ness, patience and strength. These quail
ties draw to them the weak and the sorrow
full. whom they send away with something
of that refreshment which the ailing must
have felt who followed Christ when he laid
his hand upon them.


Next to mother the sweetest word in the
English tongue is grandmother, and the



ing, spelling love has suffered an irrepara-
BILE loss. The name calls up the fragrance
OF sweet herbs and old-fashoned flowers,
those which she tended and loved to look
upon, walking up and down the garden
paths in the dusk of the summer evening
with white-headed grandchildren toddling
by her side. 1t is synonymous with de-
lightful stories and brings back recollec-
tions of the tenderest eyes that ever shone
through spectaces, the ample lap which
was an ever-present refuge in times Of
trouble. Grandmotherly intercession and
grandmotherly indulgence-they have their
place and part in all happy childhood. The
perfect old age is that which is not forbid
ding and censorious, and the most delight
full being in this world is the old woman
whose life has been full and rich and fruit
full. II is the summing up of springtime
OF blossom and LEAKAGE, Of summer ripening
and the autumn harvest. The soul has
gathered into its store-house the fruits Of
love and faith, courage and purity, and
fears nothing when the sky begins to lower
and the winter is at hand. 1t has beauty
and loneliness of its own. 1t is the con-
summation of living, the essence Of feeling,
the gold separated eternaly from the dross,
calm after tempest, and peace aud benedic-
ton after conflict

Advices from all sections of Indiana are
to the effect that the growing crops
and fruits are being badly injured by
tho drought which has prevailed for
three or four weeks. The melon crop has
already been cut down one-half and the berry
crop has been unusually small. The growing
corn, owing to late planting, is very backward.
and the drought has proved so disastrous that
but little will silk-out unless rains come within
a few days. Pastures are burned out and in
many sections the new hay is being fed to
stock. Wells have become dry and in Jackson
and other counties the people are obliged to
haul water for domestic purposes.

New YORK, Nov. 15.-The stock mark

the same time. The only cause of ex-
citement was the announcement from

crisis, and the holders of stocks became
panic-stricken over the news, without
rejecting that the danger had really al
ready passed when the Bank of England

Early advices from London were re-

PoRr TOWNSEND. July 16.-Particulars of
a horrible murder aboard the steam
schooner Jeanne, in Cooks inlet, Alaska,
have just been received by the arrival of
the steam schooner Francis Cutting. In
an alteration between First Engineer De-
we're and the second engineer. whose name
could not be learned, Devere struck his an
tagonist, knocking him senseless. and then
deliberately picked him up and threw him
into the moving machinery. Several of the
crew hurriedly stopped the engine, but too
late to be of avail to the unfortunate man.
Upon examination, it was found that his
right arm was crushed, several bones were
broken. and he was otherwise fearfully
mangled. Medical assistance from q sal
mon cannery was summoned and the arm
amputated, but in few minutes he was
dead.


The captain and third officer were ashore
temporarily and the Jeanne was exercising
her engines. The murderer defied the
ships crew to modest him, and taking
ships boat with a few supplies, started
down the coast. There were no officials in
Cooks inlet and the murderer was not pur-
sued. he travelled several miles along the
barren. uninhabited coast to small can
merry, where he took passage on the steam
schooner Francis Cutting for Puget sound.


Meagre particulars were received the day
the vessel sailed. When Devere arrived
here and before his arrest could be made,
he escaped and cannot be found, although
officers are searching diligently.

Martin Houck shot and fatally wounded his
wife Louise in Baltimore yesterday afternoon


as she was coming out of her bath room.
They had been married only three weeks. but


owing to Martins jealousy, could not live in
harmony. The day after their marriage the
bride returned to her sisters where she has
since lived. Houck tried persuasion. but his
wife had had enough of her jealous husband
and refused to return. During the past two
days he has been hanging about the house
watching for her. but. as she remained indoors,
his efforts to get an interview proved unsuc-
cessful. About noon yesterday he gained an
entrance and met his wife as she stepped from
the bath room. He asked her whether she
would like to be single. If were single
again / would not marry the best man in the
world" she replied. With this she was about
to turn away, when Houck drew his revolver
and fired three times. Every shot took effect
One ball entered the abdomen, and the other
two the back. She ran screaming down stairs
and fell In the hallway. Meanwhile the muir
derer coolly walked after her, and stepped
over her PROSTATE body as he made his exit from
the house. A neighbor, who heard the shots.
tried to detain him, but he broke away and
after wandering about for several hours gave
himself up. Mrs. Houck's maiden name was
Telger. She is remarkably pretty and about
twenty-three years Of age. In her ante mortem
statement she said her husband was so exacting
and Jealous that she could not live with him.

The most serious casualty on the Sound
for many months occurred Monday even
ing off the south shore of Lopez island,
where the steamer Ferndale caught ire,
drifted on the rocks and went TO pieces.
The Ferndale had taken on 500 barrels of
lime at Roche Harbor, some hay and grain
and valuable horse at other points in the
islands, and left San Juan Monday evening
for Port Townsend. After passing Smiths
island she met very heavy sea. and soon
found it too rough TO proceed. The
steamer was put about, to return to San
Juan, and soon afterward was struck with
increased fury by the storm. She rolled
fearfully. and the guys of her smokestack
parting, the great iron chimney was broken
down and went overheard. The sparks
from her lire passed up into the house, and
in a few minutes the boat was in danes.
The crew used every effort 10 extingliish
the fire, and were successful after
a time, but during the excitement
it was discovered that the steam
pipe of the engine was broken and no
more power could be expected. The YES
sci was rapidly drifting toward the shore,
and three anchors were got out and
dropped, but they were not sufficient TO
hold her. Had the steamer been 100 yards
farther out she would have missed the
point at Lopez island and reached safely a
little bay on the lee side, but she was too
far in and struck the rocks. The sea
washed the decks, and the cargo of lime
was soon wet and began generating great
heat. Steam and smoke poured out of
every creyice, and in few minutes the
flames were again eating away furiously at
the woodwork. The crew were driven on
deck, and all realized that there was no
possibility of saving the vessel. Mrs. Ben
jamin, the captain 5 wife, was on board, and
the first work was to make her es-
cape certain. Captain Benjamin had
boat lowered with difficulty


and his wife was soon safe on shore. The
horse could not be driven overheard, al
though every effort was used, 10 give it
chance to swim to land. The crew nnally
left the vessel, and saw her burn to the
waters edge. She struck not far from
land, and was going 10 pieces when the
members of the crew, who reported her
loss, left the scene. Captain Benjamin
had not come in from the wreck last even
ing, and all that is known of the casualty
was learned from a member of the crew.
The Ferndale was 10 years old, and owned
by her master, Captain A. O. Benjamin.
She has been in service on the Sound for
years, and is well known. Ii is said that
she was insured for $40, COO Her cargo of
lime was for Gillette & Wiley, of this city,
and the hrm's loss will be about 81 800.

The color of trout's back depends on
the color Of the bottom of the river, but
the trout which grow rapidly differ
greatly in spots and color from those
which grow slowly and thrive badly
and middle aged trout differs in color
from an aged trout. Speaking general
ly. the young, healthy, fast growing fish
will have silvery sides, white belly and
plenty of well defined spots. The poorly
fed fish Will have few or no spots, a drab
belly and muddy yellow sides. The old
trout will be much the same in appear
ance, only more so, and will be particu-
larly lank and large headed. This accounts
for those trout which have access to salt
water being brighter and more beautiful
than others which do not. The variety
and abundance of their food make them
so.-American Angler.

LONDON, Oct. 14.-The funeral of Mrs.
Catherine Booth, the wife of General Booth,
who was known as ''the mother of the Sal
yati0n Army took place to-day and was
made the occasion of a great demonstration
by that organization. The weather was ex-
ceedingly disagreeable, murky fog envel-
oping the city. But despite this, thousands
of persons assembled in the streets to wit
ness the funeral procession. The route from
the Thames embankment, where the army
was mustered, to Abney Park Cemetery,
where the remains were inferred, lay
through the densely populated district of
Stoke Newington. The entire route was
lined with dense crowds, and the windows
of the houses were thronged. All the rail-
ways entering London ran excursion trains,
and the throng in the city was augmented
by immense numbers of Salvatiopists and
friends from the provinces; also large at
tendance from foreign countries. The army,
attired In uniform, wearing white badge
of mourning, was everywhere nspicuous
The crowd surpassed in numbers that which
gathered to witness the show on Lord
Mayors day. The demonstration is con-
vincing proof that the Salvation Army
wields a powerful influence throughout the
.ountry.


The remains of Mrs. Booth were taken
from the Olympia duling the night and con-
veyed to the headquarters of the army. on
Queen Victoria street. Here the coffin was
placed upon a kind of gun carriage, on
which We're the deceased's bonnet and Bible.
When the procession had been formed to-
day the gun-carriage was drawn into posi-
tion in the line. the members of the Booth
family took their places and the procession
started from the embankment. rhere were
fifteen bands in line. All those who took
part in the procession were officers of the
army, privates and friends not being allowed
to march. Thousands of persons entered
the cemetery to witness the last rites.
The gloOminesS of the scene was addei to
by the dense fog, which never lifted during
the proceedings. When the procession en-
tered the cemetery the gun-carriage was
drawn beside the open grave, the coffin re-
moved by officers of the army aud lowered
into the earth. General Booth stood at the
head Of the grave and read the burial serv-
ice. The officers of tile army from various

Little Jennie Rosenthal, the two-year-old
daughter Of John Rosenthal of 40 Grove
street, Jersey City, was playing yesterday
near rear window on the second floor of
her nome, and another child who was
downstairs in the yard called to her. She
ran to the window and leaned over the sill
so far that she lost her balance and fell
head foremost. There were two pillows
resting on the sill, where they had been
placed to be aired. AS the child fell she
seized these and pulled them out with her.
She clutched them fast.


She turned half over in the air, and that
brought the pillows directly beneath her.
When she struck the ground she lay there
stunned. The accident was witnessed by a
number of women, who ran Screaming into
the yard expecting to find the child dead.
Before DR.. Heating arrived the child
had recovered from the shock and
was PLAYING about the house. The dis
lance the child fell was twenty five feet,
and the SPOT where she struck was paved
with coDblestones. If it had not been for
the pillows she would surely have been
killed.-N- Y. Sun, Aug. I'd.

NEEDLES, Cal, August pa wreck
and explosion occurred on the Atlantic
and Pacific road near Homer, about 80
O'Clock this morning. A double header
freight train was coming into Needles,
when the train parted, and afterwards
collided, causing the explosion OF some
powder in one of the cars. Eleven cars
were derailed, and some Of them blown
to pieces. Freight and merchandise
were scattered around for several hun
,dred yards, and the ground for some dis
tance was excavated by the explosion.


Mike Cramer, Of Los Angeles, boiler
maker, sustained fracture of the thigh,
and internal injuries which may prove
fatal. An Indian trackman was fatally
injured. Fireman Tison was seriously
injured about the body and knee, and
seI eral Indian railroad hands more or
less hurt.


Just after the explosion occurred, the
head engine became disconnected, and
having no one in the cab, tore down the
track at a frightful rate of speed, just
behind the east bound mail and express
train, and had not a night yardman
changed the switch in time, would have
dashed into the rear end of
the Pullman and car doubtless caused a
fearful loss of life. AS it was, she
collided in the Needles yard with
another engine, completely wrecking
the two.


The wreck is being cleared and travel
will be resumed tonight.

NEW YORK, Nov. pa terrible acci-
dent occurred at Eastern Park, Brook
lyn, before the Yale-Princeton football
game today. The big free stand on the
eastern side of the grounds suddenly
collapsed, carrying down the entire load
of human beings.


More than 1000 people were in the
structure at the time. The scene was
indescribable. Confusion and panic
followed the crash. The occupants were
mostly men, the great majority of them
students from Yale and Princeton.
There were also many women. They all
lay in struggling mass upon the
ground, many completely buried under
the wreckage. The screams and groans
were awful, and many tainted away from
the injuries they received.


In an instant there was a rush for that
part of the field, and score of police
men were engaged in pulling the manned
and wounded from the wreck; others
lent assistance, and within ten minutes
the whole place was cleared. At first it
was feared some were killed, but this
fear proved unfounded. great many,
however, were severely hurt, and broken
limbs and bruised heads and bodies are
numerous. Many of the injured were
carried away by their friends before
their names could be learned.


Among those whose names were
learned are: Charles Wilson, ankle dis
located; Cadets John A. Quillar and
Perrin Fancy, of the military institute
at Peekskill, backs badly sprained; E.
b. Remington, Princeton '93, leg
broken; a Yale man, name not learned,
conclusion of the spine; two Rutgers
college students, heads bruised and cut
John Monroe, Princeton, confusion of
the legs; S. G. Dunning, Princeton 81,
broken ankle; G. A. Wylie, thigh
broken; James McGlone, internal
injuries; E. S. Keller, Columbia '9l,
broken wrist; John Weed, Yale, injured
internally; Stephen p. Spear. Yale, arm
broken John Carruthers, Wesylan
university, badly cut head; Eldridge,
Princeton '04, both legs badly injured
Curley, '94, Princeton, conclusion of the
brain, very serious; Edward Moran,
Yale, leg broken Mexican, Princeton,
fractured leg; Bradley 1872, Princeton,
both legs badly hurt; H. w. Fuller,
scalp wound; George a. Johnson, con-
fusion OF the spine.


A lot OF boys, names not learned, who
stood upon the top row OF bleachers,
were badly bruised.


The only ladies hurt were five Brook
lyn women, whose names could not be
learned


The number of people injured is about
fifty to sixty. The stand was evidently
in most unsafe condition, for the
broken timbers showed that many of
them were rotten, while the whole
structure was the most fimsy affair i'm
aginable. Every one claimed that a
very superficial examination of the
structure would show that it was totally
insufficient to support the crowd which
would occupy it.

March % for Hamburg, arrived at dock this

full of water. She in collision at midnight

badly damaged that she sank. No lives were
lost

ships with great force and cut halt way through

children. A scene of wild confusion followed

rushed half clad from their berths
to the deck. The live boats
belonging to the steamer were cleared away

them. Rowing a short distance the boat lay
to for two hours until the Avoca sunk. The
North Cambria then picked up the people in

the personal effects Of the passengers and crew
were saved.

Twenty young men of Williams and vicin-

weeks recreation. They pitched their camp
on the east side of Snow Mountain, where

walled mountain side, while they lured the
shy trout, the innocent deer and the fierce
bear from their haunts in the unbroken
mounta fastness. The boys enjoyed the
alurements of the wilderness, and the
wild game furnished their table with an
abunda nee of the most delicate vlands.
During the evenings when all were about
the campfire they at various times paused
in the telling of mirthful tales. thinking

of the night, when all was still about the
place and wrapped in slumber, one OF the

noise, and upon opening his eyes his vision
rested for minute on the face of strange
man, whose beard and hair were unkempt
hatless and in taltered clothing. As soon as
the stranger found that he was observed he
disappeared into the faSlneSs of the jungle.


There was no more sleep for the young
man although he remained In his bed. In
about two hours the strange figure returned,
his long hair floating in the midnight breezes,
his chin almost resting on his sunken chest
his bony fingers bent like cats paw when
about to spring, and from his eyes shOne an
unnatural light. Breathless did the young
man, who had the day before bravely faced
an enraged BEAR watch the approaching fig
ure, whose countenance looked ghOst-like in
the light Of the moon. This strange man
approached the impr 0vised table of thecamp,
where meat and bread from the last meal
remained, and he ate ravenously, more like
a wild beast than human being. Presently
the young man saluted him with a friendly
greeting. Had an electric shock passed
through his system he could not have acted
more quickly. In an instant the wild man,
for such he really appeared, sprang up the
almost impas sable mountainside as fleet as
deer. Excited and hardly knowing what he

precipitous side Of the mountain, evidently
loosened by the wild being which had passed
up.


The boys from that on lost their appetite
for the juicy venison and delicate trout.
They only remained day OF so after, but
during that time the strange figure was often
seen skulking near the camp like wild an
imal, but invariably upon being discovered
he would swiftly disappear into the almost
lmpeDetrable jungle.


The description of this wild man of the
hills" tallies exactly with that OF Sam Well
ing who murdered Stafford near Willows
three years ago 1t is presumed that it is
the murderer. who escaped and went into
the mountains, and that his crime, ever eat
ing at his mind, together with the loneliness
and hardNhips of such life. drove him in

Commodore Sutton Of the police boat Joe

dore well-dressed man with watch chain

When the end OF the route was reached he
muttered something about going into the river
and then walked hurriedly toward the wharf
just TINS side Of the Inland and Seaboard Coast.
ing Company's wharf. The conductor ON the
car walked down to the wharf after him, but
when he reached the wharf the stranger was
not visible. There were several persons about

driver Of the car concluded however. that the
stranger had committed suicide and they re.

Express Messenger Geo. A. Taylor, who has
a run OH the Chicago and Alton railroad be-
tween Kansas City and St Louis, had a desper
ate struggle with two wild cats in his car We'd
nesday The animals had just been captured
i'll the Indian territory on order of the zoologi-
cal gardens of st. Louis and were on their way
there. About an hour out of Kansas City,
while Taylor was busy in the end OF the car, he
heard a cracking noise and turning saw the
largest of the two wild cats coming out of the
cage, the Stats Of which had been gnawed
apart. Taylor seized tarpaulin just in time,
for the gray belly of the animal was dragging
on the floor and instant later came the
spring. The wild cat struck the tarpaulin with
such force as almost to knock the messenger
down, but he recovered himself and gave the
wild cat a fearful kick through the tarpaulin,
in which its claws had caught.


The train was running fast and his car was
locked to prevent robbery, and there he was
pitted against two wild beasts. Again and again
did the wildcat spring. Sometimes Taylor
would get it covered with the tarpaulin and
then before it could get away he would kick the
enraged beast beneath the tarpaulin with all
his power. Finally the kicks began to tell and
at last the wildcat no longer sprang at him but
crouched upon the floor. Seeing his chance
Taylor grasped piece OF gas pipe, and pro-
tecting himself with the tarpaulin he boldly
approached the animal and attacked it. 1t
turned and with two jumps regained its cage
and companion. Taylor stood guard over the
cage with the gas pipe until the train stopprd
when he sprang from the car and gave the
alarm. The animals were soon safely Gagged
and are now at the gardens.

text:
A Terrible Tragedy in West Virginia


Brought on by jealousy.


A telephone dispatch fIGm Grantsville,
Pa. says that Adam and Grant Richards,
who were visiting an uncle at Oxford, went
to corn-husking a few nights since, Adam
taking his young and pretty wife with him.
During the evening the usual country games,
in which kissing takes prominent part,
came off. Grant universally selected his
Cousins petty wife as his choice among the
many misses, maids and matrons, and there
by excited Adams jealousy. On their way
home Adam chided his cousin, and warned
him to desist In future.


In the morning at the breakfast table the
subject came up again, but the men left the
house apparently good friends. They had
not left the yard, however, before Grant
drew knife and attacked his cousin, cutting
him almost in pieces. He then walked into
the house and told the woman that she was
to blame for the murder, picked up his gun
and made for the hills, but was overtaken
and captured that night. Adams heart was
completely severed and two ribs cut away.
Many threats of lynchng the murderer were
made, but he was hustled off to the county
seat and safely lodged in jail.-Pittsburg
Dispatch,

Marie Gagnors troubles are over. She died
early yesterday morning at the Lariboisiere Hos
pital in Paris. After severe operation We'd
nesday the poor girl lay for hours in state of ap-
parent calm, but real stupor. Toward g. IN
she breathed her last, carrying with her to the
grave the secret Of her death. Just before the
end Marie made terrible effort and, raising
herself slightly, pronounced the name Emile. !"
There WAS no mistake about the word, for the
director OF the hospital and two internes watch
ing at her bedside heard it disti nctly and their
testimony agrees. Strain their ears as they
might they were unable to make any sense out
OF the unintelligible tumble which followed
The girls eyes stood out from their sockets,
the right eye bruised and blackened and the
cords OF her neck frightened. She clutched the
air with her bloodless hands and her voice died
away in . series Of gasps. Plainly there was
something she wished to say before she died,
but she could not say it. What that some thing
was human justice will never know.

The tow boat Port Eads, Capt. Nelson Davis,

portation company. was sunk yesterday at the
site of the railroad bridge, two miles below

mine-inspectors, District Master Workman

tombei men. Fifteen and a half days

abandoned this evening at 6 o'clock, and
the dust or ashes of the thirty-one impris-

till the last day shall come. This is because

After being driven from the mine by

one more attempt to rescue their comrades,
and at . o'clock they again entered the
burning pit Three of the party returned
to within few hundred yards of the burn
ing subterranean fire and satisfied them
selves that the men were dead and further
search was useless.


The stencil of burning human flesh sick
ened them, but they visited nine places
where the men were known to have been
at work. Two dinner pals were found
with the dinners untouched and two coats.
The picks and shOvels were all lying just

on a run for his life. Otherwise no trace Of
the men could be found.


While prosecuting the search further, res
cuers ran into dense cloud Of black damp,
which put out their lights. A struggle for
life then followed, but they succeeded in
getting back to the rest of the party. Alter
sad consultation it was decided to aban-
don the search, and the company will now
make an effort to eXtinguish the fires and
save some of their property.

MIssoULA, Mont, Dec. 19.-The great
est hanging which eyer took place in
the Northwest, occurred this morning,
when Lola See, Pierre Paul, Antley and
Pascale, four Indian murderers, were
hanged at the court house here. All
died game, Pierre Paul and Antley
smilingly bidding their friends good bye
Twenty minutes after the trap was
sprung, all were dead. Their necks
were broken.


The four Indians protested their inno-
cence before dying. Their bodies will
be taken to st. Ignatius mission for
burial. Several prominent chiefs were
in attendance at the execution, but
there was no protesting demonstration
on their part, or from members of the
tribe as had been anticipated. About
one hundred persons were present.


THEIR CowARDLY CRIMES.


The crimes for which the four Indians
were hanged we,e most cowardly and
brutal. Pascale killed prospector
named j. NJ. Dunn, in the spring of
1889, near Demersville. Dunn traded
horses with him, and when he refused
to trade back the Indian shot him, tax
ing his horse and what money he had.
Pascale hid the body in the brush where
the bones were discovered some months
later by another Indian, to whom Pas
Gale admitted the crime. The bones
were identified by remnants Of clothing,
and Pascale was arrested.


Antley's crime was his participation
in the murder of three white prospect
ors, Mcdonald, Seely and Thompson, in
the fall of 1887 lat lfcreek, near Tobacco
plains. The prospectors were surprised at
their camp fire, by party of six Koot-
enai Indians, and murdered in cold
blood. Two of the Indians were cap
tured soon after, and lynched by the
people of Demersvlle. The Antleys
remained at large till last summer.


Lola See and Pierre Paul killed two
white men, names not known, in Au-
gust, 1887, and threw the bodies into
the Jack river, where they were found by
a half-breed woman, who was cautioned
by the murderers to say nothing about
the bodies. They notified the author
tiles and the murderers were arrested
last summer. The murders were un-
provoked.


The four prisoners were tried and con-
victed before Judge Marshall, at Mis-
soula, last fall.

Irene Allen, the pretty fifteen-year-old daugh-
ter Of Andrew Allen, n porter, mysteriously
disappeared from her home at 1923 Broadway,
Brooklyn, on the night Of September 80, 1889.
The fact that the girl was stage struck and had
some merit as an actress caused detectives to
conclude that she had gone off with some the
atricai company. Her parents, however, con-
tinued to suspect that she had been kidnapped,
until after the lapse Of several months when
they learned, through one Of her companions,
that she had gone of on her own account; that
she was getting along well and that it would be
useless for her family or friends to make any
inquiries about her.


Mr.. Allen, on receiving this information, had
the search renewed, but without success, and
lrenes whereabouts and fate remained o mys-
terry until yesterday afternoon, when she reap
peared at her home as suddenly as she had dis
appeared over o year ago. She had grown
prettier and looked in no way the worse for her
prolonged absence from home. She explained
that she had been travelling with the Howard
Dramatic Company and had not only earned
enough to support herself, but had been able
to save enough for the purchase of Christmas
presents. During her years theatrical expert
ence she had journeyed over big part Of the
country and learned more, she thought, than il
she had remained in Brooklyn for twenty years.

PTTsBURG, Dec. 26.-A conspiracy to
flood the United States with counterfeit
silver dollars has been unearthed. Nine
teen persons are already nnder arrest,
and $1l00 spurious coin has been Sc
cured. The money was brought from
the central depot in New York to Pitts
burg, by gang of Italians employed to
pass it. The money was all in silver
dollars, and is the best counterfeit
standard silver dollar ever made. Two
Italians and their wives were arrested
while trying to pass some of the spurious
money The house where they lived
was surrounded and fifteen other Ital-
ians were arrested, and the counterfeit
money secured. According to the infor-
nation given by the prisoners, similar
gang was sent out from New York to
other cities, but the men could not tell
what particular cities were being oper-
ated.

PARIS, April 27.-The municipal cleo

suburbs the police destroyed a number
of Orleanist and Boulangist placards.

fifty-nine new ballots will be necessary.
OF the latter, the voting today favored
the Republicans in forty-two cases, the
Boulangists in thirteen and the Conser-
vatives in four.


The Royalist deputy for Belleville has
been sentenced to 1,500 franks fine and
10000 francs damages for ibeling G OBJ
let.


President Carnot has received letter
from the King of Dahomey, complaining
that the French attacked him without
warning and without declaring war
against him. The French merchants
now in his power will be kept as host
ages.


Comtesse Kessler, daughter of Ad-
miral Lynch, has brought actions
against the Matin, Soir and Parti National
(newspapers) for accusing her of being a
Prussian spy and giving receptions with
sinister ends; also for accusing her of
stealing Boulanger's mobilizing scheme.

LONG ISLAND Cry, April 27.-There
was lively time at the Recreation ball
grounds this afternoon. The Metropoli-
tan baseball nine were to have played
the Senators, and 900 people paid admis-
sion. The Senators failed to appear.
The Metropolitans offered to
play a picked nine, but the

who shouted for the return of their ad-
mission money. Manager Ryan offered
to give checks good for next Sundays
game. This made the crowd angry, and
they set upon the manager, whose
clothing was nearly torn off his back
before he could announce he would pay
back the admission money.

tempests and mishap. When the ship was one
day out from Liverpool a woman among the
steerage passengers rolled over OH her fve-

it The child was buried on the following day.


On Saturday last an electric light wire on the
starboard side came in contact with the wood
work on the deck aud for two hours there was

this city, Judge Kinkead of Kentucky, and
Judge Cumback of Indiana, comprising the
Puyallup Indian Commission, had final
conference with tie Secretary of the Inter-
ior to-day. and received their final instruc-

of the land fronting on Puget Sound.

elderly man, named Schweitzer, and his
wife were walking across Yolo bridge, over
the Sacramento River, when the woman
crept through the railing and leaped into the
water. thirty feet below. Her clothing kept
her afioat, and she drifted several
hundred yards down the stream before
George FAY and Jesse Dolan, railroad en-
ployes, could get boat and reach her. She
is all right tonight and says she has been
an invalid for several years, and subject to
attacks of mental alteration. She thinks
she will not be tempted to Try the river
again in the winter time.

QUEENSTOWN, April 1.-The City of
Paris has sailed for Liverpool.


LONDON, April 1.-The agents of the
Inman line telegraph from Queenstown
as follows: The flooded compartments of
the City of Paris have been pumped
dry. A close examination shows that
the bottom of the vessel is uninjured,
and all the bulkheads are sound, except
those of the engine-room, which were
somewhat damaged from the pounding
OF the broken machinery. The port
engines are in working condition, and
the steamer will leave Queenstown for
Liverpool under her own steam. In our
judgment the vessel throughout was per-
fectly safe, and everything indicates
that she would have continued to float
indefinitely, as she was without further
submerson or risk after the original
disaster occurred.
