MONTREAL, Aug. 11.-Twenty-fye hun
dred Grand Army men, with their wives
and children. left Chicago for Boston via
Niagara Falls, ST. Lawrence River and Mon
treal on Friday. Most of them were from
posts in cities outside Of Chicago, and many
came from Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska.
Kansas. Missouri and Wisconsin. At 4
o'clock yesterday morning five big steamer
loads left Kingston to go through the rapids
of the st. Lawrence. All the boats were
packed with Grand Army men and their
families. The Bohemian, the largest of the
boats, was the last. She had between six
hundred and seven hundred passengers
aboard. The Long Sault rapid was passed
safely and the entire day was very pleasant
ly spent. The hurricane deck was fearful
ly crowded.


About o'clock great thunder clouds be-
gan to gather in the west and the sky to
darken. The wind freshened considerably,
too, and big storm was predicted. There
was yet one series OF rapids TO go through,
the Cretan, as dangerous as any on the
river, and the captain of the Bohemian
thought he could reach there before dark
ness set in. The upper deck forward of the
boat was packed with people, watching the
first plunge of the steamer, when there was
brilliant flash of lightning, the rain began
to fall in sheets, and the people made rush
for the cabin and shelter as the steamer
entered the rapids. She rolled fearfully,
and the people surged from side to SIDE.
Suddenly the sound of cracking timbers was
heard, and women shrieked and tainted.
Then there were heard several hOarse COM
mands from the pilot-h0use to the crew to
clear the tiller chains. Tie upper-deck
beams had cracked, and the floor in sinking
had jammed the tiller chains leading from
the pilot-hOuse aft, and the steamer. in the
midst of the boiling rapids, was entirely
beyond control.


When it was known that the boat was
unmanageaDle, a panic ensued. Women
rushed here and there. Those that had not
tainted did so then, and worse than all, the
crew and walters on board made a rush for
the pile of lfe-preservers in the center of
the cabin and on the after-deck, and began
strapping them on.


The war veterans aboard kept their wits
about them and fought the towards away
from the lIfe-preservers, while as quickly
as possible they strapped as many as they
could find on to the women and children.
There were not enough TO half go round.


The boat meantime had turned entirely
around and was now going down the rapids
stern first Suddenly there was terrible
jar. The steamer had struck a rock The
steamer slowly began to turn around again.
ana then came another shock, followed by
another, each one heavier than the first,
and the steamer gave mighty heave and
plunge as if she was going down head first,
and then slowly turned her head to the
rapids. There was still another shock and
another rock was touched, and plunge
followed. which was the last jump through
the rapids out into the open, clear waters,
and the captain yelled, "We are all right
now."


The crew had got over their panic and
were working hard clearing the tiller-chains
during the most critical time, and by the
lime they cleared the rapids the steamer
was under control again. Her head was
turned Shoreward, and within twenty min
utes the party were disembarking ut the
Beauharnais Canal Pier.

flowed. Two mill dams were swept

midst OF the river, which poured

moving houses from their foundations.

the infant of Mrs. Olsen, which was

Probably most men, and certainly most

environments that their immediate circle

heroine, the homely heroine, the poor and

miliar and favorite characters in young
women's literature. Probably the authors
of these interesting characters took to lit
erature because at some time of their ca
reer they had been thrown back upon
themselves. They began to write when
circumstances made them feel isolated
from the rest of the world, and in spirit
Of morbid concentration upon their own
thoughts.-Illustrated American.

At one time it looked little serious

mitted the crime to secure the room

Countess Frances Aurelia Bartlett Won
Glumer, who arrived in the Cuban steamer
Yumuri Monday, is at the Park Avenue Hotel,
New York, for stay of several months. She
Is better known by the name Of her first hus-
band, whom she married at st. Patrick's
Cathedral October Is, 1859. That wedding,
which has passed into history as the diamond
wedding" was perhaps the most brilliant ever
celebrated on this continent The bride was a
beautiful young woman. the daughter of Lieut..
Bartlett, U.s.N.. and the groom was Spanish
nobleman of great wealth, Don Estaban Santa
Cruz de Ovieda, a descendant of one of the
companions Of Columbus, and a man of
gorgeous ideas about spending money.


For weeks before the wedding all classes of
society we're talking about it. Don Estaban
had given his fiance rings valued at $50 900,
other jewels costing nearly as much more, be-
sides eighty gowns of various styles and of
great beauty. Among them were the wedding
gown, which cost $4,000, and four others cost
ing $1,000 each. 1t was said that Don Estaban
spent over $50, 600 in preparation for the we'd
ding. When the day came all New York tried
to get into the cathedral, where Archbishop
Hughes celebrated the wedding. The news
papers OF the day devoted great space to it,
and Edmund Clarence Stedman wrote some
famous verses about 1t.


Miss Bartlett was nearly thirty years the
junior OF Don Estaban. She and her first hus-
band lived for macy years on one of his Cuban
plantations, frequently visiting Europe and
this country, and each time attracting atten-
ton by the magnificent way in which they
lived. After Don Ovieda's death his widow
married Count Won Gunner, who had an old
and honored name, youth and good looks to
make up for his lack Of estates


Countess Won Gunner 10 now . widow about
fifty years Of age, tall, slender and white haired
with traces Of her former beauty left She is
living in the City of Mexico surrounded by all
the luxury her wealth enables her to command.
She has not been in this country for four years
and will make her stay the longer on that ac-
count. Tuesday afternoon she drove down to
the dock where the Yumuri had Just landed and
personally superintendent the bringing ashore
Of her pet saddle horse. When he was safely
landed she threw her arms about his neck and
covered his head with kissee Her parents are
long since dead, and the old homestead ut 80
West l4th street, where the reception following
the diamond wedding was held, has passed to
strangers.

Capt. Vim. Brown arrived in San Francisco

at the stake for witchcraft


The tribe had been attacked with ala grippe +"

After the deliberations of the council the

bound TO a. stake for seven days during very

The worst fears in regard TO the Walnut
Grove disaster are more than realized,
although particulars come in slowly and are
still meager. Two prospectors arrived ~
Prescott late Monday night from the upper
dam. They say that they camped above the
dam on Friday night. At about o'clock on
Saturday morning the dam broke, the water
rushing down the narrow steep canyon in .
solid body eighty feet high. One man was
rescued from the top Of tree. They state not
even a remnant OF the dam exists. The i'm
mense body of water, one aud 9 half miles
square and sixty feet deep, was emptied in an
hour.


They had talked with many from the smaller
dam, fifteen miles below, who said that up 10
Saturday evening twenty-five bodies had been
recovered, but could give no additional names
The survivors were in the greatest restitution,
having neither provisions nor clothing.
Coarse grain sacks were being used in lieu OF
clothing. The camp Of workmen engaged in
building fiume has not been heard from At
all and II il feared that all are lost

Wickenberg or from the settlements below the
dam. More detailed particulars are looked for
now every moment.


A conservative estimate places the loss Of life
at nearly forty. 1t is known that at least
thirty men and women were lost from the little
settlement that had been built at the foot Of
the lower dam.

OAKLAND, Cal, March 25.-An elderly
woman, who has not yet been identified,
was killed by one of the dirt cars on the
Broadway grade, near the Tabiolo hos
pital, today The cars, which are filled
with rock at the hill near the old Hale
place, are allowed to run down by
gravity to the fill near Twentieth street
IN Broadway. A car was coming down
the grade in charge of two men, who saw
the woman walking beside the track.
They shouted to her to get out of the
way, but when the car was within about
two lengths Of her, she stepped upon the
track, and. was struck. She was run
over and terribly mangled. Her left arm
and leg were crushed, and she received
internal injuries, causing almost instant
death

TRUCKEE, CAL, February 25.-A reg
ular Eastern blizzard has been coming
on the Sierras during the last twenty.
four hours. At Essex the people left
some of their houses, fearing they would
blow over. Considerable snow has
fallen, but the amount can hardly be
told from the drifting masses which con-
stantly fill the air. The snow completely
covers many of the houses in Truckee,
and tunnels have been run to the win.
dows and doors. The storm is still rag
ing. The barometer is going down.
Train No. 8 srrised at s O'Clock tonight,
nearly twelve hours late.


THE STORM ON LAKE TAHOE.


VIRdINfA, New, February 2S.-lhe
most violent wind and snow storm ever
known in this vicinity has been raging
on Lake Tahoe for the past forty.eight
hours, and up to the present hour shows
no signs of abating. AT present it can
not be learned that the storm has done
any serious damage to the wharves or
buildings about the lake. The waves
have been breaking over the wharves at
Glenbrook at furious rate, but so far
they have withstood the storm. Fortu-
nately the mill company's steamer and
all the small boats had been placed be-
yond the reach of the waves before the
storm set in.


HEAVY SHOWS IN THE NORTH.


SPOKANE FALLS, Wyo., February 25.-
Snow storms have again interfered with
all the roads leading into this city, with
the exception of the Spokane Falls and
Northern. No trains have moved over
the Union Pacific since Thursday. The
east-bound Northern Pacific passenger
train was delayed twelve hours by heavy
snow drifts between here and Cheney.
The west-bound Northern Pacific train
was several hours late.


POMONA, CAL, February 25 Since
noon there has been steady rain in the
Pomona valley, and this evening it looks
as if the rain will continue another day.
The rainfall in this locality this season
has been nearly double the average an

LOUISVILLE, June 13.-At Bull Creek,
six miles above Marysville, last night, there
was cloudburst The cIeek rose suddenly
and swept away several dwelling-houses
and occupants. A dozen persons living on
the banks of Bull Creek are reported
drowned. The following bodies were
found: John Ruggles, fisherman; Lucy P.
Estler, widow, and her two daughters, Bet
tie and Julia, and two sons.


While the storm was at its height a
freight train on the Chesapeake and Ohio
Railroad ran into a washed out culyert,
causing fearful wreck. Engineer C. C.
Roadcap, Fireman Morris Honaker and
Brakeman Charles Eaton were buried be-
meath the wreck. The bodies have not yet
been recovered.


4 little later mixed passenger train
would have passed over the fatal culVert
where the freight train went down, when
the loss OF life would have been appalling
The clouds suddenly burst aud caused a
rapid rise in the creek. Farmers say
the creek rose two feet per minute and
the water looked like wall twenty-five feet
high when it got to the railroad. Twins
portable saw-mill was lifted from its fasten-
ings and, with over 100 big logs, was hurled
violently against the railroad stone eulvert.
This IS probably what caused it to give
way. The creek was raised two feet higher
than it has been in forty years.


The fury of the storm caused many per-
sons on Bull Creek to abandon their homes
and take to the hills, else the loss of life
would have been greater. The storm did
much damage to buildings, fences and crops
in that portion of the country. Some half
a dozen persons are yet missing, but it is
believed they will turn up all right.

brutes life extinct the Young lady united
the rope from the pommel of her saddle. leav-

went to the spot where the dead panther Law

A special to the Philadelphia Times from
Tucson, Ariz., says: Arthur Stanley is miner
who lives near Tucson, and it was his habit
always to 60 armed in hopes of killing off the
mountain lions which came down from the
hills in the night and carried away his young
sheep. The old man had two sons James and
BERTHE, the first sixteen and the latter five
years younger. The elder Stanley always
warned his boys to take the family rife with
them when they went to hunt the cows. For
getfulness came near costing both the boys
their lives recently. One day last week at
sunset after finding the cows the BOYS were on
their way home when their dog brought lion
to bay on the top of high rock. James didn't
want to lose SO good chance to bag lions skin,
so he told BERTHE to run all the way home and
get the rifle, promising to keep the lion at bay
till the little boy got back with his fathers gun
Through fright and fatigue the little fellow lost
his way and didn't reach home at all that night.
James, who had been reinforced by a neigh
boris dog. set both animals to worrying the en-
ragged lion. which came down from its perch
and attacked the boy. James was saved by a
big hickory club and by the pluck of the two
bull dogs. All were badly bitten. James left
arm was torn, and when the dogs finally drove
the lion up tree, wearying Of the doubtful
struggle, he hobbied home for the rife, hobbled
back and brought the lion down from the top of
the tree after it had fatally wounded one of the
dogs. The lion was a full-grown male and
measured 81 feet from tip to tip. BERTHE Stan
ley was found at daylight two miles from home
asleep in the woods and James is now the hero
OF the Tucson valley.

Little Baby Morgan still lies lowering be-

through an open window of a PHILADELPHIA,
Wilmington and Baltimore train Just this side
of the Darby station. He landed on a pile of
rocks and was picked up unconscious suffering
from confusion of the brain. Since then he has

day Ire seemed trile better. Baby" Morgan's

He was sturdy little chap with golden hair.
rudy cheeks and the brightest of big blue

morning. Mrs. Morgan was arranging her

window was open. Rob stood there until

PORTLAND, April 29.-Eary this morning
shooting scrape occurred at Dandy, q
small fishing station about forty-fve miles
from Portland on the Oregon side of the
Columbia River, between union and non
union fishermen, in which two men were
dangerously shot. 1t is known that a party
OF union fishermen came last night to
Danny from Astoria and rumors were rife
yesterday that In case the two crowds came
together somebody would get hurt.


Captain Share OF the steamer MarvSville
says in regard to the trouble that all the
nOn-union men below Wood Point have quit
fishing, owing to the murderous demonstra-
tons OF the members of the union. Night
before last party of union men fired four
teen shots, but fortunately no one was
killed.


The, steamer Telephone has brought the
wounded men here. One of them was shot
through the abdomen, and will die. The
other was shot three times in the leg. Both
were removed TO the hospital. The officers
Of the steamer say they passed a number OF
boats containing fishermen few miles be-
low the scene of the shooting. In one boat
were three men, who were either wounded
or dead. The shooting was all done by non
union men, who were in an old stranded
boat-house, land fired upon feet of union
lists with Winchester rifles.


Great excitement prevails and more blood
shed Is anticipated. The cause of all the
trouble Is that the cannerieS are all filled
and now have more fish than they can han
die, and the fishermen are eEdeavoring to
form trust and force the cannerymen to
pay big price for what they do buy The
union demands 81 % per fish, and the nom
union men are now furnishing fish for 3

The steamship Professor Morse arrived at New
Orleans yesterday with 262 passengers aboard
The Morse halls from Central America and
reached the quarantine station ten days ago,
with 163 of her 262 passengers sick. A death
occurred at Militia On board the steamship
Oteri, from which the pa 'sengers were taken.
which was regarded as suspicious and four
more have occurred at quarantine.


A committee of experts visited the vessel
yesterday to determine whether the disease
from which the passengers were suffering was
contagious or not. The visitors found 1863 Of
the passengers sick from malarial and bilious
fever and dysentery and that the five deaths
had occurred all from the same disease, there
being no contagious disease among them The
passengerj wer3 accordingly allowed to dis
embark.


They ara Americans from all parts of the
country who went down to Central America in
April to work Oh banana plantations at Sacete,

The Fourth of July exercises Of the reunion
OF the confederate veterans at Chattanooga
took the form of monster parade yesterday
morning. Two thousand veterans were in line,
together with the three regiments OF Tennes-
see state guards, encamped near the city, and
several military companies from other southern
cities. Gen. John B. Gordon WAS commander
in-chief, Gen. Z. Kirby Smith, attired in suit
of confederate gray, commanded the military
division. Fifty thousand people witnessed the
parade. In all the line not single confeder-
ate flag was displayed. but every command car
rled the national colors.


In the afternoon five thousand people crowded
into the great tent and listened to Fourth of
July oratlons, war "reminiscences and patriotic
music. At night the whole city was illumi-
mated and Roman lights and fireworks of var
lous kinds made the night brilliant. Lookout
Mountain aud Missionary Ridge were ablaze
with bright Nights and on the Tennessee river
and Cameron Hill there were monster pyro-
technic displays.


In speech at the tent Gen. Gordon of Louis
lana made the remark that time had shown
that slavery was wrong and consequently that
the south had been on the wrong side of the
fight. Today the veterans will go to Chicka-
manga battlefield, the proposed national park,
and attend great picnic.

Deputy Coroner Schaeffer spent his Fourth
OF July morning at the morgue making an
autopsy on the body Of colored woman named
Mary Ellen Warren, whose sudden death under
mysterious circumstances was reported to the
officers Of the third precinct station early yes.
terday.


Mary was about twenty-five years old and her
home was in Georgetown. She was well known
to the police, having been arrested many times.
Her mother died in Georgetown about six
months ago and since that time Mary lived
among her friends in Georgetown and the first
ward.


About week ago she went to live at the
house Of an elderly colored woman named
Frances Day, who resides in an alley between
18th and 18th, L and NJ streets.


While living at Mrs. Days house Mary
behaved herself well and was in the house
every night until Thursday night, when she
went out with some friends 1t was after
O'Clock In the evening when Mary left the
house. She was perfectly well and In the best
OF spirits. Mrs. Day waited for her return
until a late hour and then concluding that
Mary had again fallen slave to the liquor habit
retired for the night


LYING DEAD AT THE DOOR.


She heard no more Of Mary until between S
and o'clock yesterday morning, when boy
",
out here dead"


Mrs. Day imagined that Mary was only
dead drunk, and it was not until she gave
the matter q second thought that she went
down stairs to inquire into the truth of what
the boy had said. Sure enough Mary was dead
and her body was lying in a woodshed adjoin-
ing Mrs. Days property. Her shoes had been
taken of her feet and placed near her head
and her hat was on her bosom. Her dress
looked rs though her body had been dragged
some distance through the alley. Some per-
sons made statements that they heard the
woman scream, and it was claimed by some of
the colored people that she was assaulted while
others thought she made the noise on account
OF the whisky and other intoxicants she had
drank.


THE POLICE INVESTIGATION


When the body was taken in charge by the
police several colored boys were arrested They
were Thomas Jackson Daniel Gill; Gus Null
len, Ben Wayne and Samuel Thompson. Sew
eral witnesses we're examined by the coroner,
but none of them could say that Mary had in
any way been assaulted, although Mrs Day
thought she had. 1t was shown by the wit
nesses that Mary met two of the boys arrested
and borrowed 20 cents with which she bought
a pint OF gin. She drank the whole pint
OF liquor. DIR. Schaeffer described the ari-
topsy and said that there were no indica-
tons of violence about the body. Death re-
suited from congestion of the brain, probably
from the excessive use of alcoholic stimulants
The jury returned verdict of death from the
effects Of alcoholism and exposure, and the
prisoners were released. The body Of the
woman was turned over to her friends for
burial.

Yesterdays race for the Goelet cups at New

that there is only one sloop yacht in America
capable Of beating all others in any kind Of
wind or weather. The day was one Of fiukes,
and although there appeared to be plenty Of

For some unexplained reason the schooners
we're slow in getting away after the gun was
Marguerite was the first to cross and then came

the wind appeared to be. The Katrina,
Oracle and the schooners kept away out and
seemed TO be steadily falling behind. The
first leg OF the course took the yachts to
the Sow and Pigs light ship, and the big white
volunteer was first to round at 2:20:40. Twelve
minutes and two seconds later the Puritan.got
around and twenty minutes elapsed before the
next boat came. The saucy Katrina was the
third yacht to tack around, and then the Cos
soon arrived at 10000. The schooner NJ lin
nearly covered her up as she went away one
minute and ten seconds later, sailing better
than she had ever sailed before and showing Q
clean pair of heels to every other schooner hi
the race. Mayhower, once a single stick
Americas cup defender and now a schooner.
came next at 500 S. and the feet sloop Oracle





at 3.1450 and Sea Fox, last year the
winner of the cup, came behind all the others

Clara for the Gossoon had beaten her eleven

disastrous confiagrations that was ever wit

not gotten under control for five hours, and
then only after a favorable change of wind.
The Fire Department and volunteers worked

Railroad Wharf, the cottonseed-on mills,
eight warehouses, three cotton-compressers,
with probably 10000 bales Of cotton, big
ice factory, box factory and some large
coal-sheds were destroyed. In fact, the
buildings bounded by the river front from
Knox street on the northern boundary of

The losses will probably reach S3,000,O0O,

loss of life, although many firemen were
overcome with heat and smoke and had
narrow escapes from falling walls.


The alarm for the fire at Stewart & Butts

port was spread that the entire business

The first worm | brought to them was

yet about three feet away from the glass

scarcely dropped from the forceps in my

land snakes, when immature, feed upon
earthworms. DR.. Hoibrook, in his work.

the little brown snake. Stoysyia De Kayi,

worms we're their only food. The mature
garter snakes feed mainly upon tc ads and
frogs have never known them to be IN
seciiverous. In captivity l have seen them
swallow salamanders and small fishes, but
/ doubt very much If they ever pursue and
capture the latter in the water.

sent his brother, General Antonio Ezeta,

sanguinary conflict the body of

the plaza of the battle-torn town,

The article in yesterdays HERALD
stirred up the baseball enthusiasts in
this city, and the result will be series
of games. Yesterday the San Francisco
team arrived here from San Diego, and
intended going north on the evening
train. Two Los Angeles enthusiasts
came to the rescue, and guaranteed the
visitors their expenses if they would
stay over until next Monday.
The necessary arrangements were
completed without delay. The open
ing game will be played on
Thursday at the Temple-street grounds,
between the San Francisco and Los
Angeles clubs. The same clubs will
also play again on Saturday and Sun
day. The visiting club is very formid-
able one. Phil. Knell, the celebrated
south-paw of the Philadelphia club, will
do the twirling for the San Francisco
team. Stevens will be at the receiving
end of the battery. "Buck" Ebright
and Charley Dooley, of the visiting
team, are old favorites here. They
played with the strong club that repre-
sented this city over two years ago.
Both have won fame on the diamond
field since leaving Los Angeles. Knell
needs no introduction here. He is al
most an Angelefo. Rube Levy, Jim
Mcdonald and O'Day, the boy wonder,
have all played in Los Angeles before.
Dan Sweeny, the sensational midget, is
with the team. He is the player
who has captured the northern part of
the state with his wonderful ball toss
ing. Roscoe Coughlin, pitcher Of rep
utation, also accompanies the team and
will be in the box on Saturday.


Jim Fogarty, the champion out fielder
of the Philadelphia club, will play with
the Los Angeles club. Carsey, the ris-
ing young twirler, will pitch for Los An
geles, and Pete Lohman will catch.
Carsey pitched for Oakland on the day
they defeated the All California team.
Included in the Los Angeles team will be
such old favorites as Goldie, Holiday,
Isaacson, Young, Jack Fogarty and
others. These series of three games will
in all probability be the only games
played in this city this winter, and a
large attendance is confidently expected,
as itsis not often that so many star play
ers can be seen at one game.

and the Neg Perez campaigns. 1t is because the

admitted making the erasure, but
claimed that he did so to protect Miss
Marshall. He declined to answer the
question in regard to changing the fig
ures. The letter was then admitted in
evidence. Mrs. Wilson then took the
witness stand again. She testified that
she had written the letter in question
for the purpose of testing O'Brien's
friendship for her daughter.


Jessie, the pretty plaintiff, was placed
on the stand for cross-examination, but
the closest questioning failed to shake
her testimony, which in the main was
as follows:


In San Diego she secured employment
as a waitress in a hotel. In 1888 she
procured employment in Taylor's hotel
at Del Mar, and it was there that she
met her ruin. She said that Taylor ap-
peared to take great interest in her;
asked her great many questions about
herself and parents. She told him
frankly all about herself, and gave the
reason she was working out-the neces-
sity Of earning her own living. Taylor
asked her if her father left any insur-
ance money when he died, and if
he belonged to secret society. Miss
Marshall told him her father had been
Mason. Taylor said he also was
Mason. Learning this the girl placed
confidence in him, for she had heard her
father say that if she or her mother was
ever in trouble or distress to make the
fact known to member of that order
and they would be rendered aid and
sympathy. The witness next stated
how Taylor invited her to partake of
glass of wine. She had scarcely swal
lowed the liquid when she began to feel
sick and tingling sensation crept over
her. She could not remain on her feet,
and sank upon the bed. The last she
remembers was that Taylor had his
arms about her and expressed sorrow
that she felt ill, and that he loved her.
The next morning she realized what
had happened. She adhered to her
original statement that Taylor had
never given her more than $3.50. One
hundred of this was given her when she
was i'll and about to become a mother.

LONDON, January 1.-The boys Sec
ton of the paupers' school in the district
of Forest Dale, in connection with the
Whitechapel and Poplar Unions, took
fire last night while the inmates were
asleep, and was burned with terrible re-
suits. Twenty-six boys in the upper
stories we're suffocated. Fifty-eight were
safely taken from the burning building
amid terrible excitement. Two matrons
escaped by sliding down the watsr-pipes.
Several boys escaped in the same way.
The Superintendent repeatedly rushed
through the flames and brought out q
humber of inmates. There were 600
persons in the institution. The bodies
of those suffocated were carried to the
main hall of the building, which was
profusely decorated with Christmas
green's. The fire was caused by an over
heated stove. The female department,
in which were $50 girls, was not touched.


The boys retired last evening in the
highest spirits. having been promised
preeents and New Years fetes today.
The scene in the main hall, where the
bodies of the dead boys lie, is harrow
ing. The relatives and schoolfellows of
those who perished are loud in their
lamentations.


Further reports of the fire show that it
originated in the clothing room beneath
the boys dormitory. The smoke and
flames issuing from the stove fiue
alarmed those sleeping on the top floors
and they escaped. The fire engines were
promptly on the spot. Employees of the
adjacent railway station rushed to the
scene and rendered valuable assistance.
The cries of boys unable to escape were
terrible. The bodies of two boys we're
badly burned but it is believed that they
were suffocated before burned. The
ages of the dead range from seven to
twelve.

text:
Associated Press Dispatches to the HERALD.


WASHINGTON, January 1.-The New
Year began here with q cold, disagreea-
BILE rain, which continued throughout
the day. The White House was. as
usual, the central point of interest. No
one of its predecessors excelled in bril-
liancy the first official reception given by
the head of the present administration.
Certainly never before has been at
White House reception such large and
distinguished representation from other
nations. This was due to the presence,
in addition to the regular diplomatic
and consular officers, of the delegates to
the International Maritime and Pan
American conferences. The Interior
decorations, while not elaborate, were
very effective, consisting of liberal dis.
tribution of tropical and towering plants
and cut flowers. The reception was
held in the blue parlor from IL till 2.
THE RECEIVING PARTY


Entered the parlor in the following Or
der: The President and Mrs. Mckee /;
the Vice. President and Mrs. Morton !;
the Secretary of State and Mrs. S. B.
Elkins; the Secretary of the Treasury
and Mrs. Window the Attorney General
and Mrs. Miller; the Postmaster Gen.
eral and Mrs. Wanamaker; the Secre-
tary of the Navy and Mrs. Tracy the
Secretary of the Interior and Mrs. Noble
the Secretary of Agriculture and Mrs.
Rusk; the Secretary of War and Mrs.
Logan.


Mrs. Mckee occupied place next to
the President. The other ladies assist.
ing were ranged next in order as follows:
Mrs. Morton, Mrs. Window, Mrs. Miller,
Mrs. Wanamaker, Mrs. Tracy, Mrs.
Noble and Mrs. Rusk. The toilettes of
the ladies were singulsrly rich and be-
co ming.


| THE PRESENTATION
Was in the following order: Diplomatic
corps, Judiciary and members of Cen.
gress.


The reception OF the officers of the
army and navy and the marine corps,
which followed, was probably the show
lest feature of the day, they being in full
dress uniform, and resplendent with
brass buttons. bright epaulets, gaudy
sashes, gold lace, etc. Msjor-General
Schofield headed the army, and Rear
Admiral Jouett the navy. Admiral Por-
ter did not attend on account of the bad
weather.


1t was now IL O'Clock, and the recep-
tion became more general in it's charac-
ter /; indeed, the callers became SO numer-
GUS and followed each other 80 closely
that the President was compelled to re-
strict his welcome to a single shake of
the hand and simple "Glad to see you."
Those received in this manner included
the officers of the Smithsonian Institu.
ton, Civil Service Commissioners, Inter
state Commerce Commissioners, assist
ant secretaries and the chief officers of
the various departments, and the faculty
of the Columbian Institute for the Deaf
and Dumb,


| The next section of callers was headed
by a few survivors of the war of '46,
closely followed by large representa-
ton of Grand Army men and smaller
body of gray-haired, venerable looking
men, known as the oldest inhabitants of
the District of Columbia. The reception
of the public generally, was the next in
order, and the gates to the grounds,
which had been closed up to this time
except to the privileged few, were thrown
open and the crowd thronged rapidly
into the mansion.


The reception lasted until 2 O'Clock,
and it is estimated that during that time
the President shook hands with nearly
5000 persons. When it was over the
President invited the ladies who assisted
him, and number of others, to join him
in luncheon. which had been prepared
expressly tor them, in the hall. way up
stairs.


Mrs. Harrison's absence was due to
the recent death of her sister, and it was
at her request that her daughter, Mrs.
Mckee, assumed the responsibility of
hostess on this occasion. Mrs. Blaine
was unable to assist by reason of the
recent death of her sister. Mrs. Proctor
is in bad health and was also unable to
be present. Following are the names of
the


LADIES WHO RECEIVED:


Mrs. Logan, Mrs. Hale, Mrs. G mman,
Mrs. Mcmillan, Mrs. Hiscock, Mrs.
Plat. Mrs. Pugh, Mrs. Quay, Mrs. Cock.
rell, Mrs. Reed, Mrs. Carlisle, Mrs. Bur.
rows, Mrs. Springer, Mrs. Lodge, Mrs.
Butterworth, the Misses Blaine and

Schulze is president. and the Central Street

franchise over a portion OF South Sixth
street. Last Monday morning 300 men

struction pushed. The same activity was
displayed yesterday.

been temporarily enjoined until the merits

hearing to show cause will come before the

When people read the paragraphs in the
funny papers about the buttons and the
punched and the counterfeit coins which are
dropped in the contribution boxes, they usually
give the man who wrote the article credit for
drawing largely upon his imagination. The
fact of the matter is however that the truth
is funnier than all the humorous mems fictions.
The treasurers of nearly every church in the
city send regularly to the United States sub.
treasury lot of.punched coins, on which they
realize not much more than half their face
value. The counterfeit coins are usually de-
stroyed.


The treasurer of one of the best known Cath
Ollie churches in the city showed the writer a
collection Of punched coins the other DAY the
face value OF which amounted to about SlO
and all OF which were put into the contribution
boxes In one month. A queer-looking collec-
ton it was, too. There were coins represent
ing nearly every civilized nation in the world.
Among the collection were German pfennings
English sixpences, shillings and half-crown
pieces and sixpence struck in honor of Queen
Victoria in the year of her Jubilee: Canadian
pieces, French fifty Genuine pieces of the time
when Napoleon ruled that country and pieces
OF the same denomination struck since the
country became a republic; Mexican coins,
pieces from Venezuela and coins from numer-
Gus other countries


The largest piece was a United States half
dollar; there were several of these. There were
a number of quarters, dimes, half dimes, FIVE
cent and three-cent silver and nickel pieces
and copper one-cent pieces, ali mutilated,
either by having a hole punched In them or q
piece cut out of the edge. Each hole was care
fully plugged with lead SO that the sharp-eyed
collector would not observe that the piece was
mutilated unless he inspected it closely. There
were more dimes than pieces Of all the other
denominations put together.


No doubt many of these pieces have an in
teresting history, for the reason that many of
them contain monographs, and during the time
that bangle bracelets were the rage they IN
doubleday adorned some fair wrist Some of
them were undoubtedly tokens of love, and
how they found their way into the contribu-
ton box will probably remain a mystery. Per-
haps some Of them were spent in dire necessity
and finally reached the contribution box after
passing through several hands. Maybe some
of them were spent for caramels by a proud
beauty to show her disdain for her former
admirer. Possibly some Of them were lost

The strike of the police in the Bow street
station. London took place at IL o'clock last
night, being preceded by riotous proceedings
in the streets, and as a result the people of
London are panic stricken. Merchants and
the bank men barricaded their property and
awaited the morning with great anxiety.
Tho trouble began yesterday morning, and the
disaffection, instead of being suppressed or
allayed, spread everywhere through the force
The vicinity Of the Bow street police court
presented remarkable scene. Thousands of
the criminal classes helped to swell the excited
crowd. The spectators seemed to sympathize
with the police mutineers. The thoroughfare
was completely biockaded, and at 3 o'clock
affairs became so threatening that squadron
of Life Guards were hastily summoned and
arrived on a trot, and simultaneously the
mounted police dashed upon the scene and
charged the crowd. There was a stampede in
every direction. Hundreds of people were
Guards followed the police, dashing right and
left into the surging throng. At IL o'clock the
mob still kept up the rioting and pelted their
pursuers with stones, bottles and bags of -four
kissing and hooting the superior police officers


No men had as yet gone out, but 1t was not
long after IL o'clock before the initiative was
taken and the great strike inaueurated The
force of Z division went into the station at the
usual time, but refused to parade for duty
Assistant Commissioner Howard and Col
MOused were in charge and vainly tried to in
duce the men to alter their determination,
which they absolutely refused to do. The
superior officers then tried to exert their au-
thority, but without avail and disturbance
ensued. Meanwhile the reserves were being
quietly sent out of the station in squads of five
or six. They took their places at different
points in the street. Men were drafted from
other stations for a similar purpose. While
the mob was waiting for the reserves to march
out the streets were quietly Differed


The disorder. however, increased instead of
diminished. bag Of flour and dried fruit
we're hurled ut the police on duty. Commits
sioner Howard was mobbed near the station,
the policemen assisting in the outrage. and it
was with great difficulty that he forced his way
into the station. In the wild disorder outside
men were trampled upon in large numbers.
Every moment the crowd grew larger more
dense and more turbulent. Cheers were
mingled with Kisses. Some jeered the police
and others Missed the officials of the home Sec
rotary. The mob sang the 'Marseillaise,"
Rule Britannia" and other popular songs


ROYALTY IN THE MOB.


Opposite the Bow street station is the Co
vent Garden Theater, where the performance
of an opera was spoiled by the hubbub in the
street The audience withdrew and viewed the
rioters from the balcony. When the mounted
police arrived the good humor of the crowd
quickly turned to bitter opposition. The re-
suit was soon apparent. The mounted men
formed at the top of the street and charged
the mob. desperate struggle followed; men
attempted to drag officers from their horses
The policemen struck their assailants with
their fists and sticks The crowd was broken
by the repeated charges, but reformed as soon
as the mounted officers passed. This was re-
peated for two hours Finally the squadron of
Life Guards arrived Immediately d rumor
spread that the Princess of Wales was in the
theater and had asked for a cavalry escort The
people cheered. Then upon hearing q report
that the squad was bro ught to clear the streets
the mob yelled, hooted, Kissed and cursed
The prince and princess finally left the theater;
the former was cheered and the escort hooted.


The greatest difficulty experienced in
driving the people away from the theater until
forced to quit by the cavalry. Scores of thieves
were ut work IN the crowds, and many rob-
berries were reported. One of the objects of
the mob was to imprison the foot police in the
Bow street barracks The younger men in
sympathy with the strikers and mixed with the
crowd, urging 1t Oh.


At midnight the thoroughfares we're blocked,
ana two-thirds OF the police force were not on
duty: and the old hands were weak in assisting
to preserve order The mounted police acted
with great brutality, many people being in
Jured and several were reported killed. The
mob, angered beyond endurance became revo-
Iutlonary, and groans were uttered for the queen.
AeahhhBs "SIc tcTu Ou TOu SHOPS ana lalQ In
the street to obstruct. and, if possible upset
the cavalry. The policemen cried anarchy"
and shouted like madmen. More Life Guards
came to the rescue, but heavy rain storm
that had just set in. did what the police and
cavalry failed to do-dispersed the mob. At 1
am. Bow street became auieter. The striking
postmen passed through the crowd and were
loudly cheered. Several hundred postmen
went ont last night and the rest will strike in
the morning. The strikers held a meeting,
which was noisy one, and in which the out
break was loudly cheered.


With the policemen and postmen on strike
and signs of mutiny among the soldiers the
situation is not pleasant one, and uneasiness
is felt everywhere.


The men, it is said, propose to follow the
course pursued by the dock strikers When
three-quarters of the night force have arrived
the men will form three deep and await the
appearance of the men inside the station
houses. When the latter come out they will
be called upon to join the movement. This
process it is expected will induce all who may
be doubtful to cast their fortunes with the
strikers. and the night men will then await the
arrival of the morning reliefs and endeavor to
persuade them also to join the strikers ranks
Afterward all the various contingents will
hold a mass meeting in Bond street.

LOUISVILLE, KY, March 3O.--A Dixon

passed through Webster county Thurs
day evening. The tornado proper lastet

The property loss will amount to 5000,

tered all over the country. A large

the earth, and buildings of every descrip-
tion demolished and scattered for miles

from the place where the havoc was
wrought. Only meagre account of the
casualties has yet been gathered, as the
physicians have not yet returned from
the desolated districts Some people who
have come here for surgical aid, give
terrible reports of the destruction,
and say seventeen deaths are reported

GRANADA, Nicaragua, Sept. 2l.-
Twelve thousand people, terror-stricken
by earthquake shocks and the continued
rumbling Of the ancient volcano OF Nom
bacho, have fled from this city since
Sunday. Internal sounds resembling
distant thunder were heard. Almost
Immediately the earth heaved violently
and has continued to vibrate at brief in
tervals ever since, shattering nearly every
house in a city of $4,000 souls. Nom
bacho has been considered extinct for CEN
turies, no eruptions having taken place
since the discovery of the country. There
is now daily dread lest the long closed
crater should open and bury the town
in lava and ashes. A heavy shock came
Monday morning that caused immense
damage, cracking walls in all parts of
the city. 1t was felt at towns sixty and
seventy miles distant. Other shocks
equally heavy followed, though no dam
age has been done outside the city, where
there is hardly house that does not
threaten to fall. Avid panic has seized
the residents. Everyone is making des-
perate efforts to leave the city. The
government is running trains for that
purpose.

Strife.


LAMAR, Col, Sept. 25.-Word is
received of serious county-seat strife
between the towns of Boston and Spring
field in Baca county. Springfield
secured the seat at the election held last
fall. The only available building in the
county for court house, was hotel
building in Boston. A few weeks ago
this was sold at sheriff's sale, and
bought by Springfield parties. Satur-
day night a party left Spring
field for Boston to move the building to
the former town, and use it as court
house, thus preventing the county-seat
issue from being raised this fall. The
building was moved about five miles
toward Springfield, which is about
twenty-five miles from Boston, when
the people of the latter place discovered
the trick and Immediately organized.
All the available horses and rifles
were brought into requisition and
pursuit made. Upon overtaking
the party, battle began, which
ended in the Springfield party being
driven from the building, which was
then burned by the Bostonians. Great
excitement prevailed, but owing to the
isolation of the towns, news is hard to
obtain. Several parties arrived here
from Springfield last night and departed
hurriedly after buying all the cartridges
they could find in town. There is re-
port that several parties were seriously
wounded and two killed during the
fight, but no news was authentic.

SAN QUENTIN PRISON, July 6.-When
Captain Slipping of the first night-watch
reached his bedroom last night he heard
gr0ans issuing from the room underneath,
occupied by Guard john M. Massey. He
quickly dressed. broke into the room and

Coroner from San Rafael took his body.

guard at the Carson Penitentiary, and has
had the position of guard here for five
years. He was native of Alabama, and
was 81 years of age.

vessel was running at a reduced speed

yards. The engines were reversed

vessel, so that the berg was struck at
slant. The iron plates grated alongside

the sails touched the water. There was

from high bunk and slightly injured.

very long. After the collision the Hiber-

veloped in thick fog. During this time

chief witness against him and the latter
swore vengeance. Mock was seen in this
city this morning. but has not yet been ar
rested. During the excitement last night

reached his feet ten seconds had passed

PORT TOWNSEND. July 29.-Dominico
Cecilia, alias Joe Smith, Who murdered
John Diletis, fruit merchant, was
lodged in jail this morning.


Chief of Police Delany and Sheriff
Jones arrested the murderer under ex-
citing circumstances. The officers had
had information for the last two weeks

A Lively Fusilade In Chesapeake Bay.


An Annapolis special gives the following de-
tails of the exciting encounter on the Chesa-
peake bay between the police sloop Daisy
Archer, Mate Phipps commanding, and the
oyster-dredging schooner Virginia F. Lawson,
Capt John Lutts, which was briefly mentioned
in Saturdays STAR. The schooners crew were
detected at work with their dredge on forbid
den grounds, between Hockett's and Tolley's
Point. The Daisy bore down upon her, Mate
Phipps meanwhile preparing for battle The
crew were armed with repeating rifles and lib
orally supplied with small arms When the
schoOners captain was able to make out the cut
OF the Daisy he weighed anchor with all haste
and was soon under way. The Daisy. however,
Is the smartest sailer in the state police navy
and soon gained upon the Virginia. An easterly
gale was blowing and the chase was exciting,
When within gunshot Commander Phipps sent
heavy shot whistling through the rigging of
the dredger. The only answer was regular
broadslde Of musketry from the oysterman.
The sails OF the police sloop were clipped by
the balls and the crew lay low as the shots
came thick and fast from the Lawson. Com
mander Phipps soon had his small battery in
good order and the rattle OF the guns reused
the naval academy and caused considerable ex-
element along shore. After a chase of several
miles the dredger hove to and stood the fight
fer some time, but finally was compelled to
surrender or be riddled with the shot from
the police boat, whose store of ammunition
was the more plentiful. Commander Phipps
towed his prize into Annapolis and Justice
Gassaway fined Capt Lutts $50 and costs and
released him on bail for court

on the eve Of being closed. On Thursday
dispatches were received here from Sydney
stating that unless the United States con-
tributed toward the mail subsidy the Sydney
Government would withdraw the mail
service.


Robert ]. Creighton, agent of the New
Zealand Government, confirms these dis
patches and states that he has had official
advices by cable of the same purport. Last
year Australia was in favor of close and di-
rect intercourse with the United States.
The Chambers of Commerce of Sydney and
Melbourne passed strong resolutions favor
ing that end and recommending a contnu-
ance Of the mail service via San Francisco,
on the condition, however, that the United
States should contribute equally with them
toward the cost of the service.


Recent events and these dispatches
would indicate that the Sydney Govern
ment had concluded that this Government
was Indifferent to Australian trade. This
trade amounted last year to nearly $780,
100000 for total population of 1900, O0C
people.

The steamer Rhynland, which sailed from
Antwerp January and arrived at New York
yesterday, experienced some of the toughest
weather ever known on the Atlantic While in
the English channel she encountered strong
gales from the west, with heavy seas, but in
the Atlantic the gale became a perfect hurri-
cane, with mountainous seas which swept ever
her decks. The Rhynland withstood these gales
easily until January r. when one of the most
terrific storms ever experienced came on. The
sea was terrible, and mountainous waves swept
over the decks with such fury that six of the
life boats on the upper deck were stove. At
about the same time terrific wave boarded
the ship astern, crushing in the turtle back over
the steering machinery and rendering all steer
ing impossible.


Then it was that the steamer was saved from
almost inevitable wreck through the heroic ex.
ertlons OF Capt. Weyer and his efficient officers,
Tor the sailors, fearing to expose themselves.
where the huge seas were continually sweeping
over the decks, were only encouraged by the
noble example of their captain and his officers,
who went Immediately, at the risk of their lives,
to the scene of the disaster. The damage was
temporarily repaired, SO as to render steering
possible. The weather continued stormy up TO
January II, when it abated, and the wind blow
ing from INV. the steamer was enabled to
put on all sail and hopes of reaching New York
In few days were entertained but the next day
dispelled these illusions, for a gale even more
terrific than the former one came on, lasting
to the following morning.


At this time it was found that the coal was
running short, so the ship was headed for Hal
flax. where she arrived at about noon on the
10th. She proceeded again, and during the re-
malnder of the voyage had heavy westerly gales
and high southerly sea with frequent snow
squalls and intensely cold weather.

The long-looked-for rain came down last
night in copious streams, after a whole
days gloomy forebodng. Shortly after
nightfall big drops began to fall slowly and
the gusts of wind carried slight mist,
which grew denser until about 9:30 o'clock,
when the rain first fell Before two hours
had passed, the city was treated to char
acteristic San Francisco winter storm, and
all night long water was precipitated from
the clouds necessarily and plcntifully.


Suddenly umbrellas appeared on all sides.
1t seemed that everybody had umbrellas or
that these very useful companions on the
right occasions are not noticed nor seen in
dry weather. And the streets changed
crowded, while the sidewalks were almost
deserted, only comparatively few pedes-
TRANS remaining to brave the storm. A
remarkable result of the rain was also OBJ
served in the strange freaks played by cleo
trio lights all over the city. The mean
descent lamps fiickered ftfully. and the
greater number refused to glow at all.


The arc lights also flickered, but in long
drawn efforts, often becoming dark for
minute or two, then shining again. or some
times failing to give out more light. At the
corner of Pine and Kearny streets, wire
that touched the woodwork and awning
lost its covering with the sudden change
from dry weather, and emitted a light that
Illuminated the vicinity and ignited the
building. In several places similar occur
rences were noted.


In its impetuosty, the wind raised and
moaned In the chimneys and through WIN
dows. The storm had all the appearance of
having come to remain for the season.

ard street October 25, 1888, had been

Savage. Savage knocked Mcdonald

head heavily on the sidewalk McDon-

sat him on the doorway of the Cali
fornia Athletic Club, where he was
found dead next morning. Clark says a
person presumed to be his wife) who
was in the saloon at the time told him
the facts above related. The police are
looking for Savage.

dense fog. The steamer was making, ac-
cording to her master, not more than six
knots per hour, and, being in the way of

intervals. Captain Dittman says he listened
for the Point Robinson fos-horn, but not
hearing it for twenty minutes had calculated

aground. An effort to back her off proved
futile and nothing remained to be dons but
to pump out her water ballast and await the
rising tide. AT tluod-lide, about 10 o'clock,

Ell PAso Tex, July 3.-Joseph D.
Brown, an expert telegrapher and railroad
clerk, was wantonly murdered in the Gem
saloon yesterday morning by William G.
Colwell, engineer at the steam pumping
station. The latter had been out drinking
and gambling all night, and about o'clock
in the morning left the Gem in an irritable
mood, having met with losses at the faro
table. The man he killed was standing
outside the door and jeeringly asked Col
well how much he lost, to which he replied
it was none Of his business. After more
words Colwell whipped out his pistol and
fired twice. The man ran into the saloon
and Colwell pursued him inside and found
him lying on his face and hands on the
floor. Walking deliberately up to the pros
trate man Colwell placed QUE foot between
his legs, and bending forward fired two
more bullets into his back. They entered
his heart and killed him instantly.

plete mass of ruins. The firemen scarcely

ASTORIA, IL. July 5.--The coast-steamer
Eleanora, while bound eastward through
He'll Gate this evening collided with the
Walter Sands, one of two barges lashed
together, upon which were between 800
and 1000 men, women and children, in
tow of the tugboat Idlewild 1t is almost
miracle that a terrible disaster and
great loss of life did not follow. For
tunately, however, no one was killed,
though several were injured. Eight OF
those whose injuries are most serious
were taken to the hospital.


Captain Connerton, OF the barge
Walter Sands, says that while passing
through He'll Gale, the Eleanora was
seen steaming to the east. The tug sig
nailed her by whistling twice to keep to
the port side, and the steamer appar-
emily obeyed she signal until about op-
posite the barges. Her bow then sud
denly turned, and in moment crashed
against the side of the barge amidships,
almost throwing the latter on its beam
ends, though it was lashed to the other
barge. In second the rear half OF the
guard rail and the bulwarks of the up
per deck were cut clean away. Along
the rail or bench sets running around
the upper deck, were seated many men,
women and children, upon whom the
broken supports and splinters of the
timbers fell. About twenty persons in
all were injured by these flying
pieces. Had the steamer struck the
barge more squarely there is no telling
what the result would have been. At
the time of the collision the larger por-
ton OF the excursionists were dancing,
and the moment the crash was heard a
scene OF most intense excitement began.
Men ran hither and thither searching
for their wives, children and sweet
hearts, and shouting for life preservers,
while the women screamed and tainted,
and children joined in with chorus OF
cries. The officers of the barge soon
succeeded, however, in restoring order.

The funeral train reached Ridge avenue
Philadelphia, at pm. Thousands of citizens
and various organizations were there waiting.
First came one hundred members of George G.
Meade Post, in blue fatigue suits and caps car
rying their flags and marshaled by Comrade G.
Harry DAVIS. The Samuel J. Randall Associa-
ton numbered two hundred men, under the
guidance of George H. Hoffman. They wore
black suits and black silk hats, and at their
breasts were pinned black satin badge let
tered in gold with the inscription: Samuel J.
Randall Association" Select Councilman Peter
Monroe led one hundred and fifty members Of
the Continental Democratic Club wearing
black suits, silk hats and satin badges which
bore the name Of the organization. Fiftv
members of the Young Mems Democratic Bat
talon, commanded by Maj. NORMAN; the Mu-
nicipa1 Council Of the Irish National League,
with Vice President Hugh McCaffrey and Pat
rick Dunley at their head; the James Page Lib
rary Assoc ation. marshaled by Dennis Brad
ley, and the Jackson Democratic Club OF the
twentieth ward, led by James c. Galusha, were
the uniformed bodies that awaited the arrival
of the funeral train.


There was multitude around Ridpe-ayenue
station, the overhead bridge was crowded with
them and along the sloping banks on either
side OF the railroad track were gathered hun
dreds of people. In all this throng there was
not loud word spoken and the deep silence
was a more eloquent tribute of honor to the
dead than the ioudest words OF praise.


The committees of House and Senate. led by
Mr.. Carlisle, were first to alight. Then came
the honorary palbearers. When these had as
cended the steps the coffin containing the re-
mains OF the honored dead was tenderly lifted
from the funeral car and with an escort of six
stalwart reserve policemen under command of
Lieut.. Malin and the direction OF Undertaken
VIM. Brlnghurst, was carried to the hearse in
waiting. AS the casket was lifted from the
train Comrade Thos Thompson OF Meade Post
covered 1t with the American flag and reyer-
emily laid beautiful wreath of white
flowers at the head with the inscription, Our
Comrade," III blue immortelles in the center.
Then the family of the dead statesman followed
to their carriages and the long cortege took I'D
its way to Laurel Hill Cemetery. A great
square OF the cemetery was reserved for those
taking part In the services. and this was roped
off and protected by Gordon of 100 policemen.
commanded by Lieut.. Wolf and Sergeants
Richards. Norberry and Fulton. Outside the
square were gathered nearly ten thousand
people, who stood i'll silence during the brief
ceremonies. Rev. DIR. Chester, Mr.. Randalls
pastor, announced that any who 80 desired
might take last look at the remains before
the funeral services began and while the coffin
lid was reverentiaily held open many looked at
their friend with moistened eyes. just before
DIR. Chester began the reading of the simple
burial service OF the Presbyterian Church
VIM. McMullen, Randalfs tried and lifelong
friend, Postmaster General Wanamaker and
ex-Cong ressman Sowden moved "a few steps
nearer the coffin, and stood there until the
benediction had been pronounced. quar-
tette OF Meade Post. consisting of VIM. A. Bris-
coe, John Graeff, q. L. II. knorr and George
Ford, sang Remember thy Creator in the
days of thy youth" and Immediately follow
ing them DIR. Chester read the burial service


The quartet then sang Nearer, My God, to
Thee" and it was rendered with such deep
sentiment and feeling that silent tears found
their way unbidden to the eyes Of many in the
multitude and coursed down rugged cheeks
Rev. DIR. Henry c. McCOok, who had been spe-
cially requested by Mrs. Randall, delivered
the prayer over the body OF the dead states
man.


At the close OF the prayer Rev. /. Newton
Ritner. chaplain OF Post l, pronounced the ben
ediction and the great cortege and the throngs
of sympathetic people silently melted away
The family returned with the delegations to
Washington and the local organizations
marched down Ridge avenue.

WASHINGTON, June 1.-THE senate
committee on finance today considered
and amended the house silver bill. The
provision making the certificates issued
in payment of bullion legal tender for
public and private debts, was struck out
leaving them receivable for customs,
taxes and public dues. The bullion re-
demption clause was struck out; also the
section providing for the free coinage OF
silver whenever the market price is one
dollar for 37114 grains of pure silver. The
act is made to take effect in thirty days
after its passage, and shall terminate at
the expiration of ten years therefrom.


This action of the committee was not
unanimous, but the minority will make
no report, reserving the right to offer
amendments on the floor of the senate.
The striking out Of the bullion redemp-
ton clause was practically unanimous.

GUTHRIE (Oklahoma), Oct 2.-To-day was
one of tremendous excitement in the Terri
torial Legislature. The bill for the per-
manent location OF the CAPITAL at Okl ahoma
City passed the House yesterday. Before
action was taken in the upper House to-day,
however, motion in the lower House for
reconsideration was adopted. Friends of
Speaker Daniels had induced him to sign
the bill and Representative Perry was
hurrying over to the upper House with it.
When the enemies of the measure discovered
this the Legislature was turned into howl
ing mob. Perry was pursued. When over
taken in the street some one yelled, Hang
him." and the proposition was nearly carried
into effect. The unfortunate legislator con-
vinced the mob, however, that he had
handed the bill to Representative Nesbit
and that gentleman made wild break down
the street with the mob in full pursuit. Nes-
bit managed to distance them for four
blocks when his strength gave out and he
surrendered. The bill was taken back to
the House and the Speaker in the presence
of the Governor and ether witnesses erased
his signature saying lie signed the measure
under Misrepresentation. The United States
Marshal and Captain Havenaugh, command
ing the United States forces, calmed the eX-
cited crowd, which was still demanding the
punishment of Perry and NeSbit.

SALMON CANNING.


George 7. Meyers has forty men actively
at work getting ready for the canning sea-
son.


The salmon season is near at hand.
These fish. making their way toward the
small streams, are getting to be plentiful
and fishermen have begun to get out their
nets to supply the canneries. The salmon
are caught for the canneries mostly with
seins and drag nets; but parties for an &C.
casional catch use gill nets and trolling
hooks. The salmon begin running Sep
TENDER of each year. and continue
through October and November, during
which period the fish find their way into
the different arms of the Sound
and the streams which flow into it.
The "Jack" salmon appear first. They are
caught as early as July 80, and are of an
inferior variety. The "Tyee' and silver
salmon follow four weeks after. The
former are the largest of the salmon tribe,
~-H~ I~.k t. III
yer salmon are the most choice, and are
usually the ones used for canning. They
are more gamey, smaller and fatter than
the Jack" salmon, averaging about eight
pounds They come in larger schools, and
hence larger hauls are made OF them with
nets. The silver salmon season lasts
about six weeks. The Jack" tribe go up
the streams after the first fall rains, while
the silver varieties wait until the streams
are swollen quite high. They form i'll
large schools at the mouths of the rivers,
and there they are principally caught.


Another variety, commonly known as the
dog" salmon. follow later. Their proper
name is calico salmon, the former name
having been given them by the fishermen
because these fish often bite the nets when
ensnared in them. They seem bound to
get a mouthfui. They are not of
very good favor but are often
smoked and canned and sold
cheap. The female are the best, as the
male fish are not of good favor. The fish
of this type weigh generally about eight
pounds, and in their season are extremely
abundant. They ascend smaller streams
than any other salmon. The three types
given above are the only salmon that have
large fall runs on the Sound.


The very late class is the winter salmon
or "steel heads" They are found in small
schools and are of good size.

The tactics OF the Dahoman army are to
surprise the enemy, attack him in mass early
In the morning and surround him if possible.
This was the scheme at about 4:30 O'Clock on
the morning Of March 4, when the enemy in
compact masses, emerged on the dead run
from the palm groves and hurled themselves
upon the French works. The Amazons formed
the left flank of the assaulting column, and
they poured with almost resistless impetus
across the level plain upon the little fort oc-
cuped by force under Lieut.. Comperat.
At a distance of 600 feet the musketry began
to hail shot among them. 1t thnned their
ranks, but did not stay their progress. Up to
the very wall they surged, bowling like de-
mons, showering their bullets as they ran and
began to scale the fertilization. Lieut.. Com
perat and one Of his white sergeants were
wounded at their first fire. At short range the
French troops bayOneted them and kept their
repeating rifles busy. Some Of the women who
reached the top OF the wall fell dead among
the troops.


Meanwhile a few volleys from the cannon
further south, together with a rafting fire Of
musketry, had scattered the swarms of warriors
in front OF the other Notifications and they
made for the woods.


1t seemed to tho troops that Lieut.. Com
perats force was being eaten up and reinforce
ments were hurried to him. The Amazons "a
them coming and turned and fed. They rallied
before they reached the timber and made an
other furious charge. but under a deadly fire
they wavered and fell back before they reached
the fort Then the troops poured over the
wall and pursued them into the timber. Dying
women caught some Of them by the legs and
tried to throw them down and stab them with
their swords. The bodies of nearly 200 women
were scattered over that little plain.

DUBUQUE, Iowa, June 12.-The death

probably without parallel. A year
and half ago the boy, then IA years of
age, fell from butchers wagon and
hurt his spine. About four months ago
paralysis set in, his stomach became
affected, and for ninety-six days,
ending at the time of his death,
not morsel of food passed
his lips. For while a glass
of wine was given each twenty-four
hours. His stomach soon refused even
this nourishment Then soda-water was
substituted, and for the last thirty days
only pure water was used to moisten his
lips. At the time of his death he
weighed but trife over fifty pounds.
His shrunken skin barely covered his
bones, and he presented terrible pic
ture of emaciation. Through all this
time young Sutton retained his con-
sciousness and recognized his friends
and relatives.

LEwEs Del.), Sept. 5.-The British steam
er Haygreen arrived at the Breakwater
this morning, having on board nine men,
the crew of the Swedish bark Anna Maria,
from Mobile, bound for Wolgast, Germany,
with a cargo of lumber. The bark was
struck by hurricane August 18th, when
about 200 miles north of Bermuda. She
was dismantled and completely disabled.
Her seams opened and she leaked badly.
The men were kept at work at the pumps
until they became completely exhausted.
They were entirely helpless and were res
cued with the greatest difficulty. Captain
Martins of the bark was dead, from the
effects of injuries received during the storm
and the subsequent exposure. The bark
had nine feet Of water in her hold.

WASHINGTON, April 1.-THE House
and Senate Republican caucus commit
tees are hopelessly apart on the silver
question. After the last Intellectual meet
ing of the joint subcommittee, the
House contingent reported that the full
committee failed to agree. Thereupon,
Walker, of Massachusetts, addressed the
committee, holding that conces-
sions to the extreme silver men

derstanding that something positive
be achieved but that as they failed to
reach an agreement the House commit
tee should have it's modified Window
bill reported by the coinage committee.

vailed--10 to 5. The next step will be
to report to the House Republican
caucus, probably about Monday night.

accept the House committees bill, and
that it will pass the House. Meanwhile
the. Senate will probably pass its bill
and the matter will be turned over to a
conference committee.

Johnston, the mind reader, performed

pearances disproves the theory that a
man possesses only five senses,

hands. He then requested the proprie-

Panfc-Stricken Pasnengers on Board the


steamer Tiburon.


There was much excitement among the
passengers on board the San francisco and
North Pacific Railroad Company's steamer
Tiburon yesterday afternoon, and it almost
amounted to panic.


Tie steamer left Tiburon at 4:10 o'clock
for this city. having about 800 passengers
on board. When she left Tiburon the regu-
lar through train from Ukiah had not yet
arrived nor the Veteran Firemen or Paint
ers and Decorators, who had been holding
picnics on the line of the road, or the boat
would have been crowded and serious
panic must have ensued.


The boat had left her slip about ten
minutes and was just off Bird Rock, when
a great crash was heard and the boats
Roadway was stopped. Instantly there was
the greatest excitement among the pas
sengers and rush was made for the life
belts which were slowed in racks all ready
for use in case of emergency. Many of the
lady passengers screamed in fright, not
knowing what had happened. and large
number, both male and female, adjusted
life-preServers around their bodies think
ing the boat was about to sink Collector
Kelly on the lower deck and porter Manuel
Enos on the saloon deck went around, calm
ing the passengers fears, telling them that
it was only a log that had got in the wheel
and that there was no Hanger.


When the crash occurred Captain Van
Pelt and Chief Officer Gus Dorges were 10
the pilot-house. The captain at once sig
nailed the engineer and asked what was the
matter. The reply was that there was
probably a log in the wheel. In few
minutes the engineer reported that the shaft
was broken just outside the bulkhead on
the port side. He told the captain that he
could 90 ahead slowly with one wheel, and
WAS told to do so. Captain Van Pelt after
giving the order descended to the saloon
deck and Gained the passengers, his
presence assisting materially in allaying
their fears With one wheel working the
Tiburon arrived on this side shortly after 8
O'Clock, being only about twenty minutes
late.


As soon as she arrived a telephone mes
sage was sent to the steamer James Nj.
D0nahue at Tiburon and Captain Hughes at
once strained over and took the;pasSengerS
who should have been carried on the IL
huron, and continued making trips during
the evening. On account of the accident
the Ukiah passengers were delayed about
an hour, while those who attended the
Painters and Decorators picnic did not
get back to the city until after ten o'clock.

Once again has Yale won. 1t was hard pull
at first but when Yale finally begaA pulling in
good shape the eight oars did the work and
carried off all the honors. 1t was great race,
and it was nip and tuck from the start, until

times in succession has Yale now defeated
Harvard and the score now stands with nine
victories in favor of the hardy Yale boys and
six to the credit OF old Harvard. The course
was a straight one from Gales Ferry to Win
throp Point, on the Thames at New London,
and Yale came in three and one-half lengths
ahead in q minutes and 20 seconds while Har-
ward followed, completing the four miles
eleven seconds later.


THOUSANDS OF SPECTATORS.


Never has the Thames river been in better
condition for racing during the whole season
than it was this evening, when great crowds
began to gather along the shore. Almost along
the entire course the banks were lined with
excited humanity and the water itself closely
resembled a checker board, SO thickly was it
crowded with craft of all kinds. All along the
course from start to finish were scattered scores
OF large sail and steam yachts. large excursion
steamers like the Rhode Island, City of Worces-
ter, Elm City and others, and countless small
yachts and open boats of every description





bank was the moving observation train of
thlrty-four cars at the navy yard opposite the
two-mile flag the large wharf and the man-of-
war fantic and the sioping banks at the finish
we're black with people.


ONE DESPERATE STRUGGLE.


There was just the suspicion Of a breeze and
the water rippled pleasantly when at $50 the
Yale students leisurely padded to the starting
point They had barely reached the line when
their formidable rivals pushed out Every
timing was done IN q business-lke way, and in
less than minute more the word had been
given and away went the light boats. Harvard
had the best of it at the start and by the first
few strokes led the Yale shell by full length
Harvard kept this lead to the quarter, where
Iaie's powerful and machine-like stroke
changed matters very decidedly. Yale's boat
began to move up, and by magnificent exhi-
bition of rowing the shells were again on even
terms, half a length before reaching the half
mile flag. Some idea OF this desperate struggle
may be had from the fact that the bow of
Iale's boat gained on Harvard at the rate Of
one man for each four strokes. This was kept
up until tales shell was half length in front


Yale held this advantage to the tbree-quarter,
where Harvard succeeded in reducing it to
one-quarter length. These positions were
maintained to the mile flag. Just after passing
the flag Harvard increased their stroke and
again pushed their shell up even with Yale
Here another splendid exhibition of rowing
was gwen by both crews. 1t was difficult to
tell which crew was ahead. so evenly we're they
matched, but as they passed the mile and half
point Harvard apparently had slight advan-
tage. Nearing the navy yard Yale struck q
strip OF smoother water under the lee and by
another squirt again took the lead. passing the
two-mile flag with lead of half a length.
Harvard tried hard to respond to Yale's squirt.
but its effect resulted in giving slight roll to
their boat, causing the cOxswain to swerve
tribe.


Harvard had evidently made their greatest
effort and. failing to hold their position, drop
ped gradually behind until the end of the third
mile Yale was one length ahead. Here both
crews we're pulling thirty six strokes and nothing
was gained or lost during the next half mile.
At three ana one-half miles Yale began to show

Unusually Late season for Forest Fires.


The dense smoke of the past four or five
DAYS has been unusual even for this sea-
son for forest fires. In the evenings it has
been 20 dense as to make the eyes and
throat smart. while the arc lights struggled
vainiy to pierce the cloud. The shores of
West Seattle have been scarcely visible for
week. and shipping has grouped about
the harbor sounding fog signals The
smoke Friday evening was denser than has
been experienced here for years.
The burnings are heavy on all sides of the
city. The forest fires began unusually late
this year. The heavy June rains and rank
verdure resulting from it, kept the fires
from spreading to any serious extent dur
ing July and the early part of August.
Summer tourists this year have therefore
had better opportunity OF seeing our
matchless mountain scenery unobscured by
smoke.


Major Pond has made three visits To
the sound. and each time the horizon has
been hidden in . dense cloud of smoke
from burning forests. Many other emin.
ent visitors have been disappointed in the
same way. The landscape is usually OBJ
scured by smoke from the middle of July
until the fall rains begin.


The delightful season in the East il
known as Indian summer. lasting two or
three weeks in September ana October
over which poets rave, is prolonged on the
Sound as many months.

The coast seamen are preparing for an
important event just now, namely, the
election of three delegates to the inter-
national convention of the seamen of the
world, which will be held in Glasgow
during the first week in October next.


This convention will comprise delegates
from Australia, Europe, the Atlantic and
Pacific coasts and the lake seamen. Five
nominees are now in the field, named at
last nights meeting, three of whom will be
chosen at the election which will take
place about the middle of August. The
nominees are: Andrew Furiseth, Frank
Warehouse, W. Macarthur, Edward
Crangle and John HAST.


The Banking Committee, composed of W.
A. Bushnell, Joseph Trewren, Edward
Andersen, Thomas Finnerty and George
HOen. was elected.


The Secretary read the resignation of the
unions agent Mt San Pedro, which was re-
ceived and ii. Jorgensen elected to succeed
him.


The meeting was also visited by Miss
Elsie Herman and Miss Katie Thurman,
delegates from the Girls Cooperative
Union, who asked the support and co-opera-
ton of the seamen. They were favorably
received and given every assurance of the
Seamen'S support.

dispatch sent from this city few days
ago to the effect that an irrigation dis
trict was being organized under the
Wright act, to include the water rights
and canal of the Gage canal system, is
without foundation. A press representa-
tive has investigated the matter
thoroughly, finding the district to be Or
ganized included in such lands as lie
above the Gage system which are entirely
separate and distinct from the aforesaid
property. All the leading landowners
under the Gage system have signed q
protest against such measure, and those
citizens interested in the lands above the
Gage canal have abandoned the scheme
as impractical.

KANSAS CRY, Nov. 25.-A special from
Arkansas City tells of excitement among
the Indians in Indian territory over the
Messiah craze. A delegation OF Poncas,
Otaes, Missouris and Iowas returned to
the reservation today from a pilgrimage
to the Cheyennes, where they learned
all the latest news of the Messiah. These
Indians dwell on adjoining reservations,
and will inaugurate ghost dance Fri
day.


LAWRENCE, Kan, Nov. 25.-Joe Alb
ner, Cheyenne Indian, from the Chey-
enne and Arapahoe reservation, Indian
territory, says the Messiah craze has
taken hold of the Indians there. They
are arming and becoming very restless.
A Sioux, acting as a missionary, came
from the north to teach the new religion
the southern tribe. He breaches to
them that anyone who does not believe
in the new religion will be destroyed,
and so works upon the imaginations OF
these people that they fall PROSTATE to
the ground, and while lying there the
missionary pretends to cast some spell
on them. When they arise they declare
that they have seen the new Christ, and
at once join in the ghost dance. The
new religion has also spread to the Kio-
wos, Comanches and Apaches.
