A remarkable surgical operation was per-
formed in the Mount Sinai Hospital in Lex
ington avenue, New York, recently. 1t is
thought 1t is the first of its kind ever per-
formed in this country. The operation was
the removal of the entire left arm, shoulder
blade and cOllar-bone, and the muscles at
tached thereto, OF man "a years old. Ac-
cording to the records such an operation has
been performed only thrice before. once in
France and twice in England. The patient
is Judah Halprin. native of Russia and
tailor by trade His malady was a maljg-
nant tumor, which affected the shoulder.


1t was necessary to prevent the possibility
of a cancerous growth to remove the shOul-
der blade and collar-bone The operating
room OF the hospital was crowded with mem
bers of the medical profession. The tables
were covered with bottles and basins filled
with weak and strong solutions of bichloride
of mercury, the antiseptic used. The surgi-
cal instruments were soaking in china basins
filed with 3 per cent carbolic solution.
The patient was borne into the room under
tie influence of ether. When placed OH the
operating table he was unconscious. but was
not fully under the influence of anesthesia,
for he feebly moved his hands toward his
head as if trying to remove the cone from
his face. Soon. however, the mechanical
movements ceased, and his heavy breathing
became easier. After the parts to be am
putated had been thoroughly cleansed by
soap and water and one-thOusandth BIZ
chloride solution a March bandage "a fiat
rubber band about three inches wide) was
wound around the left arm from the hand
to above the elbow. This was to drive the
blood from the veins and capillaries back
into the general circulation, and so reduce
the loss of blood in the anputation to mill
imum. A round rubber ligature was then
tied above the bandage to prevent the re-
turn of the blood, and the bandage was re-
moved. An assistant raised the arm and
held it in position. The surgeon took the
knife and with one long sweep made an in-
cision the entire length of the colar-bone
and down back over the shoulder-blade.
There was slight rush of blood, which was
quickly sponged away by the nurse. The
hone lay bare. A few small severed ar
teries were caught with forceps and tied
with ca gut lgalures. The cartilage joining
the collar bone to the breast-bone was next
cut and the clavicle was raised and re-
moved. The sub-clayian artery. the large
vessel which supplies the arm and shoulder
with blood, was then exposed. An aneur-
ism nerdle threaded with catgut was passed
beneath the artery. This needle was then
withdrawn. leaving the double catgut be-
hind. The artery was then tied. The skin
was dissected back over the shoulder, the
remaining small arteries which run to the
back of The shoulder-blade secured, and the
Shoulder-blade exposed. The muscles which
hold 1t to the back were severed. A circu-
lar incision wa, then made beneath the arm
and through the muscles of the breast. This
left the arm, to which the shoulder blade
was still attached, joined to the body by only
little tissue, the sub-clavan vein and ar
terry and the brachial nerves. This vein
was also tied, and the parts were then sew
cred, and then the arm and shoulder-blade
we're lifted from the body and laid on the
table. The entire left side was gone, and
yet The blood lost did not amount TO table
spoonful The ribs lay exposed.


At this stage the patient breathed easy
and seemed but little exhausted. Dozens of
bright artery fofceps still hung to the body


but they were removed after the small blood
vessels which they had held had been tied
with catgut ligature. Hot bichloride sponges
were stuffed into the opening, and the sides
of the wounded parts were pressed together.
After an instant the spoDges were removed
and all bleedibg had ceased. The inside
was thoroughly washed out with one-thou-
sandth solution of bichlorde of mercury.
The loose flaps of skin were brought to-
gelher and sewed with silk, anu several
small drainage tubes inserted to keep the
inside of the wound Clean. Iodoform dust
was sprinkled over all the seams, and thin
strips of rubber protection were laid above.
Next came iodoform gauZe. followed by car
boiZed gauze, and then the body was
swathed in cotton and bound by roll after
roll OF cheese-clOth bandages, the ends be-
ing fastened with safety-pns. The opera
tiOn occupied one hour and forty minutes.
The patient will be at home next week,
minus his left arm, shoulder-blade and
colar-bone.-St. Louis Post Dispatch.

MIssoULA (Mont.), Dec. 19.-The greatest
hanging which ever took place in the North
west occurred this morning, when La La
See, Pierre Paul, Antley and Pascale, four
Indian murderers, were hanged at the Court
house here All died game, Pierre Paul and
Antley smilngly bidding their friends good
by. Twenty minutes after the trap sprung
all were dead, their necks being broken,


The crimes for which the Indians were
hanged were mcst cowardly and brutal


Pascale killed prospector named j. NJ.
Dunn in the spring of 1889, near Damers-
Vile. Dunn traded horses with him, and
when he refused to trade back the Indian
shot him. taking the horse and what money
he had. Pascale hid the body in the brush,
where the bones were discovered months
later by another Indian. to whom Pascale
admitted the crime. The bones were identi-
fed by remnants of clothing, and Pascale
was arrested.


Antley's crime was participation in the
murder OF three white prospectors, McDon-
aid, Seeley and Thompson, in the fall of
1887 at Wolf Creek, near Tobacco Plains.
The prospectors were surprised at their
campfire by party of six Kootenai Indians
and murdered in cold blood. Two Of the
Indians were captured soon after and
lynched by the people of Damersvile. Ant
ley remained at large till last summer


La La See and Pierre Paul killed two
white men, names not known, in August,
1887, and threw the bodies into Jack River,
where they were found by half-breed
woman, who was cautioned by the murderers
to say nothing about the bodies She noti-
fed the author tiles and the murderers were
arrested last summer. The murders were
unprovokad.


The four prisoners were tried and con-
victed before Judge Marshal at Missoula last
fall


The four Indians protested their innocence
before dying Their bodies will be taken
to ST. Ignatius Mission for burial. Several
prominent chiefs were in attendance at the
execution, but there was no protesting demon
stratiOn on their part or from the members
OF the tribe as had been anticipated. About
one hundred persons were present

British steamer Claymore aud the British ship
Carioianus, before reported, occurred last
Monday 400 miles west Of Fastnet.
The weather was clear, but heavy
sea was running at the time Of the collision.
The Coriolanus was lacking and the Claymore
attempted to cross her bows but failed and the
Coriolanus struck her amidship, cutting into
her engine room. The ships bows were crushed
to the keel, and her bowsprit and foremost were
carried away. The crews of both vessels be-
came panic stricken and rushed for the boats
which were Immediately lowered. Many men,
bers of the crews left their vessels without their
boots or caps. A vessel, five miles distant,
saw the collision and fastened to the rescue.

sank. The report that the Ciriolanus also sank
a short time after the collision was erroneous
as she was seen by the White Star line steamer
Brittanic on Wednesday.

CHICAGO. April 1O.-Tidal waves on a
small scale have struck terror to the hearts
OF vessel-owners on Lake Michigan. The
first OF these unpleasant visitors rolled into
the harbor and up the river Tuesday after
noon, ana was followed by others at inter
walls Of fifteen or twenty minutes for six
hours. These waves were about five feet
high, and rolled in from the lake with
great rapidity, afterward recediug with the
same speed.


Vessels were lifted and carried up the
river aud then down again, and for while
grave fears of disastrous collisions were
prevalent The Morley, Moravia and Even
were carried across the river and dumped
into the mud. For time vessels were
knocked about like corks. The lake has
settled back into its old condition


Lieutenant Beall of the Signal Service,
speaking Of the strange occurrence, said it
was due TO remarkable changes in the at
mospheric pressure on the surface of the
lake, caused by severe thunderstorm.
Similar reports come from several points on
the west shore Of the lake, notably from
Racine, where the water receded from the
shore several feet.

the Bad Lands, and there await the
coming of the troops. Scouts say that
region is better adapted for Indian pur-

the commemoration of Ash Wednesday. In
the Roman Catholic, Protestant Episcopal and
Lutheran churches Ash Wednesday marks the

events during the holy season. In the Roman
Catholic churches this morning after mass the

CHICAGO, Sept. 21.-A terrible railroad
accident occurred in the southwestern
portion of the city shortly after dark
this evening. A G. B. & @. suburban
train dashed into an Illinois Central ex-
cursion train returning from outside the
city. The collision resulted in a fright
full tragedy. For time the confusion
was so great, that even an approximate
idea of the loss of life was impossible to
obtain. The first reports from the police
had it that forty had met their death,
while the railroad officials said only two
or three persons were certainly known
to have been killed. Within half an
hour, however, five mangled corpses
had been dragged out of the heap of
broken timbers and twisted iron that
marked the spot where the collision
had taken place. By this time it had
also been ascertained that at least three
people were seriously injured and six
others slightly.


The collision took place near Douglas
park, and the victims were sundry ex-
cursionists just reaching the city on
their way home from an outing


Cause of the Wreck.


The freight train crew when uues-
toned, asserted that they passed Miilafd
avenue under clear signal. Millard
avenue is only short distance from
where the smash-up occurred, and the
freight crew claim that when the crash
came, the red lights on the rear of the
Illinois Central train were burning with
extreme dimness. To this the fearful
result following was attributed without
hesitation.


Other people state that the Burling-
ton train was behind time and running at
a reckless rate, and that to this was due
the fact that the engineer could not stop
when he saw the Illinois Central lights
The latter train was "unblocked" and
waiting to be released when run into.


The Victims.


The dead are: Lille Diener, Martha
Diener, Otto Schloef, aged II, and two
men unknown.


The fatally injured are; Lena Refs
ing, Minnie Pilgrim and Eddie Torpe.


In addition to these dozen other peo-
pie were more or less seriously bruised
and some OF them had limbs fractured.
The conductor and engineer of the sub
urban train have been arrested.

NEVADA CITY. Aug. 2S.-Thomas Jones
and Charles Cleveland, freighters between
this city and North Bloomfield, had mirac-
ulous escape this morning from frightful
death. They were descending the northern
grade of the South Yuba River. Jones
drove six horses attached to two wagons
loaded with 5000 pounds of sacked barley.
Cleveland had six horses and one wagon
loaded with baled hay, driving 200 yards be-
hind Jones. A tree came thun dering down
toward the road from the mountain side
above, where a Chinaman had cut It,
Cleveland's horses SHE'D, and one front
wheel went off thegrade. Cleveland jumped
from the wagon, and the horses, spring
Ing suddenly forward, pulled the wheel
back on the road, and breaking into a run
soon collided with Jones' outfit. Jones,
the three wagons and eight of the horses
were precipitated over the bank and went
rolling down the steep declivity toward the
river 200 feet below. The wagons were
totally wrecked. Jones and the horses
rolled over and over to the river. Two OF
the horses were perhaps fatally hurt, the
others escaping uninjured. The man was
unscratched, except having one finger
mashed. Two years ago similar accident
from like cause occurred there to a ped
dler's wagon, S. M. Shurtiiff receiving in
juries that ultimately caused his death.

Capt Campbell set to work to help the Car

HUNTINGTON, West Virginia, August
24.-There was serious and bloody
riot at performance given by the
Sunny South Theatrical company at
Ceredo Friday night, the particulars of
which have just been received. One man
was shot and over dozen badly beaten,
while the floating theatre, in which the
riot occurred, was badly wrecked. The
trouble was inaugurated by number
of toughs who persisted in insulting the
people upon the stage. During the
second act three of the performers left
the stage with clubs and attacked
several of their tormentors, but were
overpowered and cruelty beaten.


The remainder of the company went
to their assistance, when some one turn
ed out the lights. Pandemonium
reigned, and every man began an
onslaught on his neighbor in the dark,
while the women screamed. The police
arrived, but they only made matters
worse, and revolver shots began to echo
around the hall. Finally the crowd
charged into the fleeing performers, who
were unceremoniously flung into the
river, where they were stoned in the
darkness. Every one of the police and
show people were badly wounded by
stones. and the condition of several is
serious.

snow, mud and summer heat, and she

SPOKANE FALLS, August IAN acci-
dent occurred today in which five men
were seriously, and one fatally injured.
The men were raising large girder to
the second floor. The great strain broke
the ropes, causing the derrick with the
heavy girder and several joists to crash
down through the joists of the second
floor. Foreman Bailey and two men
who were placing the girder fell with
the joists. There were nine men on the
second floor working at the hoisting ap-
paratus. all of whom were injured. They
are as follows: Foreman Bailey, hip and
ribs broken; James Kinney, injured in
chest and ribs broken; Ernest Leith,
head badly cut; F. E. Elgin, head badly
bruised and cut; James Maylan, both
legs broken and arm dislocated. Maylan
died at o'clock this evening.
